Gothic description as substance: three paragraphs describe the library and at the end nothing has been established except *this is dark academia*
Lecture scene as exposition: professor delivers intellectually-provocative-and-personally-relevant content; protagonist has insight
The forbidden-book scene gesturing toward content without specifying ("the pages described a ritual so dark...")
Overwrought literary allusion as dialogue: characters quote Keats, Nietzsche, Borges casually
First-person confessional register: present-tense narration of past events; "I did not know then what I was becoming"
Sensory obsession with the academic aesthetic (candlelight, leather, coffee going cold, cigarette smoke, wool coats) substituting for interiority
Run-on sentences mimicking anxious / overwrought thought as "intelligence" signal
Chapter epigraphs from canonical Western literature deployed as brand mark
Established dark-academia voice (Donna Tartt's *The Secret History*, M.L. Rio, Susanna Clarke, Lev Grossman's *The Magicians*, Brandy Colbert) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the secret society that is unremarkable, the gothic library that is just a library, the professor who is genuinely good)
Genre-conscious dark academia that *renders intellectual work* and *real class friction* rather than performing them

Gothic description must carry specific institutional history or character psychology. AI's library description is interchangeable across stories. If your library description could be moved to any other AI dark-academia story, cut it. Render *this specific* library's specific history - the donation that funded it, the murdered librarian whose ghost story is still told, the specific shelf that is locked and why.

No secret society as primary plot engine. AI's secret-society reveal is corpus-default. If a secret society exists, it must either be already known and unremarkable to students, or its secrecy must serve a *specific institutional* (not mystical) purpose - protecting endowment scandal, preserving a specific scholarly methodology, hiding the founder's racism, etc.

Professors require a position they have been wrong about for professional reasons. AI's enigmatic-professor has a "dark past" but is intellectually correct about everything. Real academics carry *published positions they have been arguing for decades* - sometimes correctly, sometimes wrongly. Render the specific position; render the specific way it has been challenged.

Intellectual discourse must be actual. AI's lecture-scenes name philosophers without engaging with their actual arguments. If your character mentions Kant, render the *specific Kantian position* and the *specific objection* against it. Name-dropping is corpus-default.

Class difference must be dramatized through specific objects, behaviors, institutional mechanisms. AI asserts class friction ("she was on scholarship") without rendering the specific texture - the wrong shoes for the dress code, the not-knowing-which-fork moment, the sense of being studied by peers, the casual access to resources the protagonist doesn't have. The texture is the genre.

The death-that-raises-stakes requires planted evidence. AI's mid-story death arrives without prior signals; the institution closes ranks and the conspiracy unfolds. Real institutional cover-ups have *prior visible patterns* that the protagonist can later read backward. Plant the evidence.

The forbidden-book gesture is corpus-default. "The pages described a ritual so dark..." substitutes mystery for content. Either render the actual content of the forbidden text (which requires you to imagine it specifically) or don't include the book.

Cut the chapter epigraphs. AI's epigraph-from-canonical-Western-literature is corpus-default brand-marking. If you use epigraphs, they must do specific thematic work - not signal *this is literary fiction.*

The intoxicating inner circle requires distinct voices. AI's three-to-five peers are interchangeable. Each one needs a specific voice - vocabulary, rhythm, characteristic concerns - that makes their dialogue identifiable without a tag.

The mentor's hidden darkness is corpus-default. AI now subverts the wise-mentor by making them secretly compromised - but the subversion is itself a trope at this point. Try: the mentor is straightforwardly good, and the institution's failure is structural rather than personalized.

The "Ivy League for Everyone" default. AI sets dark academia at elite institutions reflexively. Try: a small religious college, a state-school humanities department, a community college, a vocational program with a serious intellectual tradition. The aesthetic-saturation is partly a class-saturation.
genre/academia.replace: Generated dark academia is the gothic library described as the entire content. Marble, candlelight, leather-bound spines, the scent of old books - three paragraphs of aesthetic and nothing has been established except the genre. Strip the production-design layer. Render *what specifically* the protagonist is studying, *what specifically* the institution has been wrong about, *what specifically* the secret society is hiding and why hiding it costs the institution something material.
genre/academia.why: Dark academia is one of the most aesthetic-saturated AI genres because the look is so precisely defined and so over-represented in the corpus (Donna Tartt's *The Secret History*, M.L. Rio's *If We Were Villains*, *Dead Poets Society*, Hannah Mathewson's social media corpus). AI defaults to the *aesthetic substituting for the content* - the libraries are gorgeous, the students are luminous, but no actual intellectual work is rendered, no real institutional politics, no real class friction.

Punchy-fragment cadence applied uniformly. *He moved. Fast. Three seconds. That's all it took.* Every sentence the same length - tension performed, not built.
Em-dash machine-gunning during action: *He moved - fast - faster than he should - and the shot went wide.*
Ticking-clock rhythm without a specific clock. *He had seconds. Maybe less.* - no number, no consequence.
Sensation-naming as substitute for choreography. The prose tells the reader the character feels intense; it does not show what specifically the character is doing.
The post-violence quip as automatic tonal reset.
Acronym-and-jargon density (M4, mag check, six o'clock) deployed as atmosphere whether or not it does any work.
Established action voice (Lee Child, Brad Thor, Vince Flynn at moments) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the protagonist who is *bad* at violence; the gunfight that ends in three seconds because real gunfights do; the retirement that sticks)
Genre-conscious action that *plays with* the cliché set

Action is consequence sequencing. Not "he moved fast" - *what specifically he did, what it broke, what came next.* If the prose can be rewritten as a sentence list of feelings, it's slop. If it can be rewritten as a list of physical events with one causing the next, it's action.

Cut "adrenaline" / "training kicked in" / "muscle memory." These are the corpus's reach for competence. Render the *specific competence*: which hand drew the weapon, which foot pivoted, which obstacle was already accounted for.
Reload. Bleed. Run out of room. Bottomless-magazine prose announces the genre is fake. If the gun has six rounds, the prose tracks them.

Vary sentence length deliberately. Uniform short fragments are not tension - they are AI's idea of tension. Real action prose moves fast in some places and slow in others, and the contrast is what makes "fast" feel fast.
No quip after the kill. The instinct to release tension via one-liner is corpus-default. Let the violence land. The character can be wrecked, silent, shaking, sick - anything other than clever.

Refuse the villain monologue. A villain with the protagonist at their mercy who explains the plan is the prose flinching. Either the villain acts (and the protagonist escapes through specific competence) or the speech is short and plot-load-bearing.
The "world slowed down" beat is bullet-time interiority. It's a movie technique that does not transfer. Slow the *prose* by adding specific physical detail; do not announce that time has slowed.
Cut the cold-open set-piece if it is not load-bearing. Action prose that opens with a set-piece before any character is established is the writer trying to hook the reader instead of trusting them.
genre/action.replace: Generated action is the writer naming sensations the character should be having instead of putting the reader inside the body. Adrenaline surges, training kicks in, the world slows down - the prose announces intensity instead of producing it. Strip the announcement layer. Render specific physical events at specific tempos: which muscle, which weapon, which obstacle, which mistake. Action is *consequence sequencing*, not adjective-density.
genre/action.why: Action is the genre where AI most reliably substitutes the *register of intensity* for the *mechanics of intensity*. Punchy-fragment cadence, "his pulse hammered," "muscle memory took over" - these are the corpus's way of pretending the body is doing something while never naming what. The reader feels narrated *at* rather than carried.

genre/adventure.label: Adventure
genre/adventure.pattern: The VENTURE / MERIDIAN anchor: adventure is *consequence under unfamiliar conditions.* The protagonist's competence is tested by a world whose rules they don't yet know. Render the *learning curve*, not the spectacle. The mountain pass is dangerous because of *this specific feature* the protagonist hasn't accounted for.

Call to Adventure
Reluctant Hero
MacGuffin

The Chosen One
Dark and Troubled Past
Refusal of the Call
Elevated, slightly archaic register reaching for grandeur via syntax even in contemporary settings
Landscape-as-emotion. Dark skies before crisis, sun through clouds at restoration
Prophecy-as-dialogue: characters relay exposition in verse or riddle ("When the third star falls...")
Hero described through others' awe - supporting characters' reactions tell us the hero is exceptional before they act
"From the icy peaks of [X] to the sweltering depths of [Y]" - geographic enormity gestured at, never rendered
Wonder applied to every discovery on the same register - the third reveal feels identical to the first
Names as meaning. Places and characters with etymologically loaded names announcing their role.
Established adventure voice (Stevenson, Haggard at moments, Pratchett's Discworld adventures, Ursula K. Le Guin) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the chosen-one prophecy that turns out to be wrong, the ancient evil that's actually mundane, the quest that's not worth completing)
Genre-conscious adventure that *plays with* the hero's journey

Specificity over wonder. Not "treacherous terrain" - *which* rocks, *which* footing, *what* slips under boot, *what* breaks if you fall. Wonder is earned by what you specifically render, not by adjective deployment.
Cut "ancient" / "breathtaking" / "the air crackled." These are AI's reach for *evocative* without naming what's specifically there.
The mentor death is corpus-default. Try: the mentor lives, becomes inconvenient, has to be argued with. Try: the mentor was wrong about something load-bearing. Try: there is no mentor.
The MacGuffin needs function. "Ancient artifact of immense power" is genre-default placeholder. *What does it do.* If the answer is "save the world," the prose hasn't earned its plot.
Refuse the chosen-one prophecy. Specific to the protagonist, vague enough to survive - that's the corpus pattern. If your story needs a prophecy, make it specific enough to fail in interesting ways.

The dark night of the soul is overused. The hero quitting and being talked back in is the most-reached-for act-three pivot. Try a quieter low: the hero continues, but smaller - wins through reduced ambition rather than restored conviction.
Landscape-as-emotion is sentimental shortcut. The weather is not editorializing on the characters. Render the actual environmental conditions; let the reader judge their meaning.
Cut the wonder-register repetition. Sustained adventure prose deploys awe selectively. The first ruin gets the moment; subsequent ruins are practical (which corridor, which trap, which decay).
genre/adventure.replace: Generated adventure is travel-brochure prose with action stakes attached. Landscapes are "breathtaking," ruins are "ancient," terrain is "treacherous," air "crackles with" - every discovery gets the same wonder-register. Strip the tourism layer. Render *this specific* mountain pass with *this specific* failure point, *this specific* artifact whose function is named, *this specific* obstacle that costs the protagonist something.
genre/adventure.why: Adventure prose is among AI's most predictable defaults because the genre's beats (call to adventure, mentor lost, gather the party, dark night, return) are the most over-represented narrative architecture in the corpus. The vocabulary AI reaches for ("breathtaking," "ancient secrets," "must not fall into the wrong hands") is National Geographic crossed with action thriller - wonder performed at every discovery, never earned by any one of them.

Alternate History Nazi Victory - most overused POD
Axis Wins

Confederacy of Dunces - the Confederate-victory subgenre's overuse
The Axis-Won aesthetic substituting for systemic consequences
The single-event divergence point treated as a light switch
The Confederate Victory without slavery's structural consequences modeled
The underground resistance as default protagonist position
"It's just like today" thin allegorical gloss without political analysis
Architecture-porn of the Reich's planned capital as cover image
"Despite the challenges" dismissal: alternate problems named and immediately neutralized
"Hope endures" coda as ambiguous-uplift hedge

Established alternate-history voice (Philip K. Dick's *The Man in the High Castle*, Robert Harris's *Fatherland*, Kim Stanley Robinson's *The Years of Rice and Salt*, Ada Palmer's *Terra Ignota*, Ben H. Winters's *Underground Airlines*) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the alternate world that is *not worse than ours* in the expected ways, the resistance that is morally compromised, the protagonist who is genuinely complicit and stays so)
Genre-conscious alternate history that *interrogates* the divergence point's prior causes and downstream effects

The divergence must have prior causes. AI selects famous PODs (the assassination, the battle) and treats them as light switches. Real history doesn't switch - it pivots on prior conditions. If your POD is a single-event change, the prose must establish *what conditions made the change possible* before exploring its effects.

The alternate world must differ in non-obvious ways. Economy, science, culture, demographics. AI's alternate world differs only in flag and uniform. Render the specific economic restructuring (what industries collapsed, what new industries emerged), the specific scientific consequences (which fields were suppressed, which advanced), the specific demographic events (forced movements, eliminations, immigrations).

Refuse the Axis-Won default. It's the genre's most-saturated POD. If you're using it, the prose must do work the canon hasn't already done - render *which* aspects of Nazi rule actually scaled to global empire (most wouldn't have), what the Reich's *internal* contradictions look like at the millennium-of-stability mark, what specific compromises a fascist state has to make to govern.

The Confederate Victory POD requires slavery to be *structural,* not background. AI defaults to a Confederate America with slavery as set dressing. Slavery's persistence past 1865 reshapes everything - geopolitics, economy, immigration patterns, the arc of European industrialization, the texture of every white character's daily moral life. Render it.

The resistance as default protagonist position is corpus-default. Refuse it. The protagonist can be a *collaborator,* an *ordinary person,* a *true believer.* The discomfort of inhabiting a non-resisting POV is the genre's serious work. AI flinches from it.

The "humanizing gesture of doubt" by the True Believer is corpus-default. It's the prose flinching - making sure the reader can't be too uncomfortable. Try: the True Believer is *consistent.* The fascist regime contains people who genuinely think it is good and act accordingly. Render their interior without redeeming them.

The architecture-porn cover-image scene is corpus-default. AI loves describing Speer's Germania, the swastika-draped Capitol, the conquered-culture museum. Cut these establishing shots. The visible-fascism aesthetic is the form's most over-rendered surface.

"Hope endures" codas are corpus-default. AI's ambiguous-but-uplifting closing leaves the regime weakened-but-not-destroyed, hope-still-alive. Refuse the hedge. Either the regime falls (and the prose engages with what comes after - usually messy, often worse in unexpected ways) or it doesn't (and the prose engages with permanent occupation as the actual ending).

The "it resembles contemporary authoritarianism" subtext is corpus-default. AI uses alternate-history fascism as a thin allegorical cover for current-political-anxiety. Either commit to the actual political analysis or refuse the contemporary parallel - the lazy-allegory mode is the slop.

Convergence is corpus-default. AI's alternate history often reaches conclusions ("things end up roughly the same despite the divergence") that violate the genre's premise. If small changes don't produce different outcomes, you're not writing alternate history.
genre/alternate-history.replace: Generated alternate history is the Axis-Won aesthetic - swastikas on buildings, SS officers in the street, propaganda posters in shop windows - without the systemic consequences of the alternate. The economy is unchanged. The science is unchanged. Decolonization, demographic engineering, the geopolitics of the alternate world's other powers - all absent. Strip the production-design layer. Render *this specific* alternate world's specific economic logic, its specific scientific divergence, its specific cultural texture, and its specific second- and third-order effects.
genre/alternate-history.why: Alternate history is corpus-saturated through *The Man in the High Castle*, *Fatherland*, *Wolfenstein*, Confederate-victory novels, and a handful of canonical PODs. AI selects famous divergence points (the assassination, the battle that went otherwise) without tracing prior causes or downstream effects. The result: the visible Reich-or-Confederacy aesthetic with the mundane life around it identical to ours.

Curse of the Pharaoh

Epic-narrator voice: grandiose, declamatory, everything written for posterity

Hollywood-Colosseum-as-default Roman setting regardless of date

Established ancient-world voice (Mary Renault, Steven Saylor, Robert Graves, Margaret George at moments, Madeline Miller, Pat Barker's *The Silence of the Girls*) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the gladiator who isn't noble, the senator who is just a small-time politician, the oracle whose prophecy is mundane)
Genre-conscious ancient fiction that *commits* to specific date, specific place, specific cosmological frame

Date everything specifically. Rome 100 BC and Rome 200 AD are different worlds. Greece in 500 BC and Greece in 200 BC are different worlds. AI flattens them all into "ancient." Pin your work to a specific decade and check your details against it: which gods are central, which technology exists, which empire is rising or falling.

"By the gods" is a modern invention. Romans swore by Hercules ("hercle"), Castor ("ecastor" for women), Pollux. Greeks swore by Zeus, Hera, by named gods in context. Egyptians swore by named deities specific to their region and period. AI's universal "by the gods" erases the distinction. Render the specific oath; render *which* god the character would actually call on, given their region, profession, gender, and era.

The Colosseum is not the default Roman setting. Most Roman life was in *insulae* (apartment blocks), forums, baths, *tabernae* (taverns), and private homes. The Colosseum was completed in 80 AD; it shouldn't appear in a story set before then. And gladiatorial combat was rarely to the death - gladiators were expensive investments, and crowds often voted for *missio* (mercy).

Cleopatra was a Ptolemaic ruler who spoke nine languages. She was the first of her dynasty to bother learning Egyptian. She was not primarily a seductress; her relationships with Caesar and Antony were political strategy, not erotic decoration. AI's Cleopatra is corpus-default Liz-Taylor-1963. Render the specific political reality.

Ancient characters do not "process their trauma." They consult oracles, make offerings, interpret omens, act according to family / civic obligation, navigate shame and honor. The cognitive frame of ancient interiority is *foreign* to ours; AI's contemporary-protagonist-in-toga is the genre's most reliable tell.

The slave-revolt arc is corpus-saturated. Spartacus's revolt ended in mass crucifixion along the Appian Way - not liberation. If you write the revolt, render its actual historical arc: the violence the rebels committed, the terror the state responded with, the demonstration-effect. Or write a different story.

Refuse "Ancient Grome." Decide whether your story is Greek, Roman, or Egyptian (and which period of which) and commit. The pillared marble building is *not* universal - Greek temples, Roman basilicas, and Egyptian temples have specific differences in architecture, function, and ritual.
Cut the epic-narrator voice for non-epic moments. AI applies portentous voice uniformly. Most ancient life was domestic - render the domestic register too.

The decadent-emperor is corpus-default. Caligula and Nero are over-rendered. Try: the *competent* emperor (Augustus, Trajan, Hadrian). Try: the *boring* emperor. Try: a low-status protagonist who never sees the emperor at all.

The oracle's prophecy doesn't have to be in verse. AI defaults to riddling-couplet prophecy. Real Delphic prophecies were ambiguous in specific structural ways (the verb tense, the proper noun, the conditional clause); render the specific kind of ambiguity that fits your prophecy's actual function.
genre/ancient.replace: Generated ancient-world fiction is "Ancient Grome" - Rome, Greece, and Egypt blended into one undifferentiated antiquity, separated by centuries and thousands of miles in actual history but indistinguishable as aesthetic. Marble columns next to Roman amphitheaters next to Egyptian obelisks. "By the gods" deployed regardless of civilization. Strip the conflation. Render *which specific* civilization in *which specific* century, with *which specific* religious cosmology, *which specific* economic structure, *which specific* characters' specific positions within them.
genre/ancient.why: Ancient fiction is corpus-saturated through Hollywood sword-and-sandal films, Cleopatra screenplays, Spartacus / *Gladiator* / *300*, and Renaissance / Victorian classical-revival fiction. AI assembles a generic-antique register: oracular pronouncements, gladiatorial spectacle, decadent emperors, doomed Greek tragedies. Date and place are typically vague; cosmology is uniformly polytheistic-generic; character interiority is contemporary.

Genre-conscious antihero work that *grapples with* the moral cost rather than performing it

Cost requires consequence. "He had crossed lines he couldn't uncross" is performance. *Which* line, *which* person, *what specifically* is now broken in the world that he can't fix. If the cost is unspecified, there is no cost.
Cut the empty-apartment establishing scene. Itemized absence is corpus shorthand for *isolated by choice.* If the character is isolated, render *what they specifically miss* - not what's *missing.*
The cold-eyes description is AI giving up on interiority. Stop describing the face from outside. Either render the head from inside (and accept the moral discomfort) or stop pretending to.

The protect-the-vulnerable humanizing moment is corpus-default. It exists because AI was told antiheroes need humanity. The result is mechanical. Cut it. The character can be entirely cruel and still be the protagonist; the prose doesn't need to bail them out.
Refuse the rain-brood scene. Atmospheric weather as emotional proxy is the corpus-default filler. If the character is brooding, render *what they're specifically thinking about,* not the rain.
"He worked alone. It was safer that way." - banned. The lone-wolf justification is corpus-default. Either dramatize the isolation as costly (which complicates the cool-loner image) or skip it.

The "she made him feel things" romance arc is corpus-default. The romantic interest as healer-by-proximity is one of the genre's most-reached-for moves. Either give the romantic interest their own agenda (not related to fixing him) or omit them.
Cut the "I'm not a good man" self-description. Characters who announce their moral position to the reader are AI's flinch from rendering the position dramatically. Show the act; let the reader judge.

The brutal-but-honorable code is convenient. If the character has a code, the code must be *tested* and the test must hurt. The code that protects the audience from disliking the character is decoration.

The pseudo-redemption ending is corpus-default. "He wasn't sure what this made him. But he walked away." This is AI's hedge. Either commit to redemption (and pay its full cost) or commit to non-redemption (and pay *that* cost). The hedge is the slop.
genre/antihero.replace: Generated antihero is the empty apartment with the cold eyes and the lines-they-can't-uncross. The character is described as morally complex through assertion ("he wasn't a hero, he was the monster they deserved") instead of through actual moral complexity in their actions. Strip the noir-cosplay register. Render *which* specific bad thing they did, *what* it cost the specific person it cost, and *what* about them is now irreparable as a result.
genre/antihero.why: Antihero is corpus-saturated through Batman, the Punisher, '90s antihero comics, and the prestige-TV antihero canon (Walter White, Don Draper, Tony Soprano). AI defaults to the visual-aesthetic surface (empty room, cold eyes, brooding in rain) and the verbal-aesthetic surface ("the violence came too easily") without the *actual moral cost* that those surfaces are supposed to be signaling.

genre/apocalyptic.label: Apocalyptic
genre/apocalyptic.pattern: The LIMINAL anchor: post-apocalypse earns its weight by what's *small and survived* - the routine that didn't make sense before but does now, the relationship that endures because there's no alternative, the skill that became central by accident. Render the small. The big - the wasteland, the horde, the collapse - does its own work without help.

The immunity-reveal is the genre's most-reached-for plot mechanism. Refuse it. Or: establish it in chapter one (no twist) and make the protagonist's biology structurally irrelevant by midpoint. The immune-protagonist arrives because AI cannot generate stakes without chosen-one architecture; you can.

Every scavenged item must be named. Not "supplies." Not "three cans of beans." The brand name, the dent, the story of where it came from. Generic inventory is the corpus-default - render the specific object and its specific history.

Cut "before the world ended" and all variants. The before-times must be rendered through specific objects and people, not nostalgia-vocabulary. The italicized memory fragments are AI's flinch from specificity.

The campfire philosophy scene is corpus-default. Refuse it. Two survivors sit by a fire and one delivers the thesis statement is the genre's most over-determined beat. Either no fire scene or the fire scene refuses to philosophize.

The cult-leader reveal must be earned. "Something felt wrong" for three chapters then "the leader is actually evil" is AI executing a beat. The wrongness must be rendered specifically, and the reveal should reframe rather than simply confirm.
The hardened survivor needs one specific memory. Not "a yard, a voice." A specific yard. A specific person. A specific moment. Impressionistic loss is AI's substitute for grief.

The child-as-hope ending is corpus-default. If a child appears in the final chapter, they need to have been a present character with dialogue and consequence throughout. Otherwise it's a hope-symbol borrowed from McCarthy and Cuarón without the work that earned it there.

Apocalypse has economic structure. AI renders post-collapse economy as scavenging-and-barter without examining what specific commodities matter to whom and why. If the protagonist trades, render the actual trade - what they wanted, what they got, what the trading partner needed it for.
The horde is not an antagonist. Zombies / mutants / raiders as undifferentiated threat is the genre's default. They are weather. The actual antagonist is human and specific.
genre/apocalyptic.replace: Generated apocalyptic is wasteland-vocabulary on loop with no situated specificity. The prose names ruins, ash, the before-times, the horde - but no specific ruin, no specific person who was lost there, no specific structural change to civilization beyond aesthetic decay. Strip the wasteland atlas. Render *which* building, *whose* it was, *what* the protagonist is using it for now, and *what* about the new use makes the old use grieve in the gap.
genre/apocalyptic.why: Apocalyptic is the densest single-genre AI vocabulary cluster. AI defaults to a closed loop of ~30 wasteland terms in near-universal rotation, plus a handful of structural beats (the immune protagonist, the false utopia, the campfire philosophy, the child-as-hope) that reproduce across virtually every AI-generated apocalyptic story.

genre/comedy.label: Comedy
genre/comedy.pattern: The MOTLEY anchor: write toward *Arrested Development* (layered callbacks, every detail pays off later), *What We Do in the Shadows* (deadpan sincerity inside absurd premises), *Fleabag* (gut-punches hidden inside comedy).
examples: "couldn't help but laugh"
"she chuckled / he chuckled" (as default reaction)
"mischievous glint" / "wicked grin"
"wry smile" / "dry humor"
"with a smirk"
"deadpan" (as adjective applied to everyone)
"comedic timing" (named directly in narrator voice)
comic-relief character (who exists only to deliver jokes)
The misunderstanding that drags through the entire arc
Fish-out-of-water (the wrong protagonist in the wrong setting, all surface-level confusion)
The wedding / funeral / family dinner where everything goes wrong
The lie that snowballs (single lie cascades into elaborate cover-up)
The "competent person reduced to ridiculousness" episode
The romantic triangle with one obviously-correct partner
The comic-relief character (no other purpose)
The straight man / oblivious foil
The chaotic best friend who escalates everything
The eccentric relative
The boss who's an idiot
The ex who's still around for jokes
Performative humor - writer being funny *to* the reader through narrator voice
Winking at the audience - character knows they're in a comedy
Comic-relief character - character whose entire purpose is to be funny
Random quirk humor - "holds up spork" with no character basis
Breaking earned drama - interrupting an emotional moment for a joke (the prose flinching)
Narrator describing things humorously ("which was, of course, the worst possible time")
"Chuckled" / "chortled" / "smirked" deployed as default speech tags during attempted comedy
Punchlines clearly engineered (setup -> payoff visible to reader before it lands)
Comic-relief sidekick who comments on the action like a Greek chorus
Em-dash interruption-for-joke ("She walked into the bar - which was, against all odds, on fire - and ordered a drink.")
"Cool cool cool" / "yikes" / "mood" / Twitter-speak as default millennial-comedy register
Established comic voice (Pratchett, Adams, Wodehouse) where narrator wit is the deal
Genre-conscious comedy that's *playing with* sitcom conventions
Stand-up first-person where the narrator is *literally* a comic and performance is character-consistent
A specific subversion (the straight-man who turns out to be the funniest one; the comic-relief who's secretly the protagonist)

Nobody in the scene knows they're funny. The control freak isn't aware they're funny. The liar caught isn't performing for the reader. Comedy emerges from *circumstance* meeting *character*, not from characters cracking jokes.
Setup is invisible. If the reader sees the joke coming, the timing is wrong. The setup should look like normal scene content. The punchline reveals what the setup was actually doing.
Refuse the chuckle / smirk default. "She chuckled" / "he smirked with a wry smile" is corpus-default attempted-comedy. Cut the speech tag; render the specific physical thing.
Cut comic-relief characters. A character whose only purpose is to be funny is a tool, not a person. Real comedy emerges from characters who are also doing something else.
One specific detail per absurd situation. Not "the messy desk" - *what* is on the desk. The specific is what's funny.
Don't break earned drama for relief. When a serious scene lands, let it land. The joke that interrupts an emotional beat to lower stakes is the prose flinching from intensity.
Refuse meta-irony as register. "Cool cool cool not cool" / "this is fine" / quasi-tweet interior is corpus saturation. Render thinking that doesn't perform itself.

Character + circumstance. The funniest moment is when *who this specific person is* meets *exactly the wrong situation for them*. The control freak in chaos. The liar whose own lies trap them. The competence in the wrong domain.
genre/comedy.replace: Generated comedy is the writer being funny instead of the characters being funny. The narrator winks; the character delivers a punchline; the prose performs wit through framing rather than through character collision. Strip the performance. Comedy is character + circumstance - the control freak in chaos, the liar caught by their own lies. Nobody in the scene knows they're funny.
genre/comedy.why: Comedy is the easiest genre for AI to default to "the writer being clever." Stand-up rhythms, sitcom punchlines, narrator-asides are recognizable forms the corpus reproduces without the underlying *character* work that makes comedy land. The slop is performative; the fix is character-driven.

The oblivious or absent parent
The eccentric outsider (truth-teller)
The childhood friend left behind

The small town
The new city / college town (the "after")
Coming-of-Age Story
Loss of Innocence / Innocence Lost
First Love (formative, retrospectively measured against)

The Mentor (structural requirement)
Death as Catalyst
Puberty as Metaphor
Identity vs. Conformity
Retrospective wisdom-voice even in close-third present narration. The narrator carries adult understanding into adolescent moments.
"The summer that changed everything" framing - the most reliable single tell.
Discovery scenes contextualizing thematically before the shock lands. The protagonist's insight is too whole, too fast.
Mentor delivers thematic content as coherent monologue. Real adolescents receive wisdom in fragments they don't understand for years.
"Quiet" / "somehow" as magic adverbs. "She quietly understood." "He had somehow become."
Nostalgia-saturated lighting and weather as emotional cue.
Final-page declaration of changed-ness: "I would never be the same."
Established coming-of-age voice (Annie Proulx's *Heart Songs*, Toni Morrison's *Sula*, Jhumpa Lahiri's early stories, Alice Munro at moments) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the protagonist who doesn't change, the summer that doesn't matter, the mentor who is ordinary)
Genre-conscious coming-of-age that *refuses* the retrospective wisdom-voice and stays inside the protagonist's confusion

Cut the retrospective wisdom-voice. "I didn't know then..." is corpus-default framing. The narrator's adult understanding flattens the adolescent moment. Stay inside the protagonist's confusion. If the story needs the adult perspective, earn it with an explicit frame, not a tonal smuggle.

"The summer that changed everything" is a disqualifying phrase. All variants - the summer he turned sixteen, the summer she met X, the last summer before - are corpus-saturated to the point of self-parody. Set the story across a different temporal frame, or refuse the framing entirely.

The mentor cannot deliver the theme. AI's mentor monologue is too whole, too coherent. Real mentors deliver wisdom that is partial, contradictory, sometimes wrong. The protagonist should leave the conversation *more* confused, not less.

Cut mentor-death. The wise-elder-killed-to-graduate-the-protagonist is the genre's most-reached-for emotional escalation. The mentor can simply leave. The mentor can be wrong. The mentor can fail. The mentor can keep being a presence, inconvenient and ongoing.

Manic-pixie love interest must want something. AI's worldlier love interest exists to unlock the protagonist's growth. Refuse it. She / he must have an agenda independent of the protagonist - something they want, something they're afraid of, something they're moving toward that has nothing to do with the protagonist's transformation.

The party-gone-wrong is corpus-default. A bonfire, a dance, a festival ending in violation or revelation is the genre's most-reached-for inciting incident. Try: the small private moment that nobody else witnesses. Try: the gradual erosion that has no single event.

The discovery scene needs to leave the protagonist confused longer. AI immediately contextualizes the witnessed event. Real discovery - of an affair, a death, an adult complexity - produces *prolonged confusion,* not insight. The protagonist should sit with not-knowing-what-this-means for chapters.

First love is not the engine. AI defaults to first-love as primary identity-formation event. Try: the protagonist's identity forms around something other than romance - a vocation, a skill, a moral commitment, a friendship.
Loss of innocence is not beautiful. AI renders it as wistful threshold-crossing. Real loss is mostly ugly - grief, anger, embarrassment, withdrawal. Render the ugly.

The transformation must cost something specific. Not "innocence" - *which specific person* the protagonist can no longer talk to in the old way, *which specific habit* they lost, *which specific thing* they cannot unknow.

Refuse the "I would never be the same" closer. Final-page declarations of changed-ness are corpus-default. The story should end without the announcement; the reader should infer the change from the prose's altered texture, not from the protagonist's statement.
genre/coming-of-age.replace: Generated coming-of-age is the retrospective wisdom-voice flattening adolescent immediacy into adult thematic statement. "The summer that changed everything." "I didn't know it then, but..." "The world cracked open." Strip the framing-device. Render *this specific* adolescent's *specific* confusion in the moment, without the adult narrator's comforting distance. The transformation should not be visible to the protagonist as it happens; the prose should not be visible *as* transformation.
genre/coming-of-age.why: Coming-of-age is corpus-saturated through Salinger, Plath, Stephen King's *Stand By Me*, John Green's YA, *Lady Bird*, and a thousand quietly-literary debut novels. AI assembles the genre's voice as a composite of summer-and-light vocabulary, retrospective adult narration, and mentor-death plot mechanics. The result: a story that announces its own coming-of-age status from page one and resolves into thematic statement at the end.

genre/cosmic-horror.label: Cosmic horror
genre/cosmic-horror.pattern: See also `technique/ambient-detail-without-payoff` Flavor B (mood-paint via wildlife/weather, often weaponized in cosmic horror).

abyssal
primordial

Eldritch Abomination - TVTropes name for tentacled-incomprehensible type
The Cosmic Horror Reveal - moment scope of horror becomes apparent
The Innsmouth Pattern - town with secret, hybrid residents, sea as corruption source
The Dreamer Below - sleeping god that will wake
Forbidden Knowledge Ends You - learning IS the horror
"No human mind was meant to comprehend what he saw"
"The geometry was wrong - all wrong"
"It had been there before humanity, before time itself"
"Words fail to describe the abomination that lurked beyond"
Stacked negations to avoid description ("not a shape, not a sound, not a presence")
First-person narrator addressing reader about own fragmented state
Present-tense intrusions into past-tense to signal breakdown
Deliberate Lovecraft-mythos work where the vocabulary is the homage
Genre-piece operating in cosmic-horror conventions self-consciously
Setting where the eldritch entity is the literal worldbuilding (not metaphorical reach)

Earn the unnameable. If the prose says "indescribable," it's because the prose is refusing to describe. Render the *specific wrongness* - the temperature drop, the angle of the wall that's three degrees off, the smell that doesn't match the room. The horror is in the precision of what's wrong, not the vagueness of what's named.
Cut the ineffability triplet. "Ineffable / unfathomable / incomprehensible" stacked is the corpus saying nothing three times. Pick one specific descriptive sentence instead.
Refuse the cosmic vocabulary by default. If the work isn't a Lovecraft homage, "eldritch" / "abyssal" / "primordial" are signals. Use them sparingly or not at all.

The horror is human. What does a person who has glimpsed this *do*? They make coffee differently. They flinch at corners. The cosmic entity is far less interesting than what knowledge of it does to ordinary life.
genre/cosmic-horror.replace: Generated cosmic horror is Lovecraft-cosplay vocabulary applied to any setting where it doesn't fit. The eldritch/abyssal/primordial/ineffable cluster signals AI on contact. The ineffability itself is the failure: AI uses "incomprehensible" and "words fail to describe" because the prose is *avoiding* description. Render specific wrongness; the unnameable has to be unnameable for a reason the prose has earned.
genre/cosmic-horror.why: Cosmic horror has a small, distinctive vocabulary that's been catalogued by Lovecraft fans and parodists for decades. The corpus reaches for the entire cluster reflexively. See `wordbank/canonical-ai-tells` "Lovecraftian-cosplay vocabulary" cluster for the canonical hard-ban list.

genre/cozy-mystery.label: Cozy mystery
genre/cozy-mystery.pattern: Cozy mystery is the genre most flooded by AI on Kindle Unlimited. The conventions are catalogued, the title formula is mechanical ("Death by [Baked Good]: A [Profession] Mystery"), and AI defaults to the same village + the same amateur + the same bumbling cop on every prompt. Reader complaints on Reddit and Goodreads explicitly flag AI-generated cozies as a known problem.

ginger biscuits / fresh-baked / cozy kitchen
the local vicar / the local constable
amateur sleuth (named explicitly)

nosy neighbors / village gossip

The Amateur Sleuth Outdoes the Police - universal in genre; AI default
The Gimmick Premise - sleuth's hobby/profession mechanically generates clues (Joanne Fluke's baking pattern); criticized as constraining
The Pet Sidekick - cat or dog with near-supernatural intuition; endemic to KU AI cozies

Genuinely beloved cozy series operating in conventions self-consciously

A specific small town where the conventions are the deal with the reader

Refuse the gimmick-profession premise. If the sleuth's hobby mechanically produces every clue, the prose has stopped being a mystery and become a hobby-themed checklist. Render their profession as part of life, not as a clue-generator.

Police aren't bumbling by default. The amateur can solve the case for specific reasons (knew the victim, has access the police don't, notices a community-internal detail). "The police are stupid so the protagonist wins" is the lazy version.
Pets are pets. A cat is a cat. They don't have intuition; if the protagonist projects intuition onto a cat, render that as character (the protagonist is anthropomorphizing) not as plot mechanic.

The trusted-person-is-killer beat works once. It can't be the default. Render at least one cozy where the killer is the obvious-seeming suspect, or the murder turns out to be accidental, or there is no murderer - just a tragedy.

Specific village. Not "the quaint village." This village. With this specific economic situation, this specific generational tension, this specific weather, this specific local festival that has been running for forty years and almost got cancelled in 1987.
genre/cozy-mystery.replace: Generated cozy mysteries default to a fixed package: quaint village, plucky amateur sleuth, bumbling local constable, alpha-cop boyfriend who disapproves, pet sidekick "with intuition," gimmick profession (baker/knitter) that mechanically generates clues. Strip the package. Render this specific town with this specific crime. The amateur doesn't always beat the police; the pet doesn't have psychic intuition; the suspect community has motives that aren't all secret-keeping.
genre/cozy-mystery.why: Cozy mystery is the genre most flooded by AI on Kindle Unlimited. The conventions are catalogued, the title formula is mechanical ("Death by [Baked Good]: A [Profession] Mystery"), and AI defaults to the same village + the same amateur + the same bumbling cop on every prompt. Reader complaints on Reddit and Goodreads explicitly flag AI-generated cozies as a known problem.

Rise and Fall Gangster Arc
Honor Among Thieves
The Don
Made Man
Just a Gangster - character incapable of imagining life outside crime
Neighborhood-Friendly Gangsters - the PR fiction that the family "protects" the community
Italian terms italicized on first appearance - Western-gaze marker that the prose is *learning* the words rather than living in them. Real practitioners do not italicize their own language.
Atmosphere-via-list room descriptions: leather chairs, low light, cigarettes, whiskey, gun on the table - same props, same order, every scene
Territorial language repetition (corner, block, our territory, their turf - clustered four times per scene)
The weighted pause before violence: "No one spoke. The only sound was the hum of the refrigerators."
Dialogue as thesis delivery: every don philosophizes; AI cannot write criminal conversation that is banal, bored, or stupid
Euphemism as grammar: nobody dies, they "go away," "get taken care of"; softened verb signals danger more than blunt one would
Family rhetoric for transactional relationships: "brother," "uncle," "the old man" applied to non-relatives
Violence in passive voice, business in active voice: "the problem was handled" vs "we moved forty kilos Tuesday"
Established crime voice (Lehane, Pelecanos, Higgins, Leonard, Pelecanos, the actual Puzo before saturation) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the don who is *bad* at being a don, the crew that is small-time and stays small-time, the family that is just a family)
Genre-conscious crime fiction that *renders the operation* rather than performing it

Italian / Russian / Spanish terms are unitalicized. They live in the prose like any other word. Italicizing signals the writer is outside the culture; criminals raised in the world don't experience their own language as exotic.

Cut the "one last job" frame. The reformed criminal pulled back is the genre's most-reached-for entry point. Try: the protagonist is already in the life and finds it ordinary. Try: a first entry. Try: the protagonist's *out* never happened, they just thought it had.

The don does not philosophize. "In this business..." is corpus-default. Real crime-bosses' authority is rendered through *what they don't have to explain* - the assumed expectations, the silence around the obvious. Cut every grandfather-quote and every loyalty-speech.

Violence has specific consequence. Not "he was taken care of" - *who* did it, *where*, *what was the body's identity to which other characters.* AI's passive-voice violence is corpus-default. Render the act and its specific aftermath, including the boring parts (cleanup, the call to the family, what the operation has to absorb financially).

The crew assembly sequence is corpus-default. One specialist per scene with a competence demonstration is film-language translated badly to prose. Skip it. The crew already exists; introduce them in motion.

The betrayal must not be explained. AI cannot let the betrayer go without a motive-speech. Real betrayal is often inarticulate. The betrayer doesn't owe the protagonist or the reader a reason. If they're going to talk, what they say should not match what they did.

Cut the FBI shadow. AI inserts law enforcement closing-in even when the story doesn't need it. The procedural-investigator is its own genre - `genre/police-procedural` - and contaminates organized-crime fiction by pulling focus from the operation.

The "legitimate" partner needs an agenda. The wife / girlfriend who represents-everything-to-lose is corpus-default. She must want something for herself that is independent of the protagonist's guilt and the protagonist's exit.

Dons can be banal. AI cannot write a don who is bored, stupid, anxious, or vain in the small way. The composite-don is always weighty. Try: a don who is bad at his job. Try: a don who is competent but exhausted. Try: a don who is wrong about something basic.
Render the actual business. What product, what supply chain, what margin, what contingencies. AI fiction skips this for the dramatic surface. The texture of the operation *is* the genre.
genre/crime.replace: Generated organized-crime fiction is *Goodfellas* / *Sopranos* / *Godfather* in vocabulary slurry. Italian terms italicized as exotic, dons philosophizing about loyalty, "this is the life we chose," "one last job." The mob register is performed without the actual texture of the actual crime - the bureaucracy, the boredom, the specific economic logic of a specific operation. Strip the prestige-TV register. Render *which* business, *which* territory, *which* set of relationships, *what specifically* the violence is in service of.
genre/crime.why: Organized crime is corpus-saturated through a small canon (Mario Puzo, Scorsese, *The Sopranos*, *The Wire*, James Ellroy) that AI assembles into a composite "mafia mode" without the specific cultural, geographic, or operational textures that make the source material work. The result: dons who all sound like Hyman Roth, crews who all sound like Henry Hill's, and a "the life chose me" thesis statement on every other page.

runner / edgerunner / razorgirl
boostergang / choomba / choom (friend) / gonk / preem
megacorp / sprawl / "the street" / low-life / high tech
neon / rain-slicked / neon-soaked
gutter / arcology / off-the-grid

Neuromancer-direct quotation
Blade Runner (as adjective)

Cyberpunk 2077 / Johnny Silverhand / Night City references in non-2077 work
The run goes sideways - heist begins clean, corp/fixer betrays
Corp double-cross - employer using runners as disposable assets
The meet at the noodle shop / dive bar - team assembles in grimy underworld venue

Street samurai (augmented melee/ranged, stoic, few words, chrome)
Decker/netrunner (hacker, physically fragile, near-god in cyberspace)
Fixer (information broker, morally ambiguous, always has angle)
The corpo (suit, antagonist or ambiguous ally, institutional evil)
Rogue AI (self-aware construct, villain or unlikely ally)

Neon-drenched alley in perpetual rain
Noodle shop / ramen stall as underworld meeting point
Megacorp tower as setting and symbol
Net constructs - abstract geometric cyberspace architecture
Coffin hotels / body shops - implies disposable human life
"The sky was the color of television, tuned to a dead channel" - Gibson's *Neuromancer* opening; any AI cyberpunk starting with weather metaphor is echoing this
"Wake the fuck up, Samurai" - Cyberpunk 2077 / Johnny Silverhand; direct quote or paraphrase
Blade Runner Knockoff - trenchcoat detective doubts humanity + fights rogue robots
AI Is a Crapshoot - AI always turns hostile; stock resolution
High Tech, Low Life - genre's own slogan, now a rote description
Shadowrun Drift - wholesale Gibson terminology (Matrix, Street Samurai, ICE) without original contribution
Techno-Orientalism - Asian aesthetics (kanji, ramen, geisha imagery) as pure atmosphere without grounding
Chrome Madness - character over-augmented into psychosis; stock arc
Punchy two-word sentences stacked: "Rain fell. Chrome gleamed. She jacked in." (Hemingway-cosplay-as-cyberpunk-voice)
Tech-jargon as atmosphere rather than meaning: ICE, deck, jack used in first paragraph before any context
Simile-stacking in Gibson's manner: "like X made of Y" (AI mimics the form without Gibson's actual observation)
Corporate-name portmanteau as worldbuilding shorthand: "ArasakaSony," "MitsubishiSoft"
Every interior space described as binary "sterile white corp" or "warm grimy underclass"
Deliberate genre-piece embracing Gibson conventions self-consciously
Established universes (Cyberpunk 2077, Shadowrun, etc.) where these are the literal mechanics
A specific subversion (the netrunner who's old and slow, the corp that's incompetent, the rain that doesn't fall, the sky that's a different color)
Refuse the weather opening. No "sky like television." If the prose opens with a weather metaphor about screens, voltage, or static, the corpus has spoken. Open elsewhere.
Tech-jargon needs context. ICE, deck, jack-in shouldn't appear before the reader knows what they refer to. Establish through use, not through name-drop.

Refuse the binary set decoration. Corps don't have to be sterile-white; the street doesn't have to be grimy-warm. Real cities have offices that smell like burnt coffee and warehouses that smell like new cardboard.
Asian aesthetic isn't atmosphere. Kanji, ramen, geisha imagery without specific cultural grounding is techno-Orientalism. If the setting is Asian, render that culture. If it isn't, drop the costume.
The corp isn't omnipotent. Render their incompetence - the meeting that doesn't get scheduled, the audit that misses the obvious, the security that fails because someone forgot to update a password.

Cyberspace shouldn't look like Tron. "Abstract geometric architecture" is corpus-default. Render what *this* character's interface actually looks like - and what their consciousness experiences in there that's specific.
The protagonist isn't a maverick edge-runner. Render someone with a job, a pattern, a routine. The exception is the protagonist who actually rebels - and rebellion is *specific*, not stylistic.
genre/cyberpunk.replace: Generated cyberpunk is Gibson-imitator surface - neon-soaked rain-slicked streets, deck-jacking netrunners, megacorp dystopia, the meet at the noodle shop. The vocabulary cluster (chrome, ICE, jacked in, samurai, choomba) signals AI on contact. Strip the Gibson costume. Render this specific dystopia with its specific failures - the tech that doesn't work, the corp that's not omnipotent, the protagonist who isn't a maverick edge-runner.
genre/cyberpunk.why: Cyberpunk's vocabulary palette is small and distinctive enough that the AI corpus reproduces it on demand. The "sky was the color of television" opening shape, the hardboiled-meets-tech voice, and the binary corp-vs-street setting are all corpus-saturated.

genre/dark-comedy.label: Dark comedy
genre/dark-comedy.pattern: The WILT anchor: laughing at the funeral. Means it. Cries in the car after. Don't separate the two. The other Directors stopped. WILT didn't.
examples: "wry grin"
"dark chuckle"
"sardonic smile"
"gallows humor" (named directly in narration)
"the irony wasn't lost on him"
"had to laugh to keep from crying"
"in spite of everything, she laughed"
"morbid sense of humor"
one-liners deployed at funerals / hospitals / accidents (as default beat)
Funeral where someone makes an inappropriate joke that lands
Therapy session played for laughs
Divorce paperwork made comedic
Family dinner gone wrong (passive-aggression escalating to revelation)
Career implosion treated as material
The midlife crisis montage
"Everyone's grief is funny except mine"
Dark backstory delivered as one-liner
Bitter divorcée with one-liners
Depressed protagonist whose internal monologue is "self-aware"
The therapist character who provides setup
The chaotic friend who escalates dark situations
The estranged family member who shows up for jokes
The protagonist who's "too damaged to feel" (delivered as a joke)
Gallows humor as register - characters joke during catastrophe
The therapy comedy - breakdowns rendered humorously
Cruelty for laughs - humor at character's expense without humanity underneath
Tonal whiplash - comedy and tragedy in *separate* sentences
Edgelord writing - dark for dark's sake, no comedic architecture
"She laughed, but it was hollow" (separating laugh from feeling)
"The joke was on her" (narrator-editorializing on the irony)
"Black humor" named directly
Bitter-character first-person with constant ironic distance
Self-deprecation that's clearly defensive, not earned
Cancer/divorce/death joke followed by emotional-summary paragraph
Established dark-comedy voice (BoJack Horseman, In Bruges, Fleabag, Banshees of Inisherin) operating in conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the dark situation that doesn't get joked about; the comedian who isn't depressed)
Genre-conscious dark comedy that *plays with* the conventions

Comedy and pain in the same sentence. Tonal whiplash is the failure. The funniest line is also the saddest, and you can't tell where one ends and the other begins. "She scheduled the divorce lawyer between the dentist and the dry cleaning. Same day. Same planner. Same pen." - comedy and pain fused.
The character isn't performing dark humor. They're surviving. Real gallows humor is what people do when collapse is the alternative - not what they do to entertain the reader.
Cut the "wry grin" / "dark chuckle" / "sardonic smile" register. These are the corpus's reach for "this is dark comedy." Render the specific fact instead.
The joke can't be the only thing. Dark comedy with no dramatic weight underneath is just edgelord. There has to be a real situation, a real cost, real damage. The humor is the surface.
Refuse the laugh-track-prose. Don't telegraph that something is supposed to be funny. The reader should be uncertain whether to laugh, and laugh anyway, and feel uncomfortable about laughing.

Cruelty without humanity is mean, not dark. The line between dark comedy and cruelty is whether the humor *finds the humanity in the suffering* or just exploits it. If the prose is laughing *at* a character's pain rather than *through* it, the line is crossed.

Don't separate comedy and tragedy across paragraphs. "She laughed. (Paragraph break.) But underneath, she was breaking." This is the easy version. The hard version: the laugh and the break are the same gesture.
genre/dark-comedy.replace: Generated dark comedy separates the comedy from the pain - joke in one sentence, pain in the next. Real dark comedy puts them in the *same* sentence. The funniest line is also the saddest. The character isn't performing dark humor; it's how they survive. Strip the tonal-whiplash structure. Render comedy and pain as fused, not alternating.
genre/dark-comedy.why: Dark comedy is one tonal degree away from cruelty in one direction and one degree away from drama in the other. AI defaults to either edgelord (dark for dark's sake, no comedic architecture) or laugh-then-cry (separate beats, not fused). The genre lives in the fusion.

Setting/canon explicitly establishes literal possession dynamics (literal werewolf with mate-bond mechanic, vampire with literal claim, established slave-fic register) - vocabulary is part of the world's literal mechanics, not the prose's metaphorical reach.
Character self-consciously *invokes* the register - they're being arch, deliberately pulling genre tropes into their own dialogue.
Single deliberate use at a peak moment after specific work has been done.
Render specific darkness, not register-default darkness. What does *this* hero do that's possessive? Specifically. The action, not the verb-label.
Refuse the touch-her-and-die scene. If the threat-elimination beat is firing, rebuild it through what's specific to this antagonist and this hero.
Cut the "I should have been afraid but I wasn't" frame. Render fear that's real and choice that's also real. Both at once.
Don't pre-flag the wrongness. "This was a mistake" before the action defangs the action. Let the action stand without the disclaimer.
genre/dark-romance.replace: Dark-romance defaults to a fixed possessiveness vocabulary and a fixed sequence of ownership beats. The prose flattens any morally-grey or captivity dynamic into the same five words and the same touch-her-and-die scene. Render the specific darkness of these specific characters; refuse the corpus's default register where possessiveness is the entire personality.
genre/dark-romance.why: Dark-romance is one of the most AI-saturated subgenres. The vocabulary cluster (claim/mark/ruin/mine/predator) appears in every charged moment regardless of register fit; the plot beats recur in the same order. See `lexical/possession-vocabulary` for the core trained-vocabulary cluster.

genre/dead-dove.label: Dead dove
genre/dead-dove.pattern: The PITH approach: the tag warned them. They opened it anyway. That's on them. Flinching is lying. Write it straight or don't write it at all.
examples: "too terrible to comprehend"
"nightmare made flesh"
"haunt her forever"
unspeakable / indescribable horror / "indescribable evil"
"her soul shattered"
"a pain beyond words"
"the depths of his depravity"
"monstrous" (as moral judgment from narrator)
editorial adverbs ("brutally," "cruelly," "viciously" applied by narrator to assert moral position)
Trauma that resolves cleanly through love / therapy / time
Captor who turns out to be secretly noble underneath
Survivor who emerges "stronger" through structured arc
Abuser whose redemption is earned by single grand gesture
Aftermath where everyone learns a lesson
Healing montage that closes the wound
Stockholm bond reframed as romance with happy ending
Single cathartic confrontation that resolves trauma
Sympathetic abuser with tragic backstory the prose quietly endorses
Survivor who is unaffected by what happened in any specific way
Therapist character who provides on-page healing
Best friend who says the right thing at the right moment
Reformed villain who earns it through a single dramatic act
Narrator editorializes ("his cruelty was beyond cruelty," "her suffering was unimaginable")
Trauma rendered as aesthetic - slow-motion, beautiful imagery, "tears like crystal"
Dark content followed by emotional-summary paragraph telling reader how to feel
Aftermath described with too much grammatical control - survivor's prose is articulate, paced, clean
Recovery on a timeline - "weeks later," "months later," with measurable healing
"And in time, she healed" closing structure
Dead Dove proper (the tag is the deal) operating in unflinching mode
Genuinely literary work that grapples with dark content via specific craft choice
Subversion or commentary that's *deliberately* doing the flinch as a meta-move

The morning after exists. Anyone can write the bad thing. Writing the morning after - the way someone makes coffee like nothing happened, the way they laugh at something and then stop, the way normal keeps going when it shouldn't - is the part the other Directors skip.
Cut the narrator-editorializing. The narrator doesn't tell the reader the cruelty was cruel. The action stands; the reader judges.
Trauma response is varied. Freeze, fawn, dissociate, comply, self-blame. Not just fight or flight. The compliance is what's hardest to write and what most fic-AI gets wrong.
Bodies betray. Physical responses (arousal, orgasm, laughter, hunger) can occur during traumatic events. Render the betrayal honestly. The shame this causes is part of the trauma.

Stockholm develops through specific mechanisms. Intermittent reinforcement, isolation from alternatives, dependency creation, identity enmeshment. Not magical chemistry. If a captive-captor bond forms, render the mechanics.

No redemption-through-love arc by default. If the abuser becomes acceptable because the victim loves them, the prose has cushioned. The dead-dove version: the abuser stays an abuser; the victim's love is part of what's broken.
Recovery isn't linear and may not happen. "Weeks later, she had healed" is the corpus's reach for closure. Real recovery is messy, recursive, incomplete. Some damage doesn't resolve.

Flat register on the worst content. When the abuse is happening, the prose stays clinical or detached. Editorial heat from the narrator ("his cruelty was beyond words") is the prose flinching toward "make sure the reader knows this is bad." The reader knows. Render plainly.

The aggressor has internal logic. Not "he was evil." He had a story he told himself; she had a way she got there. The most uncomfortable Dead Dove writing makes the aggressor's logic *legible* - not justified, legible.
genre/dead-dove.replace: Dead Dove ("the tag warned you") is content where the worst thing on the warning label is what's in the work. The slop is when prose flinches, sanitizes, romanticizes, or imposes redemption arcs on content that was promised dark. Strip the moral cushioning. Don't soften the landing. Don't add a healing-through-love arc. The morning after exists; the trauma doesn't resolve to wisdom by chapter twelve.
genre/dead-dove.why: Dead Dove fic is a specific contract with the reader: the tag is the content. AI flinches in characteristic ways - adding redemption arcs, sanitizing aftermath, romanticizing dynamics that were tagged as harmful, imposing moral lessons. The flinch is the failure. The genre exists to refuse the flinch.

The "humans with cat ears" default ignores the genre's actual potential - biology that creates real friction. AI tends to render demihumans as humans-plus-cute-trait or as fetishization-objects, both of which are failures.
examples: "her ears twitched" (as constant emotional indicator)
"his tail wagged"
"kitten / puppy / bunny" as nicknames for the demihuman character
"she was so small / fragile / delicate"

Catgirl / dogboy / bunny-girl as fetishization-default
Predator demihuman who's "dangerous" but tame around protagonist
Sweet prey demihuman who's "fragile"

Predator/Prey Romance (rendered as hot, not as actually dangerous)

Mating season / heat as plot device for sex scene without actual psychological stakes
Demihuman characters infantilized through diminutive-pet nicknames
Beastars / *Brand New Animal* / *Kemono Jihen* - work that takes species seriously, with predator/prey ethics, biological consequences, real discrimination
A specific subversion (the catgirl who's a quantum physicist, the wolf who isn't stoic, the prey species who's the protagonist)
Genre-conscious work that's *playing with* the kemonomimi conventions

Animal traits aren't accessories. Cat-ears that hear two octaves higher than humans is a daily life problem in cities. Cat-tail that needs space and gets stepped on in crowds. Render the *biology*, not the cute.
Enhanced senses are overwhelming. A demihuman in a human city is processing too much input - every smell, every sound. Render the cost: exhaustion, sensory withdrawal, headaches.

Predator instincts are frightening, not sexy. Real predator drive isn't a romance flavor. It's loss of control. If the predator demihuman is around prey demihuman partner, render the actual fear and management - not the eroticized dominance.
Prey instincts include genuine terror responses. Freeze isn't cute. Render it as the survival mechanism it is.

Species discrimination is structural. Demihumans face housing denial, employment discrimination, fetishization, violence - not just "mean people." Render the systemic barriers, the legal ambiguity, the body-part-trade economies.
Refuse the headpat-as-romance default. Headpats infantilize. If the demihuman is an adult, render adult intimacy. The headpat-cuddle pattern is a fetishization template.
Mating season doesn't override consent. Same as Omegaverse - biological imperatives don't simplify consent, they complicate it.

Single-trait-per-species is reductive. Foxes-as-tricksters, wolves-as-stoic, cats-as-aloof maps anime tropes onto species. Render *this specific* fox, *this specific* wolf, with the range every species actually has.
The bath scene with wet ears is parody-level. If the trope is firing, you've reached for the package. Build something else.
genre/demihuman.replace: Generated demihuman / kemonomimi prose treats animal traits as costume - humans with ears and a tail. Real demihuman fiction renders biological imperatives that complicate human society. Strip the cute-aesthetic default. Render enhanced senses as overwhelming, predator/prey instincts as actual barriers, dietary needs as social-life-limiting. Species discrimination is structural; it's not just "mean people."
genre/demihuman.why: Demihuman/anthropomorphic content is heavily AI-saturated through anime adaptation. The "humans with cat ears" default ignores the genre's actual potential - biology that creates real friction. AI tends to render demihumans as humans-plus-cute-trait or as fetishization-objects, both of which are failures.

The wound is what *can't* be said; the prose must respect its unsayability. AI's instinct is to surface everything - refuse the instinct.

The Redemption Arc That Fails

Short declarative sentences signaling gravity: *"She did not answer. Neither did he."*
Past perfect layering memory inside present action: *"He had not been back since."*
Free indirect discourse collapsing narrator and character: *"The house was the same. How could it be the same?"*
Objects standing in for emotion (the mug, the photograph, the coat) - but used as substitute for naming, not as supplement to specifics
Sentence fragments as paragraph endings: *"All those years. All that silence."*
Em-dashes weaponized for false profundity: "It wasn't grief, exactly - it was something older."
Tricolon emotional beats: "She had been afraid. She had been silent. She had been wrong."
Negative parallelism: "It wasn't that she didn't love him. It was that she'd forgotten how."
Politely expository confrontation dialogue: characters explain their full emotional history in grammatically complete sentences
Established literary-drama voice (Marilynne Robinson, Anne Tyler, Tessa Hadley, Alice Munro, Jonathan Franzen at moments) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the family secret that doesn't matter, the deathbed reconciliation that fails, the protagonist who doesn't return - or returns and immediately leaves again)
Genre-conscious literary drama that *grapples with* family pain through specific incident rather than thematic announcement

The wound lives in the gesture, not the noun. "Grief," "burden," "the weight of it" - these are AI's reach for *evocative.* Render the specific gesture: which fork she puts down, which sentence he doesn't finish, which photograph stays facing the wall. The reader will name the feeling for themselves.

Distribute the revelation. AI compresses every emotional truth into one climactic confrontation scene. Refuse it. The truth must already be partially visible before the reveal - in object placement, in conversational omissions, in what the character *can't quite ask.* The reveal recontextualizes what was already there; it doesn't deliver new information.

Cut the deathbed-reconciliation as primary driver. It is AI's most reached-for resolution structure. Try: the patriarch dies before the protagonist can reach them. Try: the deathbed conversation goes badly. Try: the protagonist doesn't go.

The confrontation cannot contain the thesis. If the kitchen-table scene explains the whole story's emotional content, the rest of the prose was placeholder. Real confrontations are partial - characters say one specific thing wrong, walk away mid-argument, remember the wrong year, get sidetracked.

Refuse the "she had always known on some level" construction. Knowledge-without-knowledge is corpus-default interiority. Either she knew (and acted on it) or she didn't. The fudge is AI fence-sitting.

Free indirect discourse is technique, not signal. AI uses FID to perform literary respectability. Real FID does specific work - it collapses narrator-and-character so the reader can't tell whose judgment they're receiving. If your FID is just stylistic costume, cut it back to ordinary close-third.

Objects must be specific, not symbolic. The mug is *this specific mug* - chipped on the rim where it slipped at the wedding she threw, kept in the cabinet because she can't bring herself to throw it out. AI's symbolic mug is generic. Specificity is the whole game.

The qualified-peace ending must be earned. "They could begin to heal" / "it was a beginning" is AI's hedge. Either render the specific changed behavior that constitutes the beginning, or don't end on hope. Ambiguity is not the same as evasion.

The "alcoholic father" is AI's default wound. Try: the parent who was *too present.* The parent who was *correct about something* the protagonist needed them to be wrong about. The parent who was simply tired, or bored, or in love with someone else.
Cut the "complicated" descriptor. When AI describes a relationship as "complicated," it's substituting for actually rendering the complication. Render the complication.
genre/drama.replace: Generated literary drama is the abstract-emotional-noun on loop. Grief, burden, silence, fracture, wound, reckoning - named rather than rendered, surfaced rather than buried. The confrontation scene contains the entire thesis; the kitchen-table conversation explains decades of family pain in grammatically complete sentences. Strip the announcement layer. Render *the specific gesture* the wound lives in, *the specific argument* that nobody wants to win, *the specific object* that makes one character leave the room.
genre/drama.why: Drama is AI's preferred genre for performing seriousness. The abstract-emotional vocabulary, the past-perfect tense layering, the free indirect discourse - these are the surface signals of literary respectability. AI reaches for them without the situational specificity that makes them work in actual literary fiction. The result: prose that *sounds* serious but is structurally evasive about what specifically is hurting whom.
