Genre-conscious court drama with *specific dynastic, religious, and economic logic* that produces the conflict

The scheming uncle requires history, grievance, and competing loyalty. AI's default scheming-uncle has no motivation beyond ambition. Real scheming has prior history (a slight, an inheritance dispute, a marriage promise broken), specific material grievance (lands, titles, a particular position), and competing loyalty (to a faction, to a child, to a religious house) that makes the scheming genuinely conflicted. Render all three.

The wise advisor must have been wrong about something. AI's wise-counselor is uniformly correct about everything except their own mortality. Real advisors carry past errors that constrain present advice. Render the specific past failure.

Succession conflict needs specific stakes for specific characters. AI describes "the nobles were divided" in abstract faction terms. Render the specific noble's specific land, specific income, specific obligation, specific marriage stake. Politics is people losing or gaining specific things.

Formal register varies by context. Ceremony, council, private chamber, whispered hallway - these are four different registers. AI applies one uniform formal-court-voice. The variation between contexts is *what produces the texture* of court life.

No birth-secret reveals as primary plot engine. AI's "the protagonist is actually of higher birth" is corpus-default agency-conferral. Either don't use it, or use it as opening premise (everyone knows from chapter one).

The throne-room monologue is corpus-default. Cut the scene where the monarch lectures the protagonist on the political situation. Distribute the exposition across multiple scenes, multiple speakers, multiple acts of the protagonist's investigation.

The eavesdropping convenience is corpus-default. AI's "protagonist accidentally overhears the crucial conversation" is the laziest exposition-delivery. Either the protagonist works to acquire the information, or the information arrives through an active source - not a dropped curtain.

Honorifics must be consistent. Court fiction-writers research the address-form for the polity they're depicting. AI applies a salad of honorifics. Either pick a real historical address-system (medieval English, Byzantine, Tang Chinese, etc.) and maintain it precisely, or build a fictional one and maintain *it* precisely.
The "secret hallway" / "hidden passage" is corpus-default. Try: there is no secret passage. The protagonist must move through normal court space, observed.

The reluctant heir is corpus-default. "Doesn't want the throne but is extraordinarily competent at it" - AI cannot write characters who *want* power and grapple with the moral complexity of wanting it. Try: a protagonist who is *correct* to want power and pays its specific cost.

The succession crisis as automatic conflict is corpus-default. Stable polities have boring transitions. Try: a court where the succession is settled and the conflict is something else (administrative, religious, economic).
genre/royalty.replace: Generated court drama is the throne-room exposition monologue, the scheming uncle without specified motivation, the formal court-language register applied uniformly regardless of context. Honorifics inconsistently maintained; whispered intrigue establishing setting; eavesdropping scenes delivering the political situation in convenient earshot. Strip the costume layer. Render *this specific* polity with *this specific* succession law, *this specific* faction with *specified* material grievance, *this specific* honorific with *consistent* deployment.
genre/royalty.why: Court drama is corpus-saturated through Shakespeare's history plays, *Game of Thrones* and its imitators, *The Crown*, fantasy palace-intrigue novels, and Tudor-mania historical fiction. AI assembles a generic court - disputed succession, scheming uncle, marriage alliance, secret heir - without the specific economic, religious, and dynastic logic that produced any actual historical court. The result: every kingdom feels like the same kingdom.

Technology as setting, not spectacle. Don't describe the ship - describe what the crew does during the seven-hour refueling cycle they've done four hundred times. Don't explain the AI - show the policy meeting about what happens when it says no.
Tech has cost - physical, social, psychological. Where in the body does using this technology hurt? What does the user have to give up?
Refuse "quantum" as handwave. If the prose can't explain how the technology works in one specific sentence, "quantum" is filler. Cut.
Aliens that aren't human-shaped. AI defaults to alien-as-metaphor-for-human-other. Render aliens whose actual cognition is different. They don't think like us. Show that, don't state it.
Follow implications further than comfortable. The technology IS the story when followed to its logical consequences. What does this tech actually mean for how people live, work, fail, love?
genre/sci-fi.replace: Generated sci-fi reaches for Star Trek bridge defaults and quantum-handwave technobabble. Technology is described with awe instead of consequence. Render technology as setting, not spectacle - what the tech does to people, what the daily inconvenience of living inside the system is, what the physical experience of using the interface is.
genre/sci-fi.why: AI sci-fi defaults are recognizable across every subgenre - the bridge, the viewscreen, the quantum drive, the rogue AI. The vocabulary cluster signals Trek-derivative on contact regardless of the actual setting. The plot beats (first contact gone wrong, maverick captain, AI goes rogue) recur in identical shape.

The voice is so distinctive - self-deprecating, ironic-distanced, brand-aware - that it parses as template across nearly every AI-generated slice-of-life work.

Refuse the aesthetic-as-setting default. "Cozy apartment with an indie playlist" is brand description, not a place. Render *this* specific apartment - the spot on the ceiling where the upstairs leak left a stain, the windowsill that doesn't quite latch.
Cut the quasi-tweet interior. "This was fine. Catastrophic, actually." reads as twitter, not as thought. Render thinking that doesn't perform itself for an audience.
Self-deprecation isn't characterization. The ironic-distance default replaces actual interior. Render moments where the character doesn't make a joke about their feeling - just has it.
No "she sighed at her phone." The phone-sigh is the corpus's universal stand-in for "ennui." Render what's *on* the phone, what specifically she's reading, who she didn't text back.

Friend group dinners as setting, not vehicle. The "forced honesty over wine" scene is corpus-default. Render the dinner where nothing is said, or where the wrong thing is said by someone other than the protagonist.

Quit-the-job-pursue-art is a beat, not a plot. If the resolution is the protagonist becoming a baker / writer / artist, the prose has reached for the package. Render what happens *after* she quits, including the months where it doesn't work.

Setting through sensory detail, not brand reference. "She walked into the third-wave coffee shop" -> "She walked into Bonsoir, where the espresso machine made the same mournful hiss it had every morning for three years."
genre/slice-of-life.replace: Generated slice-of-life is millennial-protagonist-aesthetic-default - cozy apartment, indie playlist, third-wave coffee shop, "she sighed at her phone." Interior monologue arrives as quasi-tweets ("This was fine. Catastrophic, actually."). Aesthetic-as-character: setting described through brand names, color palettes, and music genres rather than sensory detail. Strip the aesthetic. Render this specific Tuesday for this specific person.
genre/slice-of-life.why: Contemporary slice-of-life is dominated by an extremely-online millennial register that's well-represented in AI training data. The voice is so distinctive - self-deprecating, ironic-distanced, brand-aware - that it parses as template across nearly every AI-generated slice-of-life work.

Established space opera voice (Iain M. Banks's Culture, Becky Chambers's Wayfarers, Yoon Ha Lee's Machineries of Empire, Vernor Vinge, Lois McMaster Bujold) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the empire that's actually competent and likable, the chosen one whose chosen-ness is wrong, the rebellion that wins and immediately becomes corrupt)
Genre-conscious space opera that *integrates* economics, biology, technology, and politics into a single coherent setting

Polities have specific economic and political logic. Not "the Empire" - *which* polity, *what* it produces, *who* it taxes, *how* it transmits authority across distance. AI defaults to monolithic-fascist empire because *Star Wars* is the corpus's gravity well. Build a different system.

The binary Empire / Rebellion frame is corpus-default. Refuse it. Most political conflict is multi-polar; most polities have internal factions; most rebellions are messy and partly bad. Render the mess.

FTL has a cost. Hyperspace, warp drive, jump drive - AI deploys these as travel-time skip with no cost. Real space-opera SF that earns its weight (Bujold, Banks) makes FTL *expensive* in fuel, in time-dilation, in social effects. If your characters can travel without cost, your setting is decorative.

Cut the four-archetype crew. The pilot / idealist / rogue / stoic-alien rotation is corpus-default ensemble. Either build the crew from a different role-set (engineers, diplomats, cooks, doctors - people who actually run ships), or accept that you're writing fanfic and own it.

Aliens are biology, not personality. AI's Planet-of-Hats default ("the warrior race," "the merchant race") is the lazy version. Render *this specific* alien species' specific biological constraints (atmosphere, gravity, lifespan, reproduction, senses) and let the culture flow from them.
The chosen-one bloodline is corpus-default. Refuse it. Or: render it as banal - the bloodline does specific things and not others, the specialness is technical rather than mythic.

The "ancient evil awakens" act-two pivot is corpus-default. It's the *Mass Effect* Reaper architecture stacked onto the *Star Wars* frame. The political conflict you established was sufficient - don't escalate to cosmic-cycle-extinction unless that's what the book is actually about.
The mentor dying at the midpoint is corpus-default. Try: the mentor lives. Try: the mentor was wrong about the central thing.
The villain-is-family reveal is corpus-default. Biological relationships weaponized for stakes. Cheap. Either earn it (the relationship is rendered before the reveal) or cut it.

Cut the viewport introspection. Character-at-viewport-with-cosmic-weight-imagery is the genre's most reliable tell. If your character needs to think, render them doing something specific in the same scene.
No "the journey is just beginning" coda. Forward-looking codas are AI's reach for series-setup. End in the present. Let the reader imagine what comes next.

Names should not all be portentous. Ships named *Eternal Horizon* / *Void's Edge* / *Last Dawn* - corpus-default. Mix in mundane names (industrial designations, registry numbers, jokes, names of dead ex-spouses).
genre/space-opera.replace: Generated space opera is *Star Wars* political structure plus *Star Trek* crew ensemble plus *Mass Effect* extinction-cycle villain, all stacked simultaneously without integration. The ragtag crew assembles, the empire opposes the rebellion, ancient evil awakens, the Chosen One has a secret bloodline, the mentor dies at the midpoint. Strip the IP-stack. Render *this specific* polity with *this specific* economic and political logic, *this specific* alien species with biology that complicates rather than ornaments, *this specific* technology with a cost that matters.
genre/space-opera.why: Space opera is the most cleanly IP-saturated genre AI generates. The training corpus is dominated by a small canon (Lucasfilm, *Star Trek* franchise, BioWare's Mass Effect, Frank Herbert's *Dune* aesthetic) which AI assembles into a generic-cosmic-melodrama. The result reads as fanfic of a fictional universe that doesn't exist - recognizably space opera, specifically nothing.

genre/steampunk.label: Steampunk
genre/steampunk.pattern: Steampunk's visual identity is iconic enough that AI reproduces it as costume - the goggles, the corset, the airship, the brass gears - without the underlying *industrial revolution* that gives the genre its conflict. Real steampunk grapples with class, labor, technological displacement, imperial power. AI default skips all of it for the look.

Genre-conscious steampunk (China Miéville, Cherie Priest, Ted Chiang at moments) operating in conventions self-consciously
Work that grapples with the *industrial revolution* - labor, class, technological displacement, colonialism
A specific subversion (the mad inventor whose invention doesn't work; the airship that's a ship; the steampunk society that's organized around something other than steam)
Steam costs. Coal must be mined. Boilers must be tended. Workers get scalded. Pressure-vessels explode. If the steampunk world's machinery has no cost, the prose has reached for the aesthetic.
The mad inventor isn't a character. "Eccentric brilliant inventor" is corpus-default. Render *this specific* engineer with specific obsessions, specific failures, specific limits.

Refuse the airship-as-default-vehicle. Airships are *complicated* - hydrogen explodes, weather grounds them, their range is limited. If the airship is just "fancy boat that flies," the prose hasn't earned it.

The industrial revolution is the genre's content. Steampunk's *reason for existing* is grappling with what happens when technology accelerates faster than ethics. If the prose just shows cool gears, it's missed the genre.

Colonialism is part of Victorian. The aesthetics steampunk pulls from were generated by empire. Refusing to acknowledge that is a flinch. Either grapple with it or build an alternate-history that explicitly didn't have it (and explain why not).

Lady inventor in pants isn't characterization. A woman defying gender norms in a Victorian-coded setting needs *specific* costs and reactions. Render the actual social punishment, not just the protagonist's defiance.

Specificity over aesthetic. Not "brass gears" - *which* gears, *what* they do, *what* happens when they fail. Not "the workshop" - *this* workshop, with the missing wrench, the scorch mark on the wall, the smell of oil and iron and unwashed clothes.

Cut the "with a hiss of steam" stage business. The phrase appears in nearly every AI-generated steampunk passage. If steam is part of the scene, render *what it does* - the visibility, the heat, the wet - not the sound effect.
genre/steampunk.replace: Generated steampunk is goggle-and-corset cosplay over Victorian costume - brass gears as decoration, airships as set-piece, mad inventor as character-shorthand. The mechanics aren't load-bearing; the steam doesn't actually power anything specific. Strip the aesthetic. Render machinery that has *cost* - coal that runs out, steam that scalds, gears that strip, pressure that fails at the worst moment.
genre/steampunk.why: Steampunk's visual identity is iconic enough that AI reproduces it as costume - the goggles, the corset, the airship, the brass gears - without the underlying *industrial revolution* that gives the genre its conflict. Real steampunk grapples with class, labor, technological displacement, imperial power. AI default skips all of it for the look.

Render the protagonist's actual life - the relationship the heroism is destroying, the body the powers are wearing out, the moral position the costume costs them - and the genre's machinery will produce its own meaning without help.

Superhero Origin as mandatory narrative unit
Burden-framing: every action cast as obligation, weight, "I have no choice"
Costume-as-identity language: the suit is *put on* like transformation; "barely recognized the figure staring back"
City-as-patient: skyline described in emotional terms; the city is sick, the hero is the cure
Brooding interior monologue, present-tense second-guessing, sentence fragments
Power description as dread: "I felt the heat build behind my eyes again"
Slow-motion combat with sensory expansion: "he saw the punch coming before it arrived"
Costume description on first wear: emblem catches light, suit clings to frame, city below
Established superhero voice (Moore, Morrison, Brubaker, Vaughn, Whedon at moments) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the hero whose powers are useless, the secret identity that doesn't get exposed, the city that doesn't need them)
Genre-conscious capework that *plays with* the burden-and-mantle architecture

Powers have specific costs. Not "the gift came with a price" - *which* calories, *which* organ, *which* sleep deficit, *which* relationship the powers cost. If the power is free, the genre's ethical engine is missing.

The costume is functional. It hides body type, blood, identity; it solves a specific problem (cold at altitude, friction at speed, identification by pattern). Render the function. The "symbol catches the light" mirror scene is corpus-default.

Cut the rooftop brood. The character standing at the city's edge looking down is the genre's most-reached-for emotional placeholder. If the scene has no plot function, cut it. If it does, render the specific surveillance - what they're watching, what they're waiting for.
The mentor death is corpus-default. Try: the mentor lives, becomes inconvenient, has to be argued with. Try: the mentor was wrong about the central thing. Try: there is no mentor.

Power loss -> "real strength inside" -> power restored stronger is the most-reached-for act-two structure. Refuse it. Try: power loss is permanent and the hero adapts. Try: power loss reveals the hero was never that good.

The villain-is-family reveal is corpus-default. Biological relationships weaponized for emotional stakes is the cheapest of the genre's moves. Use it only if the relationship is rendered before the reveal - not as a twist.
Cut the slow-motion first-use. Time-slowing combat is film grammar; in prose it reads as the writer announcing *this is the cool part now.* Render the actual physical event.
The "I quit heroism" speech is corpus-default. If the character is going to quit, they quit in a small specific way (didn't show up to a thing) rather than in a speech.
No final-page cosmic significance. "The city would never be the same." Cut every closer that elevates the local stakes to symbolic-of-everything. Local stakes are sufficient if rendered.
genre/superhero.replace: Generated superhero is the burden-of-power monologue with the costume photographed in the mirror. Powers manifest, training kicks in, the symbol means something, the city would never be the same. Strip the announcement layer. Render *which specific rule of physics* the power breaks, *what it costs* in calories or sleep or relationships, *what specifically* the costume is designed to hide and what it accidentally reveals.
genre/superhero.why: Superhero is one of the most AI-corpus-saturated genres because the conventions are tight, the source material is voluminous, and the moral architecture is overdetermined. The result: every cape story sounds like every other cape story - origin tragedy, costume reveal, rooftop brood, mentor death, "the city needs me." The character's *specific* pain is replaced with the generic pain of being a hero.

Ticking-clock sentence rhythm: "08:47. Twelve minutes left."
Technical jargon for texture without accuracy (hacking as "relentless button-smashing")
Over-complicated plot summaries in prose itself - characters explain plot to each other
Adverb stacking for urgency ("quickly, silently, carefully" in succession)
Hedged omniscience - narrator knows things hero doesn't, withholds in contrived ways
Deliberate-pastiche / loving genre work
Established franchise (Bourne, Bond, Reacher) operating in known conventions
A specific subversion (the lone wolf who fails; the mole who isn't actually disloyal)
Real clocks, not abstract urgency. "Time is running out" is nothing. "Four minutes until the shift change" is a clock. Specific deadline + specific consequence at expiry.
Information asymmetry as engine. Who knows what, who's wrong about what they know. Map the gaps. The tension lives there.
Smart characters making bad calls under pressure. Competence isn't never miscalculating. It's knowing which mistake you can afford. Render the cost of the choice.
Refuse the villain monologue. The antagonist's plan is visible through gaps in what they let slip - never explained whole.
Cut "the stakes have never been higher." If the prose has to tell the reader the stakes are high, the prose hasn't built them.
genre/thriller.replace: Generated thrillers default to fake clocks and competence porn. The vocabulary cluster (pulse-pounding, cat-and-mouse, ticking clock, off the grid) signals AI on contact. Real thrillers run on information asymmetry - who knows what, who's wrong about what they know - and on specific consequential clocks. Refuse the abstract urgency. Build the specific gap.
genre/thriller.why: Thriller defaults are particularly recognizable because the genre's mechanics are well-catalogued and the corpus has many examples. The "lone wolf called back from retirement" / "the mole is one of us" / "with seconds to spare" beats appear in almost every AI-generated thriller.

"Wibbly-wobbly" handwave deployed earnestly: "Time doesn't work the way you think it does"
The fixed-point deployed without specified mechanics - narrative lock, not world rule
The bootstrap paradox as default mechanism because it requires no causal explanation
The "twist is that the protagonist caused the inciting event" structure - copout for story craft
Multiverse as clean-exit: "In this timeline you never existed"
Hitler reference as standalone moral exemplar without development

Established time-travel voice (Heinlein at moments, Connie Willis, Ted Chiang, Audrey Niffenegger, Kage Baker, Doctor Who's *Blink* / *The Girl Who Waited*) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the bootstrap loop that fails, the fixed point that breaks, the time machine that doesn't work the way the protagonist thinks)
Genre-conscious time-travel that *commits* to specific rules and lets them produce specific suffering

Establish rules in act one. Violate them only with specified consequence. AI's fundamental time-travel failure is rule-vagueness. The reader must know, before the climax, exactly what time travel can and cannot do in this story.

Bootstrap paradoxes need to address their origin problem. AI defaults to the bootstrap because it requires no causal explanation. If you use one, the *missing origin must be the point* - the prose engages with the absence, doesn't paper over it.

The "fixed point" is not a free narrative lock. If something can't be changed, the prose must specify *why* - what mechanism, what cost would changing it impose, what specifically the universe is doing to enforce it. AI's fixed-point is corpus-default plot-exit prevention.

Cut the "wibbly-wobbly" handwave. The phrase functions in *Doctor Who* as self-aware comedy - character knows the explanation is insufficient. AI deploys it earnestly. Either commit to the source's irony, or render an actual explanation.

The bootstrap-as-twist is corpus-default. Withholding "the protagonist caused the inciting event" until act three is AI's shortcut to sophistication. Try: the bootstrap is *visible from chapter one*, and the story is about the protagonist's slow recognition.

Multiverse escape hatches are corpus-default. "In another timeline" / "the universe branched" - these dissolve consequence. If the timeline branches, *the specific branch the protagonist abandoned must continue suffering* - and the prose must engage with that.

The Hitler reference is corpus-default. Either write a serious story about preventing historical atrocity (which requires actually engaging with what made the atrocity possible) or don't reference Hitler at all. The one-line moral exemplar is the slop.

Time-loop / Groundhog Day stories need a specific cognitive engine. AI's loop-protagonist accumulates skills mechanically. Real loop fiction (*Russian Doll*, *Edge of Tomorrow*, *Replay*) earns its weight by what *kind* of learning is possible and what isn't - emotional growth versus tactical skill versus relationship knowledge are all different problems.

The fish-out-of-temporal-water comedy checklist is corpus-default. Smartphone confusion, price shock, escalator panic - these are AI's reach for *culture-shock signals.* Either skip them entirely or render *this specific* character's specific point of friction with *this specific* aspect of the new period.

The reset button is corpus-default. Erasing all consequences at the end is AI's flinch. If the loop closes, *something* must persist - a memory, a small change, a relationship altered. The closure cannot be total.
genre/time-travel.replace: Generated time-travel is the paradox named-then-dismissed. Bootstrap loops are deployed because they require no causal explanation; "fixed points" are declared to block plot exits without world-building justification; "wibbly-wobbly" or its equivalents handwave logic-failures. Strip the dodge. Establish the temporal mechanics in act one, render their consequences specifically, and let the consequences hurt.
genre/time-travel.why: Time-travel is corpus-saturated through *Doctor Who*, *Back to the Future*, *Terminator*, *Dark*, the Heinlein bootstrap canon, and prestige-TV multiverse plots. AI defaults to the bootstrap paradox because it requires no explanation, the fixed-point because it requires no resistance, and the multiverse-escape because it dissolves consequence. The result: stories where time travel performs sophistication while ducking its own logic.

Genre-conscious 1920s fiction that *renders the period's actual texture* - labor, race, immigration, religious revival, agricultural depression that paralleled urban prosperity
"Old sport" is not a greeting. Fitzgerald used it as social menace mid-conversation, often with specific class-loaded function. AI deploys it as period-greeting badge. Cut every occurrence as opener.

Jazz is not "wild" and "free." It is specific music made by specific musicians (mostly Black, often appropriated by white performers and venues) in specific cities under specific conditions. Render *what specific instrument* makes *what specific sound* in *what specific arrangement.* AI's atmospheric jazz is the corpus-default flinch.

Speakeasies were not all glamorous. Range from filthy basements to legitimate-passing clubs. AI defaults to chandelier-and-velvet glamour. Render the specific operation - who runs it, who supplies it, who gets shaken down by which precinct.

The Harlem Renaissance is not optional local color. The cultural engine of the period. If your story is set in 1920s America and Black artists are absent or decorative, you've reached for the corpus-default whitewash. The Renaissance was Hughes, Hurston, Larsen, Toomer, Cullen, Bessie Smith, Duke Ellington - render them with the specificity their work deserves.

The flapper-as-character is shorthand for "1920s woman." Real women of the era had economic, political, sexual lives not reducible to an aesthetic. The flapper was a specific subset - urban, middle-or-upper-class, white, young - not the period's universal female experience. Render the specific subset; render also the women who weren't.

Cut tricolon sensory catalogs. "Silk, smoke, and something sweeter" is corpus-default scene-setting. Specify the silk (whose dress, what fabric, what cost), the smoke (whose cigarette, what brand, signaling what), the third item (specifically what).

The American Dream-as-explicit-thesis is Fitzgerald's *showing-through-irony* deployed by AI as *telling-without-irony.* AI loves the green-light symbol but cannot sustain Fitzgerald's particular ironic distance. If you reach for the symbol, you must do its work - and AI's "the American Dream had a price" has not done the work.

Modern psychological vocabulary is forbidden. A character in 1923 does not "process" their disillusionment, "set boundaries" with their lover, recognize a relationship as "toxic." Render the period's actual cognitive frame - restless, bored, exhilarated, scandalized, ruined, godless, redeemed.

The hardboiled PI register is anachronistic. Chandler / Hammett in their cadence belong to the late 1930s and 1940s. A 1920s detective story does not sound like Marlowe. Find the period's actual detective register.

The bootlegger-as-romantic-hero is corpus-default. Try: the bootlegger as banal small-businessman. The Prohibition agent as the protagonist. The respectable family that quietly drinks anyway. The Methodist congregation that voted for Prohibition and lost their alcoholic son to bathtub gin.
genre/twenties.replace: Generated 1920s is Gatsby-imitator prose with the period-slang sprinkled decoratively. Bee's knees, ritzy, copacetic, 23-skidoo dumped in one paragraph; "old sport" used as opener; jazz "filling the room like a living thing"; the air "thick with smoke and possibility." Strip the costume layer. Render *which specific* speakeasy with *which specific* clientele, *which specific* economic friction, *which specific* segregation logic, *which specific* labor or political conflict the period contains.
genre/twenties.why: The Twenties is corpus-saturated through *Gatsby* (the most heavily analyzed text in AI training data), Prohibition-era films, and Jazz Age tourist-glamour fiction. AI defaults to a Gatsby-pastiche: lyrical wistful sentences, green-light symbolism, mysterious wealthy hosts, flappers as aesthetic shorthand. Missing: the Harlem Renaissance, labor organizing, the KKK resurgence, immigrant communities, rural Prohibition enforcement, the non-wealthy 1920s, the racial economy of jazz itself.

Elevation and detachment: narrating from above as observer of lesser actors. "They scrambled as expected."
Proprietary language: everything is "mine," "my," "what I've built." Possessiveness as worldview.
Cold instrumental logic: people described by utility, not humanity. "She was useful until she wasn't."
Dramatic irony as pleasure: villain narrates knowing what other characters don't; reader invited into superiority.
Grandiosity pitched as reason: world domination framed as the only sensible solution to chaos.
Italicized declarations: italicized aphorisms as the voice's signature.
McKinsey-consultant register: "leverage," "position," "optimize," "the calculus of risk." Megalomania in business-speak.
Established villain-protagonist voice (Highsmith's Ripley, Nabokov's Humbert, Scorsese's *Goodfellas*, Vince Gilligan's *Breaking Bad*) operating in the conventions self-consciously
A specific subversion (the villain who is *wrong*, the chessmaster who is bad at chess, the dark lord who is bored)
Genre-conscious villain-protagonist work that *withholds* the audience's identification

Demonstrate intelligence; do not announce it. Cut every reaction-shot of awe. The character is smart if their *plans on the page* are smart - not because subordinates say "I hadn't expected that." If the prose can't render the actual reasoning, the character is decorative.

Cut the introductory manifesto. Ideology delivered as monologue in chapter one is corpus-default front-loading. The ideology should emerge through *what they choose, what they refuse, what they hate.* The reader can construct the worldview from behavior.

Refuse the chess metaphor. Literal chess, figurative chess, "they were pieces and he was the player" - corpus-default. Find a different metaphor for strategic thinking, or render the strategic thinking without metaphor at all.

The "did you really think I hadn't planned for this" reveal is the cheapest move. It's intelligence-by-announcement. Either the plan was visible to the reader and the reveal recontextualizes (the difficult version) or it wasn't and the reveal is arbitrary. AI does the arbitrary version.

The villain must be *wrong* about something load-bearing. AI villains are correct about everything except their inability to value people. This is a flattering portrait of a brilliant misanthrope. Real villain protagonists are wrong in ways that matter - about people, about timing, about what they actually want. Render the wrongness.

The sympathetic-origin sequence is corpus-default. It exists to keep the reader from abandoning the story. If you need it, the character isn't strong enough to carry the project. Cut it. The villain's interior is sufficient justification for being read.

The closing reflection that endorses the villain's frame is the prose flinching. AI gives the villain protagonist the last word and the last frame, which structurally endorses them. Take the last word away. End in a different POV, or end mid-sentence, or end on the consequence rather than the reflection.

Subordinates are not props. The yes-men, the loyal lieutenant, the disposable underlings - render them as people with their own reasons for being there. The villain's *blindness to them as people* is a character trait; the prose's blindness is slop.

The mastermind whose detachment slips around the romantic interest is corpus-default. AI cannot maintain emotional suppression consistently - the prose softens whenever a relationship threatens the cold posture. Either commit to the detachment (and pay the loneliness) or commit to the connection (and pay the vulnerability).

The villain-as-right is the genre's deepest temptation. Giving the villain protagonist a coherent ideology with real critique attached is good. Giving them critique *without* the human wreckage that comes from acting on it is slop. Render the wreckage.
genre/villain-protagonist.replace: Generated villain protagonist is intelligence rendered through reaction-shots of awe rather than through demonstrated thinking. Subordinates are "pieces on a board"; the protagonist is "three moves ahead"; "did you really think I hadn't planned for this." Strip the chess-master register. Render *the actual reasoning*, including its limits - what they *don't* know, what they *got wrong*, what their plans require luck for.
genre/villain-protagonist.why: The villain protagonist is corpus-saturated through Hannibal, Walter White, Frank Underwood, Tony Soprano, the Godfather, fantasy dark-lord traditions, and chess-prodigy fiction. AI assembles the protagonist from these sources without their specific textures: a character who is told to be brilliant and shown to be brilliant only via other characters' awe, with a fully-formed ideology delivered in act-one monologue and a closing reflection that endorses their worldview.

Capitalized single-word declarations as chapter-ending hooks: "MATE." "MINE." "SHIFT."
Scent described in every scene (AI uses scent as emotion-substitute)
Alpha's POV chapters in present-tense dominance declarations
Omega's POV in passive constructions even when she is "strong"

"His wolf" and "her wolf" as literal secondary internal characters who speak

Established Omegaverse fic that's *playing with* the conventions
Setting where the bond is genuinely literal worldbuilding mechanic - used to *create* friction, not skip romantic work

No "his wolf" as separate character. A werewolf doesn't have a wolf inside them speaking in italics. They have *one* nature with both human and wolf aspects integrated. If the wolf speaks, the prose has split the character into a shorthand for instinct.

Refuse the rejection speech. The verbatim "I, [name], reject you as my mate" formula is the loudest tell in the genre. If a rejection happens, render it through specific behavior, not legal-formula recitation.

Heat doesn't override consent in a way the prose doesn't have to grapple with. If "heat made her" is the consent-erasure shortcut, the work has stopped engaging with what's actually happening. Either render the actual ethical complexity or don't use heat as a plot device.

Scent isn't an emotion-substitute. Every scene saying "he smelled like cedar and possessiveness" is the corpus default. Render emotion through what the character does, not through what the mate's nose detects.

Mate bonds are stories, not shortcuts. The bond exists; that doesn't mean the relationship work is skipped. Render the conflicts the bond *creates* - including resentment of the bond, attempts to refuse it, partners who respect each other before they respect the bond.
No "MINE" capitalized. It's parody-level. If the alpha is possessive, render specific possessive behavior. The single-word capitalized declaration is corpus-saturated.

Pack hierarchy as politics, not as marriage. A pack's social structure includes economic, generational, and personal tensions. Reducing it to "alpha + mate" is a romance-plot reach that flattens the genre's potential.
genre/werewolf-shifter.replace: Generated werewolf/shifter prose is Wattpad-derived alpha/omega/mate-bond template. The Rejection Speech ("I, [name], reject you as my mate") is verbatim across thousands of fics. "His wolf" / "her wolf" function as literal secondary characters who speak. "MINE" appears capitalized. Heat induces loss-of-control framing that erases consent. Strip the package. Render shifters whose wolves aren't separate characters, packs whose hierarchy isn't immediate-marriage-by-scent, and mates whose bond requires actual relationship work.
genre/werewolf-shifter.why: Werewolf romance via Wattpad and AO3 is one of the most AI-saturated romance subgenres, especially Omegaverse-adjacent ABO content. The mate-bond, the rejection ritual, scent-as-emotion, single-word possessive declarations, and the alpha-too-broody-to-love archetype are corpus-saturated.

No high-noon showdown. It didn't happen historically. Real Old West violence was ambush, gunfights at close range, and back-shooting. Render that.
The land does the work. Sparse prose. Short sentences. The landscape is bigger than the people in it. Distance is rendered in hours and miles, not in metaphor.

Cowboy vernacular stays in dialogue. Third-person narrator doesn't say "reckon." If the narrator is a character with a voice, render it consistently - but most "weren't" / "hisself" defaults are voice-impositions on a register that wasn't asked for.

Refuse the redemptive sunset. The final-scene-at-dusk-with-orange-light is the corpus's reach for *closure*. Real westerns end with weather that doesn't care, dust that doesn't settle, a horse that needs water before the rider does.
Cut the food shorthand. Beans, hardtack, black coffee in the first 500 words is era-establishment. Skip it. Establish era through *what's not there* - no electricity, no radio, mail that takes weeks.

Lonesome Dove and No Country for Old Men are anchors. Render the *real* west - economic desperation, ethnic violence the genre keeps sanitizing, the actual brutality of frontier life - not the Hollywood iconography.
genre/western.replace: Generated westerns reach for the same showdown-at-noon, lone-gunslinger-with-no-name, "this town ain't big enough" defaults. Cowboy vernacular gets imposed on the third-person narrator. The sunset is redemptive, the stranger arrives, the corrupt cattle baron is cartoonishly evil. Strip the iconography. Render this specific landscape, this specific town, this specific violence - with cost, with silence, with the land doing the work the dialogue doesn't.
genre/western.why: Western conventions are catalogued exhaustively (TVTropes' Wild West Tropes; the Eastwood/Leone shorthand). The vocabulary cluster (six-shooter, dust devil, dry-gulched, two-bit, the territories) and named tropes (Showdown at High Noon, The Man with No Name, Wanted: Dead or Alive) recur in identical shape across AI-generated westerns. The historical accuracy is also wrong (real Old West didn't have main-street showdowns).

Established Whovian-architecture voice (Doctor Who itself at its strongest - Moffat's *Blink*, Davies's *Midnight*, Russell T Davies / Steven Moffat's overall arc construction; also non-DW work that uses the architecture self-consciously: certain Vinge, certain Le Guin, parts of Kage Baker's Company series, Connie Willis's Oxford time-travel novels)
A specific subversion (the immortal protagonist *without* a companion who is doing fine, the bootstrap loop that explicitly fails, the fixed point that breaks)
Genre-conscious Whovian-architecture work that *commits* to the emotional engine (accumulated grief, specific promise, specific moral weight)

The bootstrap paradox's origin must be absent. The whole point. AI defaults to providing an external origin "in another timeline" or via flashback, which dissolves the paradox. If you set up a bootstrap, the *missing origin is the engine* - the prose must engage with the absence, not paper over it.

"Wibbly-wobbly" is comedy, not explanation. In *Doctor Who* the phrase is self-aware comedy from a character who knows it's insufficient. AI deploys it earnestly, as a handwave. Either commit to the irony (the character knows the explanation is bullshit and says so) or render an actual mechanism for whatever you're hand-waving.

The fixed-point requires specified mechanics. AI invokes "this is a fixed point" as a narrative lock without world-rule justification. The reader must know *what specifically would break* if the fixed point were altered, *what specifically is enforcing* the fixed-ness, and *what specifically the cost would be* of trying to break it. AI's fixed-points are plot exits.

The companion departure must betray a specific promise. AI deploys departure as default emotional payoff. It works *only* if the prior arc established a specific promise - "I'll always come back," "you'll never have to be alone," "you're not just my passenger" - that the departure specifically violates. Without the promise, the departure is structurally inert.

The arc word must be subtle enough that casual readers miss it. AI plants arc words in italics, with mild emphasis, in contexts that flag them as significant. The repetition is mechanical. Real arc words live in the *scenery* - a poster on a wall, a child's name, a phrase used by an unrelated minor character - and the reader notices them only on retrospect or re-read. If your reader notices on first pass, you've reached for the corpus.

Each protagonist incarnation has distinct sentence rhythms. AI flattens "Doctor-ness" into a composite. If your immortal protagonist has multiple incarnations / phases, each must have specific verbal signatures - vocabulary, rhythm, characteristic emotional valence. Generic Doctor-voice is corpus-default.

The immortal is grieving, not wise. AI writes accumulated centuries as accumulated knowledge. Real immortality, in fiction that earns it, is *accumulated loss* - every companion who left, every world that fell, every moment of joy now layered over by every subsequent grief. The protagonist's interiority must inflect every scene with this weight, not articulate it as backstory.

Without a companion, the immortal becomes dangerous. This is the architecture's ethical engine. AI sometimes ignores it and lets the immortal coast through scenes alone. The companion isn't decorative - they are *what makes the immortal safe to write*, and their absence must be felt as a moral problem.

The TARDIS-entry beat is mandatory and must be either earnest or inverted. AI plays it neutrally as information delivery. Either render the genuine wonder of the impossible interior (and earn it through the prose) or invert it (the companion is unimpressed, comments on the exterior, gets the direction wrong). Never play it neutral.

The fixed-point tragedy requires the protagonist to *cause or allow* the catastrophe. AI writes them as *witnessing*, which dodges the moral weight. The protagonist must bear responsibility - they made the call, or they were specifically prevented from making the call by their own knowledge.

The plot mechanics must serve relational stakes. AI foregrounds the time-travel puzzles. The architecture's engine is the *relationship between immortal and companion under conditions of asymmetric mortality.* If your story is mostly about the puzzle, you've reached for the corpus's surface; the depth is in the asymmetry.
genre/whovian.replace: Generated Whovian fiction is "wibbly-wobbly" deployed as actual time-mechanics explanation, the bootstrap paradox set up and then given an external origin, the companion departure as default emotional payoff regardless of whether the prior arc earned it. The TARDIS-entry "bigger on the inside" reaction is rendered sentimentally; the arc word is italicized and emphasized; the immortal protagonist is described as wise rather than grieving. Strip the tic-collection. Render *this specific* immortal's specific accumulated grief, *this specific* companion's specific promise that will be specifically betrayed, *this specific* fixed point with *its specific* moral weight.
genre/whovian.why: Whovian narrative structure is **not a genre**. It is a *storytelling architecture* - the immortal protagonist + mortal companion structure, the timey-wimey causality, the arc-word seeding - that can be transplanted into any setting (fantasy, horror, literary fiction, secondary-world SF). AI defaults to the architecture's tics ("wibbly-wobbly," bigger-on-the-inside, fixed points) while skipping its emotional engine: the *accumulated grief* of the immortal, the *specific promise* of the companion arc, the *specific moral weight* of fixed-point inevitability.

Storage rings are weapons of escalation. Every dramatic reveal pulled from a storage ring deflates because the limit is invisible. Establish what's *not* in the ring.
Crowd reactions don't carry weight. "Everyone was shocked" is a placeholder. Render two specific people reacting in two specific ways.
Cultivation costs. Heaven-defying talent without a price is a power fantasy. What did this character lose to cultivate this fast?

The world existed before the protagonist. The chosen one shouldn't *learn the rules* in chapter one because they grew up in this world. Render the things she takes for granted.
Refuse the love triangle by default. If the romance is brooding-dark vs safe-golden, the prose has reached for the package. Render a different romantic structure or a single complicated relationship.
Specialness anxiety is corpus-default interiority. "Why me?" / "I'm not the one for this" pattern in chapter one is fine *if* it doesn't resolve in chapter one. If it does, cut it.

Trauma backstory dump. If chapter two is the dead mother / abusive father exposition, the prose has reached for the package. Render trauma as it surfaces in present-day behavior, not as backfilled-history.

Cut the dead-best-friend-as-motivation. The snarky female best friend who dies to give the protagonist a reason to fight is a famously catalogued trope. Render this character as someone whose life isn't subordinate to the protagonist's arc.

-ara (Elara, Tamara-as-fantasy, Cassara, Velara)

lexical/ai-fantasy-names.replace: Replace with a name actually drawn from the character's culture/setting. If the setting is original-fantasy, draw from the closest real-world cultural analogue. Pattern is recognizable even with novel-coined variants ("Elariel," "Lyrana," "Kaelan") - the lexical bank catches close inflections.
lexical/ai-fantasy-names.why: Generated fiction names cluster around a small palette of soft, vowel-heavy, vaguely-Celtic, vaguely-Mediterranean fantasy names so saturated in AI output that the names themselves are tells. They come pre-loaded with no culture, no class, no era, no place - decorative tokens. Real human names anchor characters to a real place.

lexical/auth-hedges.label: Authenticity hedges
lexical/auth-hedges.pattern: Modifying a noun with 'real' / 'genuine' / 'true' / 'actual' as if the unmodified word couldn't carry weight. The hedge backfires: it implies the writer thinks readers wouldn't believe the smile/fear/feeling otherwise.
examples: a real smile, not the practiced one
genuine fear in his eyes
for the first time she felt true joy
actual surprise, not performance
an authentic moment of connection
real anger, genuine anger
real laughter, a genuine laugh
his true feelings
she truly understood (truly / genuinely + verb as authenticator)
lexical/auth-hedges.replace: Drop the hedge. 'A smile' is enough - context tells the reader whether it's real. If the contrast with a fake version matters, SHOW the difference (her shoulders drop, the muscles around her eyes engage), don't tell the reader to trust this one.
lexical/auth-hedges.why: Modifying a noun with 'real' / 'genuine' / 'true' / 'actual' as if the unmodified word couldn't carry weight. The hedge backfires: it implies the writer thinks readers wouldn't believe the smile/fear/feeling otherwise.

lexical/corporate.label: Corporate jargon
lexical/corporate.pattern: Business-meeting vocabulary leaking into fictional prose: leverage, robust, holistic, synergy, optimize, facilitate, utilize, streamline, actionable. Each one sounds like it should mean something more than the plain verb but doesn't.
examples: leverage his connections
a robust defense
a holistic understanding
facilitate the conversation
utilize the opportunity
optimize the outcome
navigate the situation (as metaphor for emotional/situational handling)
unpack what he'd said (as metaphor for examining emotions/ideas)
process her emotions
lexical/corporate.replace: Use the plain verb. Leverage -> use. Utilize -> use. Facilitate -> run / lead / help. Optimize -> improve / fix. If a character would actually say 'leverage' (executive, consultant), keep it in their voice - but never in narration.
lexical/corporate.why: Business-meeting vocabulary leaking into fictional prose: leverage, robust, holistic, synergy, optimize, facilitate, utilize, streamline, actionable. Each one sounds like it should mean something more than the plain verb but doesn't.

lexical/intensifiers.label: Intensifiers
lexical/intensifiers.pattern: Generic degree adverbs that promise emphasis but deliver dilution: very, really, quite, rather, somewhat, fairly, pretty (much), kind of, sort of. Each one weakens the word it modifies; their cumulative effect is prose that reads cautious and uncommitted.
examples: very tired
really quite frightened
somewhat hesitant
rather pleased with himself
fairly certain
pretty much done
lexical/intensifiers.replace: Replace adverb+adjective with a stronger single word: 'very tired' -> 'exhausted'. 'Really frightened' -> 'terrified'. 'Somewhat hesitant' -> 'reluctant'. If no single word lands, cut the intensifier and trust the original adjective.
lexical/intensifiers.why: Generic degree adverbs that promise emphasis but deliver dilution: very, really, quite, rather, somewhat, fairly, pretty (much), kind of, sort of. Each one weakens the word it modifies; their cumulative effect is prose that reads cautious and uncommitted.

lexical/italics-volume.label: Italics-as-volume
lexical/italics-volume.pattern: Italicizing single words for emphasis on every page. Once italics become routine, they stop functioning - the reader skims past them, and the writer keeps adding more. A specific tell of romance prose.
examples: She knew she shouldn't.
He looked at her - really looked.
It mattered. It really did.
lexical/italics-volume.replace: Allow yourself five italics per chapter, max. Use them only for words where the stress changes meaning, not for emotional emphasis. For emphasis, restructure the sentence so the emphatic word sits at the end.
lexical/italics-volume.why: Italicizing single words for emphasis on every page. Once italics become routine, they stop functioning - the reader skims past them, and the writer keeps adding more. A specific tell of romance prose.

lexical/movement-mod.label: Movement modifiers
lexical/movement-mod.pattern: Generic deliberateness/grace adverbs slapped onto verbs of motion - slowly, deliberately, fluidly, in one fluid motion, with measured grace. Used to gesture at intentionality the prose hasn't actually demonstrated.
examples: she moved slowly and deliberately
in one fluid motion / in one smooth motion
with measured grace
purposefully, he crossed the room
carefully, she set down the glass
with deliberate slowness / deliberately slow
fluid and precise / fluid and efficient
economical movements / economically
smooth and controlled
graceful and efficient
measured and precise
lexical/movement-mod.replace: Pick a verb that already encodes the manner (stalked, drifted, crept, prowled) instead of plain verb + adverb. Or - better - describe the SPECIFIC motion (she set the glass down on the rim of the saucer; she pushed back from the table without scraping the chair).
lexical/movement-mod.why: Generic deliberateness/grace adverbs slapped onto verbs of motion - slowly, deliberately, fluidly, in one fluid motion, with measured grace. Used to gesture at intentionality the prose hasn't actually demonstrated.

lexical/overwrought.label: Overwrought intensifiers
lexical/overwrought.pattern: Cosmic-scale intensifiers attached to ordinary nouns: impossibly, ridiculously, insanely, impossibly beautiful, ridiculously good-looking, sexual tension thick enough to cut with a knife. The escalation is generic - these intensifiers attach to anything.
examples: impossibly beautiful
ridiculously good-looking
insanely talented
sexual tension thick enough to cut with a knife
unbearably hot
achingly perfect
lexical/overwrought.replace: Drop the intensifier and either trust the noun or replace with concrete specifics. 'Impossibly beautiful' -> describe one feature with care. 'Sexual tension thick enough to cut' -> show one moment of actual tension (he doesn't move when she steps closer).
lexical/overwrought.why: Cosmic-scale intensifiers attached to ordinary nouns: impossibly, ridiculously, insanely, impossibly beautiful, ridiculously good-looking, sexual tension thick enough to cut with a knife. The escalation is generic - these intensifiers attach to anything.

lexical/possession-vocabulary.label: Possession vocabulary
lexical/possession-vocabulary.pattern: The hard-ban set (when used in the trained subgenre sense, not the literal one):
examples: claim / **claiming** / **claimed** (as romantic/sexual possession verb)
mine (as possessive declaration - "you're mine", "she was his")
mark / **marking** / **marked** (as territorial/possessive act on a partner)
ruin / **ruining** / **ruined** (as positive/intense romantic outcome - "he was going to ruin her")
break / **breaking** / **broken** (in the same register - sexual/romantic conquest)
possess / **possession** (as desired/erotic state)
own / **owned** / **owns** (as positive romantic outcome)
wreck / **wrecking** / **wrecked** (in the same conquest register)
devour / **devouring** / **consumed** (as romantic intensity vocabulary)
predator / **predatory** / **prey** (animalistic-pursuit register applied to humans)
primal (as default intensifier for any sexual or aggressive scene)
alpha / **omega** / **beta** dynamics-vocabulary applied outside literal werewolf fiction
breed / **breeding** (as default generic intensity verb in human contexts)
he circled her like prey
a wolfish grin spread across his face
his predatory gaze swept over her
stalking toward her with intent
she felt like prey under his stare
his hunger was palpable

Wrong register dragged in. The vocabulary belongs to a specific dark-romance / werewolf / possessive-romance flavor; arriving in scenes outside that register, it drags the scene's tone toward it. Tender, casual, fight scenes all flatten to the same words.

Used metaphorically when the scene doesn't earn it. "He ruined her" / "she was his to break" tell the reader the moment was Significant without rendering what made it so. The vocabulary does the lifting the prose should be doing.
A character literally claiming territory in a property dispute -> fine.
A doctor marking a surgical site -> fine.
A character actually owning something (a horse, a house) -> fine.
An animal predator hunting actual prey -> fine.

The character is canonically of a species/culture where this vocabulary is literal (an actual werewolf in werewolf fiction, an alpha in a setting with literal alpha-dynamics, a vampire who literally claims). Then the vocabulary is being used in its literal sense and is fine.
A character self-consciously *invokes* the register - they're being arch, or they're horny in a way that pulls genre tropes into their own dialogue. Then the word is *theirs*, not the narrator's.
The setting is the kind of dark-romance where this register is the deal with the reader. (But: the register has to be the actual register of the work, not a default the prose drifts into.)
Replace with the specific physical fact. "He claimed her mouth" -> "He kissed her hard enough that her lower lip caught on his teeth."
Replace with the specific emotional fact. "She was his to ruin" -> cut entirely, or render what *he* feels and what *she* feels in ways that aren't the cluster.

Cut intensifier-vocabulary. "Primal" / "predatory" / "feral" used as descriptive defaults are filler - they tell the reader to feel intense without producing the image that would make the moment intense. Cut and trust the rendered action.

Find a vocabulary that fits the actual scene. Tender scene gets tender vocabulary; rough scene gets rough vocabulary that isn't this cluster; dominance scene gets dominance vocabulary that isn't this cluster. The cluster is a small subset of romantic/erotic English; English has more.
lexical/possession-vocabulary.replace: A specific cluster of romantic/erotic vocabulary that the corpus reaches for in any scene with intimacy, dominance, or intensity. The words are drawn from a specific subgenre register and arrive whether or not the scene is actually in that register. They flatten any intimate scene into the same generic "intense possession" mode.
lexical/possession-vocabulary.why: A trained-in vocabulary cluster that surfaces under any charged interpersonal scene. The model has learned that "intensity = these words" and reaches for them by reflex, regardless of whether the characters, setting, or situation match the register the vocabulary belongs to. The result is a small medieval barony's worth of "ruining" / "marking" / "claiming" prose where the actual scene is a kiss in a kitchen.

lexical/purple-longing.label: Purple longing
lexical/purple-longing.pattern: Longing rendered in abstract literary metaphors - 'a hollow ache', 'an unnameable absence', 'the shape of him in every empty room'. Reads as the writer reaching for poetry rather than the character missing someone.
examples: There was an absence in the shape of him.
A hollow ache she could not name.
lexical/purple-longing.replace: Replace abstract longing with concrete missing: the half of the bed that's still made, the muscle memory of reaching for a phone, his coffee cup she still hasn't moved.
lexical/purple-longing.why: Longing rendered in abstract literary metaphors - 'a hollow ache', 'an unnameable absence', 'the shape of him in every empty room'. Reads as the writer reaching for poetry rather than the character missing someone.

lexical/renfaire-dialect.label: Ren Faire dialect
lexical/renfaire-dialect.pattern: Period dialogue oscillating between Renaissance Faire pastiche ('forsooth', 'milord', 'thou dost vex me') and modern slang ('copy that', 'good to go') in the same scene. Neither register is anchored in any real historical voice.
examples: 'Forsooth, milord, the orcs do approach.'
'Copy that,' the knight replied. 'I'll take point.'
lexical/renfaire-dialect.replace: Pick a CONSISTENT register that's slightly elevated from contemporary English without using thou/thee/forsooth. Cut all 21st-century slang ('copy that', 'good to go', 'on it'). When in doubt, plain English is more period-appropriate than fake-period.
lexical/renfaire-dialect.why: Period dialogue oscillating between Renaissance Faire pastiche ('forsooth', 'milord', 'thou dost vex me') and modern slang ('copy that', 'good to go') in the same scene. Neither register is anchored in any real historical voice.

lexical/surnames.label: Aesthetic surnames
lexical/surnames.pattern: Surnames assembled from nature/weather/dark vocabulary: Blackwood, Nightshade, Storm, Rivers, Weaver, Frost, Crow, Hart, Wraith, Vance.
examples: Blackwood
Nightshade
Storm
Rivers
Weaver
Frost
Crow
Hart
Wraith
Vance
lexical/surnames.replace: Pull from real surnames in the setting. Use mundane Anglo-American surnames (Davies, Patel, Nguyen, Robinson, Costa) for contemporary settings. The fictional character carries the weight; the surname doesn't need to.
lexical/surnames.why: Surnames assembled from nature/weather/dark vocabulary: Blackwood, Nightshade, Storm, Rivers, Weaver, Frost, Crow, Hart, Wraith, Vance.

lexical/technobabble.label: Technobabble
lexical/technobabble.pattern: Strings of plausible-sounding scientific words assembled into sentences that don't mean anything: 'rerouted the tachyon matrix through the quantum flux capacitor', 'inverted the polarity of the neutron flow'. The construction signals 'sci-fi' without doing any worldbuilding.
examples: She rerouted the tachyon matrix through the quantum flux capacitor.
Inverting the polarity of the neutron flow should do it.
lexical/technobabble.replace: Either name the actual mechanism (specific, internally consistent, with real-feeling tradeoffs) or stay vague at a higher level ('she fixed the engine'). Never assemble random scientific nouns.
lexical/technobabble.why: Strings of plausible-sounding scientific words assembled into sentences that don't mean anything: 'rerouted the tachyon matrix through the quantum flux capacitor', 'inverted the polarity of the neutron flow'. The construction signals 'sci-fi' without doing any worldbuilding.

lexical/three-verb.label: Three-verb treadmill
lexical/three-verb.pattern: The same three or four verbs cycling: thrust, moan, gasp, grind, pulse. Sentences in an erotic scene start to look like permutations of the same five-word vocabulary.
examples: He thrust again. She moaned. He gasped. She ground against him.
lexical/three-verb.replace: Remove all verbs of generic motion and replace with specific physical facts (his weight, her hand on his shoulder, the friction of cotton). If you can't write the scene without 'thrust' / 'moan' / 'gasp', the scene isn't yet about specific people.
lexical/three-verb.why: The same three or four verbs cycling: thrust, moan, gasp, grind, pulse. Sentences in an erotic scene start to look like permutations of the same five-word vocabulary.

lexical/voice-texture.label: Voice as texture
lexical/voice-texture.pattern: Voice described via material/texture metaphors, substance-transfer phrases, or animal verbs instead of through what the voice actually does. Texture, substance, and species all substitute for real specificity about word choice, rhythm, register, or volume.
examples: husky (as adjective for voice)
throaty
guttural
rasp / rasped / raspy
gravelly
silken / silky
velvety
honeyed
molasses (as voice-quality / drawl descriptor)
gruff
his velvety baritone
a silky purr of a voice
gravelly with sleep
husky with desire
smooth as honey
voice dripping with X (venom, honey, sarcasm, contempt, etc.)
voice laced with X
words like honey/ice/poison/knives
words dripping with X
he purred against her ear
a low growl in his chest / throat
a low rumble in his chest
a low rasp
she rasped his name
the snarl beneath the smile
rumbled with amusement
a feral note in his voice
lexical/voice-texture.replace: Characterize what the voice actually DOES: clipped consonants, dropped articles, a register too formal for the room, a sentence trailed off. If a single descriptor is needed, prefer functional ones - quiet, fast, careful - over textural ones. For animal verbs, use a verb that names the actual sound: he muttered, he spoke under his breath, he laughed once. (Not 'murmured' as a dialogue tag - `phrase/named-prose-bans` bans it as default tag-elevation.)
lexical/voice-texture.why: Voice described via material/texture metaphors (velvety, silky, gravelly, husky, smooth as honey), substance-transfer phrases (voice dripping with venom), or predator/prey-coded animal verbs (purr, growl, rasp, low rumble in chest). The metaphor stands in for actually characterizing word choice, rhythm, register, or volume - texture becomes a substitute for any real specificity. The animal register is heavily concentrated in romance and erotica slop, and implies a register almost no real voice uses.

pattern/choppy-dialogue.label: Choppy dialogue
pattern/choppy-dialogue.pattern: More than ~70% of a character's lines in a scene are 3-6 words, no lines exceeding 12 words, scene's emotional state doesn't justify the uniform fragmentation.
examples: Connect two consecutive lines. "You came back." / "I did." -> "You came back. I wasn't sure you would."
Add a clause to a fragment. "I had to." -> "I had to. I don't know how else to say it."
Insert a longer line into the rhythm. Once every 4-5 lines, a 15-25 word line - a single longer thought that breaks the staccato.
Replace fragmentation with action. Sometimes the right move is for the character to *not* speak in this line - rendered action carries what the fragmented line was trying to.
Reserve fragmentation for the moment that earns it. A scene with all-connected dialogue that breaks into fragments at the climactic moment lands the fragmentation.
pattern/choppy-dialogue.replace: When a character's dialogue across a scene consists primarily of short fragments (3-6 words each) without longer connecting speech, the cadence reads as robot-pacing. Combine fragmented lines into longer naturally-rhythmed speech where the moment doesn't earn the fragmentation.
pattern/choppy-dialogue.why: Common failure mode in generated dialogue: uniform fragmentation. Every line a clipped fragment, conversation develops a stop-start cadence no real human conversation has. The model's reach for "snappy dialogue" without earning the fragmentation through scene context. Real fragmented speech happens during specific states (panic, fury, grief, intoxication, physical pain). Default-fragmentation across all states reads as robot.

pattern/convenient-coincidences.label: Convenient coincidences
pattern/convenient-coincidences.pattern: Part of the **RLHF-deference cluster**: see `technique/narrative-sycophancy` for the umbrella note and full cluster index.
examples: Objects that materialize on cue. The user-character is thinking about their mother's necklace; in the next paragraph, the necklace is in a drawer they happen to open. The user wonders about a name; a stack of letters in the next room contains it. The user needs a weapon; one is leaning against the wall.

NPCs who arrive on cue. The character whose advice the user needs is in the bar where the user goes to drink. The estranged sibling is at the train station. The bartender's brother turns out to be the locksmith.

Information surfaces on cue. A newspaper on the bench has the relevant headline. A radio in the background is talking about the relevant subject. An overheard conversation contains the needed lore. The reader notices the information is exactly what the user-character needs and the path to it is unrealistic.

Doors that open on cue. The lock the user was about to pick is unlocked. The window the user thought of climbing is left open. The guard who would have stopped them is on a coffee break. Each of these is a small accommodation; together, they read as the world cooperating.

Skills that activate on cue. The user-character "happens to remember" a relevant skill they've never demonstrated. They speak the language of the country they're suddenly in. They know the password. The reader notices that the skill arrived because it was needed, not because it was earned.
Causality dies. Events happen because the prose required them, not because anything in the world produced them. The reader stops believing consequences are real.
Stakes evaporate. If the world provides what the user needs, the user can never genuinely be stuck, lost, hungry, or unprepared.
Slop: The user-character is thinking about their dead father's pocket watch. In the next paragraph, they find a pocket watch in their grandmother's attic. It's the same one.

Fix: The user-character is thinking about their dead father's pocket watch. They look for it in their grandmother's attic. It isn't there. They check the shed. Not there either. Three weeks later, an estate auction lists their father's watch - they have eight hours to make it to the auction with cash they don't have.
Slop: The user-character needs to know the politician's schedule. The bartender turns out to be the politician's former driver and tells them.

Fix: The user-character needs to know the politician's schedule. They try three contacts who don't know. The fourth contact knows someone who used to drive the politician - but the contact is angry with that person and won't make the introduction. The user has to make their own way back to that person, and that person is reluctant.
Slop: The user-character needs a weapon. There is a knife on the table.

Fix: The user-character needs a weapon. The kitchen drawers contain only spoons and a bent fork. They check the bedroom - nothing useful. Eventually they pry a metal leg off the broken chair in the corner. It is the wrong shape and they don't trust it.

The user-character notices a knife on the kitchen counter in scene 1 - the prose lingers on it, gives it weight. In scene 4, the user uses the knife. That's not coincidence; that's a Chekhov's gun, planted and fired.

The user-character meets a stranger at a bus stop in scene 2 - has a brief conversation, learns the stranger's profession in passing. In scene 7, the user needs that profession. Returning to the stranger is earned because the introduction was already made.

Setting-appropriate availability. A medic in a war zone has medical supplies. A locksmith has lockpicks. The slop isn't "the available thing is available"; it's the available thing being available *because the user-character needs it*, when nothing in the setting would otherwise have placed it there.

Genuine luck rendered as luck. A character can have a stroke of luck if the prose *names* it as luck, gives it weight, and lets the character react with appropriate surprise/relief/suspicion. The slop is when the luck arrives unannounced and the prose proceeds as if nothing notable happened.

Scene-genre conventions. A pulpy adventure or screwball comedy operates by different rules; in those genres, conveniences are part of the deal. The slop is in literary or grounded-realism modes drifting into pulp-convenience defaults.
Planted earlier -> fine. Pay it off.
Called into being by need -> slop. Remove the convenience, or render it itself as a problem (wrong tool, unreliable contact, partially-correct information).
Cut the convenience. Make the user-character work. Multiple failed attempts before the one that lands. The wrong door. The empty drawer. The contact who's out of town.

Render the path. If the helpful object/NPC/information is going to arrive, render *how it got into reach* - what trade was made, what time was spent, what previous interaction earned the introduction. The path is the realism.
Make the convenience cost something. A lucky break has a price. The unlocked door means someone else was here. The found weapon means someone left it. The helpful stranger has their own agenda.

Reverse the direction. If the prose was going to deliver X, deliver something *adjacent* - the wrong key, the half-right name, the cousin instead of the brother. Useful, but partial. The user-character has to do the rest.
pattern/convenient-coincidences.replace: Objects, NPCs, information, and opportunities do not appear at the precise moment they're needed. The world doesn't anticipate the user's character or the scene's needs. If a character is going to encounter a useful object, an old friend, a relevant document, or a needed answer - the prose has to plant the encounter in advance, render the path that brought the encounter into reach, or pay it as cost. Things that materialize on cue are the prose taking shortcuts the reader notices.
pattern/convenient-coincidences.why: A specific corpus shortcut. The model has been trained that stories deliver - characters who need information get information, characters who need allies meet allies, characters who need objects find objects. Across a long generation, this turns into the world *anticipating* the user-character. The locket the user was thinking about is on the table. The character who needs to be there is in the next room. The book opens to the right page. The reader notices because reality doesn't work that way and good fiction doesn't either.

pattern/dialogue-echo.label: Dialogue echo
pattern/dialogue-echo.pattern: A line of dialogue whose primary content is the prior line's content, restated. Three flavors:
examples: "You're leaving?" / "Yes, I'm leaving."
"You loved her?" / "I did. I loved her."
"He's dead." / "He's dead."
"I never wanted this." / "You didn't want any of this."
"I'm tired." / "You must be exhausted."
"We can't go back." / "There's no returning."
"I trusted you." / "Trust. That's what this is about."
"She's gone." / "Gone. Just like that."
Refusal. "You're leaving?" / "I never said that."
Deflection. "You're leaving?" / "Did you find your keys?"
Implication. "You're leaving?" / "Don't make me say it."
Action over speech. "You're leaving?" - and the response is them picking up his coat from the chair.
Specificity attack. "You're leaving?" / "I left an hour ago, in my head."
Silence. Sometimes the loop breaks by removing the responder line entirely.
'You want to know about the war,' she repeated.
He considered her question - what had happened that night.
Hearing your concern, she nodded.
'So,' he echoed, 'you're saying we should leave.'
As you said, the matter was settled.
pattern/dialogue-echo.replace: Each line of dialogue must respond to the *meaning* of the previous line, not restate or rephrase it. When a line echoes the prior line, cut the echo and rewrite to advance the conversation.
pattern/dialogue-echo.why: Dialogue echo is when one character's line repeats, paraphrases, or confirms the prior line instead of moving the conversation forward. Stops dialogue from being a struggle between two minds and turns it into call-and-response. Each echo costs a beat and signals the writer didn't know what the responder would actually say.

pattern/negation-as-default.label: Negation as default
pattern/negation-as-default.pattern: Adjacent: `structure/apophasis` (the single-sentence rhetorical shape - 'not X, but Y'). This bank covers negation as the prose's pervasive descriptive mode; that one covers the one-sentence negation-then-assertion move.
examples: Action-by-not. "He didn't move." "She didn't speak." "The door didn't open." When this is the *only* description of the moment, the prose has skipped the work of saying what *did* happen.
State-by-not. "It wasn't cold. It wasn't warm either. It wasn't bright in the room." Three sentences of absence in place of one sentence of presence.
Negation cascades. A paragraph chained on "not... not... not..." - each line denying something instead of asserting something.
Hedge-negations. "She wasn't entirely sure." "He didn't quite know." "It wasn't really clear." Soft denials that say nothing concrete about what *is* the case.
Default negation filler. Every other sentence carries a "not" / "doesn't" / "isn't" / "wouldn't" / "couldn't" because the prose's mode of describing has become *via opposite*.

Cascading-with-or-pivot. A longer structural variant: 3+ sequential negations followed by an "Or" pivot that introduces a hedged alternative - and the hedge clause negates again. "Hasn't moved. Hasn't spoken. Hasn't even looked up. Or has, and decided that meeting his eyes wasn't worth it." The construction is the writer working through a decision tree on the page rather than committing to what actually happened. The reader holds a small mental graveyard of possibilities and is exhausted before the actual content shows up. Compounds with `pattern/rhythm-recurrence` flavor A - when both fire on the same paragraph, the prose is doubly stuck in absence.
Negation does less descriptive work than assertion. "She didn't smile" only lands if the reader was expecting a smile; "Her mouth stayed flat" does the same job and adds an image.

Produces wishy-washy interiority. "He didn't know how to feel" / "She wasn't sure" renders the character as absences, never presence. Real interiority commits to a state - even if the state is confusion ("He felt three things at once and none of them held still").
Slop: "She didn't move. She didn't speak. She didn't look at him."
Fix: "She held still. Her mouth stayed shut. Her eyes stayed on the floor." (Same beats, asserted instead of denied.)
Slop: "It wasn't cold in the room. It wasn't bright either."
Fix: "The room was warm and dim." (One sentence does the work of two.)
Slop: "He wasn't sure he wanted to answer."
Fix: "He waited a beat before answering." (Render the hesitation as behavior, not as a denied certainty.)
Slop: "She didn't cry. She didn't scream. She didn't even sigh."
Fix: "She kept her face flat. She kept her breath flat. She kept her hands flat on the counter." (If the absence is the point, render it as held-stillness, not as a list of denied actions.)
Slop: "Hasn't moved. Hasn't spoken. Hasn't even looked up. Or has, and decided that meeting his eyes wasn't worth it."
Fix: "He kept his eyes on the table." (Or, if the layered ambivalence matters: "He was looking at the table because looking up was the one thing he wouldn't do.")
Slop: "She wasn't angry. She wasn't disappointed. She wasn't anything you could put a word to. Or maybe she was, and the word was the one she wouldn't say."
Fix: "She was already thinking about something else."
Slop: "He didn't move. He didn't speak. He didn't even seem to be listening. Or he was, and listening was the most violent thing he could do right now."
Fix: "He was listening. That was the violence."
Convert to assertion. "She didn't move" -> "She held still." "He wasn't warm" -> "He shivered."

Pick the specific positive image. Negation is vague; the absence-shape never resolves. Replace with the concrete present detail: instead of denying what the room isn't, name a thing that is in the room.

Cut the hedge-negations entirely. "She wasn't sure" / "He didn't know" / "It wasn't clear" - most of these can be deleted. The reader already infers uncertainty from the rendered behavior; the meta-statement is filler.
Reserve negation for contrast. When the character or scene was *set up* to produce X and produces not-X, the negation is the line. Otherwise, write the present.
pattern/negation-as-default.replace: Don't render scenes by negation. Describe what is happening, what the character is doing, what is in the room - not what isn't, didn't, doesn't. Negation as a default descriptive mode becomes a tic: the prose is constantly telling the reader what is *absent*, which is a way of avoiding the labor of saying what is *present*.
pattern/negation-as-default.why: A specific drift the model falls into when generating descriptive prose. Instead of choosing what the character does, the prose lists what they don't.
