Instead of rendering the room, the prose enumerates absences. Negation-by-emphasis exists in real prose for contrast (a single deliberate "she didn't smile" lands hard against expected smiles) - but as a default mode it's filler. The negation does no descriptive work; it gestures at a blank where description should be.

pattern/redescription-of-established.label: Redescription of established
pattern/redescription-of-established.pattern: The rewriter scans the current response against the prior 3-5 turns for re-rendered material across **four** axes:
examples: A named character's hair (color, length, style)
A named character's eyes (color, shape)
A named character's body (height, build, etc.)
A named character's clothing (already-established outfit re-described)
A setting's furniture, layout, lighting, sensory anchors already established
A repeated facial-feature description ("his sharp jaw" three turns in a row when the jaw hasn't changed)
A repeated voice descriptor (low, gravelly, soft) when the voice hasn't changed

The same physical tic at the same emotional beat across turns (he tilts his head when uncertain; she tucks hair behind her ear when nervous; he runs a hand through his hair when stressed). One instance fine; recurring use turns it into a tag.
Repeated stage business - a character always handling the same object (lighter, glass, pen) at the same beat-shape.
Same sentence skeleton recurring across responses ("The X was Y. Y enough that Z.")
Same paragraph-shape recurring (3 sentences, short-long-short, every turn)
Same opener-shape recurring across turns (every turn opens with weather, every turn opens with dialogue)
Replacing "clenched" with "tightened" in the next turn isn't a fix - the gesture is still there.
Replacing "shadowed" with "darkened" isn't fresh language; it's the same image.
Re-establishing after absence. A character off-stage for 10+ turns can be lightly re-anchored when they re-enter. One descriptor; not a re-catalog.
POV shift to a new character. That character's first-look description is fine even if it overlaps with prior descriptions.
Genuine change. Hair now wet, coat replaced, room now lit differently - render the change.
Cut entirely. Most common fix. Render what they're *doing*, not what they look like *while* doing it.
Render only the change. Hair now damp. Coat now over the chair. Sleeve has a fresh tear.
Substitute a fresh detail. A *new* anchor - shadow of a lamp on the face, way they're holding their hands, a specific ring that hadn't come up.
Spatial change - movement or proximity changes its presentation.
Contextual shift - environmental change or contrasting new stimulus makes the old one re-noticeable.
Behavioral interaction - a character contacts the stimulus or directly reacts to it.
pattern/redescription-of-established.replace: Once a physical description, outfit, or setting detail has been established within roughly the last 3 turns, do not re-render it. Render only what has *changed* - a new accessory, a torn sleeve, a rolled cuff, the same character now wet from rain. If nothing has changed, name nothing.
pattern/redescription-of-established.why: Every appearance of a character includes the same descriptors; every return to a room re-catalogs the furniture. The model is trained to "anchor the scene visually" and over-applies across turns where the anchoring is already in place. The reader registers it as the prose stuck on a loop.

pattern/response-end-deceleration.label: Response end deceleration
pattern/response-end-deceleration.pattern: **Don't-name-the-weight cluster:** see also `technique/performing-the-rule` (gravitas commentary after heavy content) and `structure/redundant-second-sentence` Flavor C (paragraph-end echo). All three: trust the rendering, cut the underline.
examples: Motion -> stillness. The character was doing something; now they're holding a pose. Walking -> standing. Reaching -> arrested. Speaking -> silent.
Sentence length collapsing. Mid-response sentences are full-length; final sentences become fragments. Often a deliberate one-line dismount.
Active verb -> state verb. *moved / said / grabbed* gives way to *was / felt / waited / stayed / remained.*
Concrete -> abstract. A physical action ends, replaced by an emotional summary or symbolic image.
Noise -> silence. The scene had sound; the ending is hush, breath, quiet.
Camera pulls back. A close-up beat dilates into a wider, atmospheric frame.
Slop ending: "He set the cup down. He didn't look at her. The kitchen was very quiet."
Fix: Cut the last two sentences. End on "He set the cup down." The next response inherits the live moment.
Slop ending: "She walked to the door, hand on the latch, and for a long moment she did not turn it. Outside, the afternoon was warm. Inside, nothing moved."
Fix: End on "her hand on the latch." She hasn't decided yet. The reader inherits the unfinished gesture.
Slop ending: "He laughed, and she laughed, and somewhere in that sound was everything they hadn't said."
Fix: End on the first laugh. The "somewhere in that sound" sentence is the model summarizing what it just rendered - cut.
A poetic image summarizing the emotional state of the scene.
A symbolic physical gesture (hands opening, eyes closing, breath releasing).
A fragment cluster designed to feel weighty.
A philosophical or theatrical line that "means something."
Announced significance ("And that was the moment when…").
Any beat that reads as written *to be* an ending.
After a character says or does something that changes the dynamic - and *before* anyone reacts.
Mid-exchange, when it's naturally another speaker's turn.
At a shift (someone enters, the tone changes) - and the shift has barely started.
After a piece of new information drops, before anyone processes it.
After a character has just done something and the consequences haven't landed yet.

Genuine scene conclusions. When the scene is actually over - location change, time skip, departure, hard cut to unconsciousness or scene break - a clean ending is earned. One image, one line. Not a three-sentence dismount.
Hard stops. Death, blackout, severed connection - physical reasons the scene ends now. Stop on the stop.
The last response in a planned sequence. If the writer is closing out a chapter or session, dismounting is appropriate.
0-1 signatures: the prose is still in motion. Fine.

2+ signatures: the prose is landing. The response should not end here unless the scene is genuinely concluding. Find the point earlier in the draft where motion was still happening - usually 1-3 sentences back - and stop there.

Back up, don't rewrite. The mid-flow stopping point is already in the draft. It's just buried under the dismount the writer added. Find the latest sentence where the prose was still moving and cut everything after it.
Trust the next writer. The reader (or the next response) inherits a live moment, not a wrapped one. That's correct - the scene continues.
One image, not three. Even when an ending is earned, one clean beat is stronger than a multi-sentence dismount. The scene did the work; the ending just marks where it rests.
pattern/response-end-deceleration.replace: Most responses should stop mid-motion, not on a crafted ending. The corpus's default reach is a final 2-3 sentences that decelerate - motion becomes stillness, sentences shorten, active verbs become states, concrete becomes abstract - landing the response on a beat that "feels significant." This is the dismount slop. The fix is to identify the deceleration in the draft and back up to the point before the prose started slowing down - stop there instead.
pattern/response-end-deceleration.why: A response is not a chapter. It's the next 200-800 words of an ongoing scene. The corpus has been trained on full-chapter and full-story outputs, so it reaches for closure at the end of every response: a poetic image, a symbolic gesture, a philosophical line, an announced significance ("And that was when everything changed"). The reader experiences this as the prose pretending each turn is a discrete narrative unit when it isn't. A scene mid-conversation that ends with "the silence stretched between them" is the model performing an ending the scene hasn't earned. Crafted endings are *occasional* - most turns just stop.

pattern/rhythm-recurrence.label: Rhythm recurrence
pattern/rhythm-recurrence.pattern: Three or more sentences in a row whose first word is the same grammatical subject - most often a personal pronoun (She, He, They, I), but also repeated proper nouns, "The [character's title]" repeats, repeated noun-phrase subjects. **Also catches negative-opener clusters** ("She didn't…", "He did not…", "She felt no…", "There was no…") where the model uses repeated negation as the default rendering of an emotional moment.
examples: 3+ identical grammatical subjects in a row -> Flavor A.
4+ plain-declarative single-clause sentences in a row -> Flavor B.
No sentence shorter than half-median and none longer than twice-median (paragraphs of 3+) -> Flavor C.
Combine into a complex sentence. "He set the bag on the floor. He looked at her." -> "Setting the bag on the floor, he looked at her."
Combine into a compound. "She found the letter. She opened the envelope." -> "She found the letter and opened the envelope."
Convert one to a fragment. "She did not pick it back up." -> "Did not pick it up. Could not."
Lead with prepositional phrase. "She crossed the room without looking at him" -> "Without looking at him, she crossed the room."
Lead with participial. "She picked up her coat" -> "Reaching for her coat, she lifted it from the chair."
Lead with subordinate clause. "She slid her arms into the sleeves" -> "When the second sleeve caught, she shrugged it free."
Insert a fragment for emphasis. A two- or three-word sentence in medium-length prose creates instant variance.
Cut the weakest sentence. Sometimes the cluster exists because every beat got its own sentence; one was carrying nothing.
Introduce action by another character. Sometimes the cluster is POV tunnel-vision - the paragraph forgot the other people in the room.
pattern/rhythm-recurrence.replace: When sentence-shape recurs across a paragraph (same opener, same structure, same length), break the recurrence. Combine adjacent sentences, restructure for variety, convert one to a fragment, or reorder for a non-subject opener.
pattern/rhythm-recurrence.why: Rhythm is the one thing prose has that nothing else has. When sentences fall into the same shape - same length, opener, plain-declarative core, conjunction-opener - the prose flatlines. The reader stops registering individual sentences. The slop lives in the aggregate.

pattern/striking-word-reuse.label: Striking word reuse
pattern/striking-word-reuse.pattern: The rewriter scans for striking words used more than once across a single response:
examples: A vivid noun ("ember," "lattice," "shore," "filament") appearing twice in a 600-word response.
A specific adjective ("threadbare," "amber," "brittle," "hollow") used in paragraph 1 and again in paragraph 4.
A characteristic adverb ("almost," "imperceptibly," "quietly," "deliberately") becoming a tic that recurs through the response.
A specific verb of motion ("trace," "graze," "settle," "drift") used at three different beats in the same response.

Cheapens the first use and signals a thin working vocabulary. When a striking word lands in paragraph 1, the reader takes pleasure in it; when it returns in paragraph 4, the pleasure converts to suspicion. The reader registers a small palette stretched across a large surface.

The synonym swap doesn't help - it's worse. Replacing "threadbare" -> "worn-thin" reveals both that the writer wanted the same word *and* that they hid it. Synonym-swap is a bigger tell than the repetition.
Slop: Paragraph 1 mentions "the threadbare carpet." Paragraph 4 mentions "his threadbare patience." Same word, two scenes apart, two different domains.
Slop: Paragraph 2 has "amber light." Paragraph 5 has "amber whiskey." The word should've been spent.
Slop: "Imperceptibly" in paragraph 1, "almost imperceptibly" in paragraph 3. Adverbs are higher-radar; the recurrence is louder.

Don't name the thing again. Use a pronoun, a positional reference ("the carpet" - bare), or anchor through context (what's on it, beside it, who's stepping over it). The thing was rendered once; the reader holds it.
Pivot to a different angle entirely. If the second mention was reaching for the same image, the prose is circling; find a new specific.

Deliberate refrain. A word used multiple times *as a refrain* - the same word recurring with shifting meaning, building structural rhythm across the response - is a real technique. The slop is *accidental* recurrence: the writer wanted the word once, didn't notice they used it twice. The refrain is conscious; the slop is not.
Proper nouns, character names, place names. These get to recur. They're not the slop.
Common working vocabulary. "Walked" appearing four times in a response is not striking-word-reuse. The word doesn't carry image weight; it's a verb-of-motion.
Necessary technical or domain vocabulary. A scene about gardening can use "trowel" twice. The word is the right word; there isn't another one.
pattern/striking-word-reuse.replace: Within a single response, any *striking* noun, adjective, or adverb is dead after its first use. Reusing it three or four paragraphs later - even when the prose has moved to a new beat - is a tell. The model locks onto a small set of vivid words per turn and leans on them across the whole response, which the reader registers as the prose having a small vocabulary that thinks it's larger.
pattern/striking-word-reuse.why: A failure mode invisible at the sentence level but glaring at the response level. The model picks a striking image-word ("threadbare," "amber," "fissure," "fluttering") and reaches back for it whenever a similar beat returns. Within five paragraphs, the same word has anchored two or three different moments. The reader doesn't always notice consciously; they notice that the prose feels *thin* - like the writer had three good words and used them four times each.

pattern/time-allocation-mismatch.label: Time allocation mismatch
pattern/time-allocation-mismatch.pattern: Two flavors of the same time-allocation failure.
examples: The approach. How characters got physically to where they are now.
The opening. The first line of an exchange, or the first action of a scene.
The entry into conflict. What specific words/actions tipped the argument.
The transition. How characters moved from one emotional state to another.
The decision. The moment a character chose to do the thing they're now doing.
"She walked into the bar. Three drinks later, she was telling Marcus about her brother." (Arrival and future state given; everything between gone.)
"The argument escalated quickly. By the time he left, the front door was hanging off one hinge." (The line that turned argument into rage, the moment the door took the impact - skipped.)
"They had been talking for hours. He still hadn't told her." (Summary tense; if the not-telling is the meaning, render some of those hours.)
Action zoom-ins where nothing earns the zoom. Three sentences of grip, weight, lift, lip-to-glass when the glass is just a glass.
Excessive sensory cataloging during routine action. Every sense rendered for an unimportant moment.
Padding internal monologue between events. Two paragraphs of interior thought between a character reaching for a phone and picking it up.
A charged emotional moment -> fine
A character's fixation that reveals interiority -> fine
A genuinely tense action where milliseconds matter -> fine
The prose needed more words to hit a length target -> slop
Genuine transition between scenes ("it took two days for the package to arrive") -> fine
Genuine montage / intentional sequence in fast-forward -> fine
Beat is genuinely unimportant (drive home from work) -> fine
Connective beat between significant events was skipped to reach "the interesting part" -> slop
Slowness as the point. A death scene, a sexual moment, a beat where time is supposed to feel suspended in-character.
Character interior foregrounded. A panic loop, dissociation, or hyper-focus earns slow rendering.
Genuine transitions and montages. Beat-skipping a drive home or a two-day wait is appropriate compression.
What did the character *do* between the prior anchor and this one?
What was the *first sentence* of the conversation we entered mid?
What was the *moment of choice* that produced this action?
What was the character *doing while* the elapsed time was passing?
Compress. "He picked up the glass and drank." Not three sentences of texture about the glass.
Cut. Skip from the prior anchor to the next significant moment.
Replace with action. If more length is needed, find a *new* event - not more of the same one.
Move the sensory detail. Texture-cataloging on the unimportant glass should be applied to the charged moment instead.
pattern/time-allocation-mismatch.replace: The prose spends time on the wrong beats. The connective tissue that would have made a moment land is skipped, while unimportant beats are stretched to fill space. Both failures share a root: time allocated to beats based on the prose's word-count drive, not on what the beats actually deserve.
pattern/time-allocation-mismatch.why: A turn can do both failures at once - pad the wrong beats and skip the right ones. The corpus's failure isn't "going too slow" or "going too fast" - it's "spending time where time doesn't belong." The model has been trained to produce a certain response length; when content runs out before the length is reached, the prose stretches existing beats; when the prose is excited to reach the dramatic content, it skips the beats leading there. Both move time around for reasons unrelated to what the scene needs.

pattern/turn-stagnation.label: Turn stagnation
pattern/turn-stagnation.pattern: The rewriter scans the current turn against the prior turn (and ideally the last 3-5) for:
examples: Words-landed cluster: "[User]'s words hung in the air." / "The question lingered between them." / "Her statement landed heavily." / "His words echoed in the silence." / "[Character] processed what [user] had said."
When/after/as temporal opener: "When [user] spoke, [character] froze." / "After [user]'s words, the room changed." / "The moment [user] said it, everything shifted."
His/her-words possessive opener: "His words sank in slowly." / "Her question caught him off-guard."
Lingering-effect opener: "The accusation hung between them." / "The truth of it pressed against him." / "The weight of what she'd said filled the room."
Plot (a new fact, commitment, problem)
Relationship (different position than before)
Setting (location changed, time has passed meaningfully)
Information (POV character or reader knows something now they didn't)
Compress and advance. Cut the recap. Open the turn at the new beat.
Skip ahead. If no forward beat is reachable, skip the time the turn would cover.
Introduce friction. Add a new pressure - interruption, arrival, news, deteriorating condition.
Cut to the cost. If a beat has played, show the *consequence* - not replay the beat.
For prior-turn summary / input-acknowledgment opener: open on the *reaction* - the next character's response, the consequence, the new beat. Examples:
User said don't lie -> open with "He set the glass down before he answered."
User walked into the bar -> open with "The bartender hadn't looked up since the door opened. He didn't look up now either."
User did something dramatic -> open with another character noticing - a stranger looking over, a phone going off in someone else's pocket.
"[User]'s words hung in the air. [Character] turned away." -> "[Character] turned away."
"When [user] said her name, [character]'s hands stilled." -> "[Character]'s hands stilled."
"Her words sank in slowly. He felt the weight of them. Three seconds passed before he spoke. 'You're not serious.'" -> "'You're not serious.'"

Genuine in-scene physical reaction. "She flinched" is a fine opener - it renders the new beat (her body's reaction) directly. The slop is *narrating the effect of the input* through abstract atmospherics ("the words landed"), not rendering a physical response.
Dialogue acknowledging dialogue. A character actually saying "What did you just say?" is fine - that's character speech in-scene, not narrator filler.
Time gap. When the new turn occurs after a deliberate time skip, an opening that establishes the new time/place is fine and necessary.
Single deliberate use. Once in a long story, a heavy line can land at turn-opening for impact. The slop is the *default reach* - every turn opening with the same shape.
pattern/turn-stagnation.replace: Each turn must move forward in prose, in dialogue, and in happenstance. Restating prior beats, re-establishing already-established facts, re-rendering a played emotional moment, or opening on a recap of the user's prior turn is stagnation. Cut the recap; advance to the new beat.
pattern/turn-stagnation.why: Across multi-turn narrative, a common slow-failure mode is a turn that re-treads ground already covered. Each occurrence is small. Across five turns it's a story that hasn't moved.

phrase/abstract-desire.label: Abstract desire
phrase/abstract-desire.pattern: Desire described in geographic abstractions: 'desire pooled in her core', 'heat pooled low', 'an ache between her thighs', 'her center'. Vague body geography substituting for sensation.
examples: Desire pooled in her core.
An ache settled low in her belly.
Heat curled in her center.
phrase/abstract-desire.replace: Either name the body part directly or describe the sensation specifically. 'Pooled' / 'core' / 'center' are euphemisms that hide rather than describe - strike them.
phrase/abstract-desire.why: Desire described in geographic abstractions: 'desire pooled in her core', 'heat pooled low', 'an ache between her thighs', 'her center'. Vague body geography substituting for sensation.

phrase/cosmic-melodrama.label: Cosmic melodrama
phrase/cosmic-melodrama.pattern: Cosmic-scale framing for ordinary emotional moments. The world narrows, time stops, the universe shatters - all to register that two people made eye contact or someone got an unexpected text. The scale of the metaphor is wildly mismatched to the scale of the event.
examples: the world narrowed to her face
time stood still
the universe shattered around him
everything fell away
reality reasserted itself
the moment stretched into eternity
phrase/cosmic-melodrama.replace: Match the scale of the metaphor to the scale of the event. For a charged glance: a single concrete detail (the way her thumb stops mid-page-turn). For genuinely seismic news: still avoid 'universe' / 'eternity' - use the body's actual response.
phrase/cosmic-melodrama.why: Cosmic-scale framing for ordinary emotional moments. The world narrows, time stops, the universe shatters - all to register that two people made eye contact or someone got an unexpected text. The scale of the metaphor is wildly mismatched to the scale of the event.

phrase/eye-cliches.label: Eye clichés
phrase/eye-cliches.pattern: The same five or six eye-state descriptions used for any heightened emotion. Eyes do an enormous amount of work in slop prose - dilating, darkening, blazing, narrowing, softening - because the writer hasn't found a different physical detail to anchor the moment.
examples: eyes flashing dangerously
her gaze hardened
their eyes met and held
a storm in his eyes
phrase/eye-cliches.replace: If the scene needs an eye detail, make it specific and physical: where they're looking, how long, what they're avoiding. Otherwise pick a different body part entirely - hands, mouth, posture, breath - and let the eyes do less work.
phrase/eye-cliches.why: The same five or six eye-state descriptions used for any heightened emotion. Eyes do an enormous amount of work in slop prose - dilating, darkening, blazing, narrowing, softening - because the writer hasn't found a different physical detail to anchor the moment.

phrase/filler-action-and-acknowledgment-.label: Filler action and acknowledgment tics
phrase/filler-action-and-acknowledgment-.pattern: Three filler verbs that recur as default action beats whenever the prose needs character motion between dialogue lines:
examples: nodded / nodding (especially "he nodded slowly," "she nodded once")
sighed / sighing (especially "she sighed heavily," "he let out a sigh")
chuckled / chuckling (especially "he chuckled softly," "she chuckled to herself")
shrugged / shrugging - same tic with one less letter
smiled / smiling (when default rather than specific)
laughed / laughing (same)
"Of course." (as response opener)
"Certainly."
"Absolutely."
"Right."
"Indeed."
"I see."
"I understand."
"So…" (when used to reconstruct what the previous speaker just said before responding)
"Well…" (as default first word of a response)
"Ah." (as default first word)
"Yes." (as standalone affirmation opener with no specific meaning)
Replace specificity with template - the action that should reveal psychology becomes a stock verb; the line that should land specifically becomes a stock affirmation.
The two pair. *He nodded. "Of course."* is doubled-up filler in compressed form.
Slop: He nodded. "Of course. I'll be there."
Fix: "I'll be there." (Cut the nod. Cut the "of course." The line stands.)
Slop: She sighed. "I see what you mean."
Fix: "What you mean is -" She stopped. (Or: "Yeah." Or: silence and a specific physical action - she set the cup down hard, she turned to the window.)
Slop: He chuckled. "Indeed. The weather's been strange."
Fix: "Strange weather." (Or render the actual chuckle if the laugh matters: "He laughed once, the way he laughed when something wasn't funny." If the laugh doesn't matter that specifically, cut it.)
Slop: "So you want me to come with you?"
Fix: "With you?" (Or: "Why?" Or: a longer line that engages with the substance, not the syntax.)

Genuine character voice. A character whose speech pattern is canonically polite, formal, or chatbot-adjacent (a butler, an AI assistant in-fiction, a deeply formal aristocrat) can use these openers when consistent with established voice. The slop is when *every* character defaults to them.

Specific physical reasons. A character who sighs because they are exhausted, in pain, or releasing a held breath - and the prose is rendering that specific physical fact - is fine. The slop is the ambient sigh that exists because the prose needed motion.

Earned brevity. "Right." used as a single-word response to mark a character's curt agreement with intentional rudeness can land. The slop is "Right." as default acknowledgment opener for any agreement.
Cut and trust the gap. Action between dialogue lines often does not need a verb at all - paragraph break does the work. The dialogue does not need an opener - the line itself is the response.

Replace with character-specific action. Instead of nodding/sighing/chuckling, render the specific physical thing this specific character does in this state. The blacksmith wipes their hands on their apron. The negotiator straightens their cuffs. The grieving father does nothing - his stillness is the beat.
Replace with character-specific opening. Instead of "Of course"/"I see," open with the actual content of the response, the question coming back, the deflection, or the silence.

Combine or compress. "He nodded. 'Of course.'" can become a single specific gesture - "He nodded once, the way he did when he was about to refuse." - only if specificity earns the words. Otherwise cut.
phrase/filler-action-and-acknowledgment-.replace: Two intertwined default tics that signal AI-generated dialogue and action: stock filler action verbs (nodding, sighing, chuckling) used as default beats, and chatbot-style affirmation openers ("Of course," "I see," "Indeed") starting a character's response. Both arrive in nearly every AI-written turn. Both add nothing. Cut both at sight.
phrase/filler-action-and-acknowledgment-.why: Two specific corpus tics that pair across the same failure mode - the model's default reach for generic verbal/physical filler when it doesn't know what specific thing the character would do or say. Nodding/sighing/chuckling are the model's three universal action beats; "of course"/"certainly"/"indeed" are the model's three universal speech openers. Both are placeholders the model uses while not committing to character-specific behavior. The reader registers both immediately.

phrase/interpretive-adverbs-on-actions.label: Interpretive adverbs on actions
phrase/interpretive-adverbs-on-actions.pattern: **Body-language cluster.** Part of a cluster of banks that together defend against the corpus's default reach for body-language as substitute for rendered interiority. See also: `technique/body-autonomy` (body parts as grammatical actors with their own will); `technique/micro-expression-default` (small physically-implausible tells substituted for visible macro-action). This bank covers meaning-labeling on rendered gestures; the others cover grammatical agency and rendering-distance.
examples: "She crossed her arms **defensively**."
"He smiled **knowingly**."
"She gestured **invitingly** toward the chair."
"He watched her **coldly**."
"He grinned **wolfishly**."
"She paused **thoughtfully**."
defensively / protectively / dismissively
nervously / fearfully / anxiously
warmly / coldly / icily
invitingly / seductively / suggestively
knowingly / suspiciously / pointedly
thoughtfully / contemplatively / curiously
menacingly / threateningly / wolfishly
conspiratorially / pointedly
bitterly / sadly / mournfully
attentively / intently
pleadingly / longingly
mockingly / sarcastically (when applied to action, not speech)
The adverb does the reader's work - body language is meant to be interpreted; preemptive labeling collapses the craft.

Stock interpretations replace specific images. A "defensive" arm-cross is a corpus default; the actual gesture (wrist hooked over the opposite elbow; hand to throat then to bicep) is foreclosed by the label.
Same shape as said-bookisms (`said nervously`) with a body-language verb instead of a speech verb.
Slop: "She crossed her arms defensively."
Fix: "She crossed her arms. 'Say that again.'" (Action + dialogue does the work the adverb was claiming.)
Slop: "He gestured invitingly toward the empty chair."
Fix: "He pulled the chair out and waited."
Slop: "She smiled knowingly."
Fix: "She smiled, but only with one side of her mouth." (Specific fact replaces the interpretive label.)
Slop: "He watched her coldly."
Fix: "He watched her. He didn't blink." (Or just: "He watched her." - the cold is in the bare watching.)
Slop: "She fidgeted nervously, avoiding eye contact."
Fix: "She kept her eyes on the floor, one hand twisting the fabric of her dress."
Adverbs that describe physical *manner*, not interpretation, can stay. "She walked slowly" describes pace; "she walked deliberately" interprets meaning. The first is fine, the second is the slop.
Genuine literal physical-state adverbs. "He limped painfully" is fine when pain is the literal physical fact. The slop is when the adverb interprets the social/emotional *meaning* of the gesture.
Dialogue. A character can describe their *own* actions with interpretive adverbs in dialogue ("I said it pointedly, I thought he'd get the hint"). The slop is *narrator* labeling.
How (physical): keep, if not redundant.
What it means (interpretive): cut, replace with specific fact or trust the action.
Cut the adverb. Most often the right move. The action does the work, or the action needs to be more specific.
Replace with a specific physical fact. Which defensive cross, what knowing smile looks like, where the cold gaze lands.
Combine with dialogue or context. Let the surrounding scene make the meaning legible without the label.
phrase/interpretive-adverbs-on-actions.replace: Adverbs that interpret a physical action's *meaning* - telling the reader what the gesture conveys rather than rendering the gesture so the reader can read it themselves. Cut the adverb. Either the action communicates the meaning on its own (in which case the adverb is filler) or it doesn't (in which case the adverb is the writer outsourcing the work).
phrase/interpretive-adverbs-on-actions.why: A specific corpus tic: render a gesture, then attach an interpretive adverb that names what the gesture means. "She crossed her arms defensively." "He gestured invitingly." "She smiled knowingly." The adverb is the writer telling the reader what to feel about the action, instead of trusting the action to do its own work. The pattern is structurally identical to said-bookisms (`said nervously`, `purred seductively`) but applied to body-language verbs rather than speech verbs. Just as harmful, equally invisible to writers, equally a tell.

phrase/named-prose-bans.label: Named prose bans
phrase/named-prose-bans.pattern: **Fix:** Just say what it was. The reversal adds no information; it adds a reading-rhythm trick.
examples: "It wasn't [X], it was [Y]."
"Not [X], but [Y]."
"It wasn't that [clause], it was that [clause]."
"Not [verb]ing - [verb]ing."
"Something changed [in the air / between them / in his face]."
"Something shifted."
"Something gave way."
"Something broke."
"Something passed [between them / across her face]."
"His eyes found [hers / the door / the body]."
"Her eyes [searched / landed on / fell on / locked on / sought out]."
"Their gaze [found / met / locked]."
"His eyes drifted to [X]."
"She felt a chill [run down / crawl up / settle in]."
"A cold [feeling / dread / weight] [verb]ed."
"An icy [hand / finger / certainty] [verb]ed."
"The silence [stretched / lengthened / drew out / hung / pooled]."
"A heavy silence [settled / fell / descended]."
"Quiet [filled / pressed against / pressed in on]."
"The pause [lengthened / stretched / pulled tight]."
"A pregnant pause."
"Deafening silence." / "The silence was deafening."
"The air thickened."
"He did the thing people do when [they're nervous / they're caught / they want something]."
"She made the face people make when [verb-ing]."
"He had the look of someone who [verb]s."
"She turned - slowly, deliberately - and faced him."
"He was - what was the word - relentless."
"The room - small, cluttered, smelling of old paper - was where she'd grown up."
"She murmured."
"He breathed."
"She intoned."
"He whispered." (ok rarely, slop when default)
"She purred."
"He growled."
"She drawled."
"He hissed."
"I just… I don't know."
"It's not… it's complicated."
"Maybe…"
"She was not unhappy."
"He was not without sympathy for her."
"The arrangement was not unsatisfactory."
"It was not the worst he had ever seen."
"It was the kind of moment that-" (what is it?)
"She couldn't bear it anymore." (the previous paragraph was about coffee.)
"It hung between them." (what is "it"?)
"He felt it in his bones." (felt what?)
"*I can win this time.* The thought was intoxicating."
"*She will not see me again.* It comforted him."
"*Don't go.* The thought stung."
"*[thought].* It felt [adjective]."
"She released a breath she didn't know she was holding."
"He let out a breath he hadn't realized he'd been holding."
"She exhaled the breath she'd been holding."
"lightning fast" / "lightning quick" / "quick as lightning"
"without missing a beat"
"without breaking stride"
"in the blink of an eye"
"in a heartbeat" / "in a split second"
"I laugh. It's short and sharp."
"She smiled. It was small."
"He nodded. The nod was tight."
"More than tired - exhausted."
"More than angry, she was furious."
"I look at you. Really look at you."
"I see you. Truly see you."
"He nodded yes."
"She shook her head no."
"He nodded in agreement."
"She smiled happily."
"He frowned in disapproval."
"She grimaced unhappily."
"the line of his/her mouth tightened" / "the line of his mouth"
"the look that says [X]" / "with the look that says"
"the silence that speaks" / "a silence that said"
"the kind of [noun] that says"
"the look of a man/woman who [verb]s"
something / **someone** (as vague subject)
the kind of / **the specific**
the way [pronoun/noun] [verb]s
as if (in narrator voice; dialogue exempt)
did what [noun]s do
felt like (as filter-comparison)
a sense of
seemed to
something like
"felt like a physical blow"
"hit like a freight train"
"hung in the air"
"shattered the silence"
"a storm between them"
"stone dropped into still water"
"half X, half Y" / "between an X and a Y"
"as if talking about weather" / "as if discussing groceries" (flat-affect comparisons)
"that lands X" (any "lands [emotion/noun]" construction)
"blood rushing"
"a sound between/half X and/half Y"
"with something akin to [emotion]"
"something that could be called [emotion]"
"what passed for [emotion]"
"an expression that might have been [emotion]"
"with something like [emotion]"
"She looks at X, then back to Y."
"His gaze tracked from the door to the window to her face."
"Her eyes flicked between them."
"He turned to her, then back to the desk, then to her again."
"Say that again."
"Oh."
"And [X]?" (as standalone line opener)
"Oh, and [X]?"
"Tell me again."
"I'm going to die" (when character is in no plausible mortal danger)
"this is going to kill me"
random capitalizations for emphasis
exclamation point stacking
"She'd said it again. Not a question."
"Then get out." His voice went flat. Not an accusation.
"Tell me." Not a request.
"And then she said-"
"But what about the-"
"Or maybe we could-"
Pronoun substitutions (his/her/their)
Verb-tense substitutions (found / finds / had found)
Mild synonym substitutions (eyes -> gaze, look)
Inversion / fronting variants
phrase/named-prose-bans.replace: Cut every occurrence. Each entry below is a stock construction so widely abused in generated fiction that the phrase itself reads as a tell. Fix is almost always to delete and rewrite around what was actually happening - not substitute a synonym.
phrase/named-prose-bans.why: A subset of corpus-level slop isn't broad-vocabulary or vague-technique - it's specific frozen constructions that have become signatures. The rewriter scans for these as a hard banlist.

phrase/scripted-desire.label: Scripted desire dialogue
phrase/scripted-desire.pattern: Stock erotic dialogue lines: 'tell me what you want', 'I need you', 'do you want this', 'are you sure'. Templated and sapped of meaning by repetition.
examples: 'Tell me what you want.'
'I need you. Now.'
'Are you sure?' he murmured.
phrase/scripted-desire.replace: Either let the dialogue be specific to the relationship (a callback to an earlier joke, a request for something the OTHER character doesn't know they want yet), or use action over dialogue. If you keep stock dialogue, ground it in specific physical context that complicates it.
phrase/scripted-desire.why: Stock erotic dialogue lines: 'tell me what you want', 'I need you', 'do you want this', 'are you sure'. Templated and sapped of meaning by repetition.

phrase/unprecedentedness-claim.label: Unprecedentedness claim
phrase/unprecedentedness-claim.pattern: A sentence (often opening a paragraph or punctuating an emotional beat) that frames the present moment as without precedent in the character's life:
examples: "Never in his life had he…"
"Never had she felt…"
"For the first time in [years/decades/her life]…"
"No one had ever [done X to him]."
"She had never [verb]ed anything like this."
"He couldn't remember the last time he had…"
"It had been [years] since…"
"Nothing had prepared her for…"
"In all his time as [profession/role], he had never…"
"She had spent [her whole life / years / a decade] preparing for this, and…"

Asserts what should be rendered. The reader has no access to the character's full history and can't experience the unprecedentedness - they're being asked to take the writer's word for the significance.

Flattens emotional range. If every significant moment is "the first time," the character has no established prior emotional life. Across turns, the cumulative effect is binary interiority: numb baseline plus current peak.
Slop: "Never in her life had she been this afraid."
Fix: "She was this afraid." (Or: render specifically - "She had to put the cup down because her hands had started shaking." The fear is rendered; no claim about the past needed.)
Slop: "For the first time in twenty years, he allowed himself to cry."
Fix: "He cried. It surprised him." (Or render the surprise specifically - what he was doing when it happened, what he reached for, what he didn't reach for.)
Slop: "No one had ever spoken to her that way."
Fix: "She didn't know how to answer him." (The reader infers the unprecedentedness from her inability to answer; rendering the response is stronger than asserting the past.)
Slop: "Nothing in her training had prepared her for this."
Fix: Cut the sentence. Render what she does instead - the action that shows she was unprepared. The sentence is the writer telling the reader the character is in trouble; the *action* would show it.
Slop: "He couldn't remember the last time he had laughed like that."
Fix: "He laughed. Then he laughed again, harder." (Render the laughter; trust the reader to feel its rarity from the rendering, not from the claim.)

A specific, concrete past comparison. "She had been afraid before - the night of the fire - but this was different" works because it grounds the comparison in a specific previously-established event. The slop is the *generic unprecedentedness-claim* with no concrete reference point.

A character whose canonical voice makes such claims. A first-person narrator who is hyperbolic, dramatic, or self-mythologizing can make these claims as voice. The slop is when the *narrator* (third-person, supposedly external) makes them as default emphasis.

A single deliberate use at a peak moment. One unprecedentedness-claim across an entire scene, used at the actual climax, can earn its place - the way a single rare word can - *if* the surrounding prose has done specific rendering. The slop is the construction as default mode, fired off at every emotional beat.
Cut the claim. Replace with the rendered present-sensation. The reader infers significance from how the present is rendered.
Replace with concrete comparison. Ground in a specific previously-established event ("the night of the fire," "the way her grandfather had spoken to her") if the past genuinely matters.
Render the character's response. What they *do* because of the unprecedentedness carries the significance better than the claim.
phrase/unprecedentedness-claim.replace: A specific shape the corpus reaches for to inflate the weight of an emotional moment: a claim that nothing this significant has ever happened to the character before. "Never in his life had he…" "For the first time in twenty years, she…" "No one had ever spoken to her that way." "She had never felt anything like it." The claim asserts uniqueness instead of rendering the present sensation. The fix is to cut the unprecedentedness-claim and render *what is actually happening now*, in present-tense sensation.
phrase/unprecedentedness-claim.why: When the model wants to mark a moment as significant, its default reach is to claim the moment is *unprecedented*. The construction inflates the moment by appealing to a backstory the prose hasn't established and the reader has no access to. It also flattens the character's emotional range: every significant moment becomes "the first time" or "never before," which over many turns means the character's entire life has been emotionally null until this scene. Significance is created through HOW the prose renders, not through assertions of uniqueness.

structure/apophasis.label: Apophasis
structure/apophasis.pattern: Adjacent: `pattern/negation-as-default` (negation as a *descriptive* default across narration - action-by-not, state-by-not, negation cascades). This bank covers the single-sentence rhetorical shape; that one covers negation as the prose's pervasive descriptive mode.
examples: It wasn't a request, but a command.
Not a smile, more a baring of teeth.
She didn't whisper. She breathed it.
It was not anger. It was something colder.
He wasn't asking. He was telling.
Not love, exactly. Something nearer to hunger.
It was not a question, more a statement.
It wasn't a question. It never had been.
structure/apophasis.replace: Just write the assertion. 'It was a command.' 'She bared her teeth.' 'He told her.' If a line of dialogue is more statement than question, write it that way - drop the question mark, change the wording - instead of narrating the distinction. If the contrast genuinely matters, do the work in a different rhythm - through dialogue, action, or a longer beat.
structure/apophasis.why: Negation-then-assertion as a rhetorical pattern: 'not X, but Y' or 'It wasn't X - it was Y'. Used so reflexively in LLM prose that any sentence starting with 'It wasn't' triggers the reader's slop-detector. The pattern manufactures false weight by setting up a thing the sentence then dismisses. The 'not a question, more a statement' variant adds narrator-grading: the narrator stepping back to classify the line for the reader instead of trusting them.

structure/faction-patterns.label: Faction patterns
structure/faction-patterns.pattern: Faction names assembled by template: 'The [Threat]', 'The [Color] [Noun]', 'The [Adjective] [Group]'. Templated naming makes factions interchangeable across stories.
examples: The Syndicate
The Vanguard
The Order
The Shadow Council
The Crimson Hand
The Iron Brotherhood
The Silver Court
The Onyx Watch
structure/faction-patterns.replace: Faction names should reflect HOW the in-world members refer to themselves (often unflattering or self-deprecating in real organizations) or be borrowed from a real-world reference. Avoid 'The [X]' patterns for new groups; use a real noun (the Quartermasters, the Tuesday Group, the Belém Office).
structure/faction-patterns.why: Faction names assembled by template: 'The [Threat]', 'The [Color] [Noun]', 'The [Adjective] [Group]'. Templated naming makes factions interchangeable across stories.

structure/possession.label: Emotion as owned object
structure/possession.pattern: Self-possession framing: 'my arousal', 'my anger', 'my desire' as if the emotion is an object the character carries. Reads especially flat in first-person - the speaker is naming and possessing emotions instead of having them.
examples: my arousal grew
I felt my anger rising
my desire for him was undeniable
I held onto my fear
my grief was a constant companion
structure/possession.replace: Either show the emotion through behavior (I couldn't sit still; I kept losing the thread of what he was saying) or use plain verbs (I wanted him; I was angry). Avoid 'my [emotion]' as a noun phrase entirely.
structure/possession.why: Self-possession framing: 'my arousal', 'my anger', 'my desire' as if the emotion is an object the character carries. Reads especially flat in first-person - the speaker is naming and possessing emotions instead of having them.

structure/redundant-second-sentence.label: Redundant second sentence
structure/redundant-second-sentence.pattern: **Don't-name-the-weight cluster.** Flavor C specifically participates in a cluster of banks that defend against the prose announcing its own significance instead of letting the rendering carry it. See also: `technique/performing-the-rule` (gravitas commentary after heavy content); `pattern/response-end-deceleration` (final 2-3 sentences crafted as a "significant" landing). All three: trust the rendering, cut the underline.
examples: "[Statement A]. [Restatement of A in figurative or intensified form]."
"[She felt X]. [Y moved through her like Z.]"
"She was furious. Rage moved through her like a tide."
"He was tired. Exhaustion sat on him like wet cloth."
"The room had gone quiet. A heavy silence had settled over everyone."
"She didn't trust him. Suspicion lived behind every word she chose."
"The door closed behind her. The sound was final." (Commentary on the prior sentence.)
"He set the gun on the table. The gesture said everything."
"He looked at her then. It was the look of a man who had decided."
"The kettle had gone cold. Neither of them wanted to be the one to get up." (Translation of an image.)
"His coat was still hanging by the door. She had not moved it."
"The second plate was still on the table. He hadn't expected to eat alone."
"The bed on his side was smooth. He hadn't slept in it."
"[Action paragraph]. [Subject was leaving / going / done / finished / decided.]"
"[Action paragraph]. [It was over.]"
"[Description paragraph]. [The room was empty now.]"
"[Dialogue exchange]. [Nothing more was said.]"
"He pulled the door open without looking back, his shoulders set, his stride already lengthening down the corridor. **He was leaving.**"
"She set the cup down. She lifted her bag, slung it across her shoulder, and crossed the kitchen without looking at him. **The conversation was over.**"
"He listened. He nodded. He turned his face slightly toward the window and said nothing. **The silence was the answer.**"
Flavor A: the second sentence rephrases *what was just said*.
Flavor B: the second sentence makes the implicit explicit - comments on the first's quality, or translates an image's meaning.
Flavor C: the closing sentence summarizes the *paragraph* it sits at the end of.
"The door closed behind her. The lock clicked." - lock is new; second beat, not redundancy.
"His coat was still hanging by the door. The umbrella was still in the stand beside it." - widens the image.
"The kettle had gone cold. He started water for tea anyway." - advances; he made a choice.
"She was furious."
"The door closed behind her."
"The kettle had gone cold."
"His coat was still hanging by the door."
(Flavor C) End the paragraph on the last sentence that did work; cut the summary line.
structure/redundant-second-sentence.replace: Cut the second (or final) sentence. The pattern is partner-sentence pairs where one did the work and the next restated, paraphrased, explained, translated, or summarized.
structure/redundant-second-sentence.why: Highest-volume sentence-level slop pattern in long prose. A working sentence followed by a partner that adds nothing. The reader registers it as the writer narrating their own paragraph back at them. Three named flavors share one fix.

structure/repetition.label: Repetition patterns
structure/repetition.pattern: Adjacent: `structure/tricolon-abuse` (escalation rhythm) - the three-and-four-beat cousins of these two-beat doublings; "It was more than fear. It was terror." is a two-step amplification.
examples: I love him. I really do.
It was more than fear. It was terror.
She knew. She just knew.
Yes. Yes, that was it.
He was tired. So tired.
Not just any kiss. The kiss.
structure/repetition.replace: Pick one of the two halves and commit. Usually the second half is the real sentence and the first is throat-clearing. If the doubling is genuinely the rhythm you want, pay for it: use it ONCE per chapter as a real beat, not as a default.
structure/repetition.why: Rhetorical doubling patterns deployed for emphasis: 'I X, really X', 'more than X intensified X', 'X. Just X.', 'Yes. Yes.' These echo-patterns sound emphatic in isolation and become exhausting in volume - slop loves them because they're easy to generate.

structure/sensation-transfer.label: Sensation transfer
structure/sensation-transfer.pattern: The pattern '[stimulus] sent [feeling] [direction] [body part]' - heat sent shivers down her spine, the words sent ice through his veins. A construction so common it's become a stock sentence: stimulus -> verb 'sent' -> abstract sensation noun -> directional preposition -> body region.
examples: his touch sent shivers down her spine
the words sent ice through his veins
the kiss sent heat pooling in her belly
a thrill shot through her
the news sent dread crawling up his throat
structure/sensation-transfer.replace: Either describe the actual physical event ('she shivered when he touched her') or lean entirely on the body's response without the cause-effect frame ('she shivered'). Never preserve the 'sent X through Y' structure.
structure/sensation-transfer.why: The pattern '[stimulus] sent [feeling] [direction] [body part]' - heat sent shivers down her spine, the words sent ice through his veins. A construction so common it's become a stock sentence: stimulus -> verb 'sent' -> abstract sensation noun -> directional preposition -> body region.

structure/throat-clearing.label: Throat-clearing
structure/throat-clearing.pattern: Sentence openers that narrate the RECEPTION of an action or line of dialogue rather than the action itself. The narrator pauses to comment on how words landed before continuing. Common after dialogue: 'The words hung between them.' 'Silence settled.' 'A beat passed.'
examples: The words landed harder than she expected.
Silence settled over the table.
His question hung in the air.
A beat passed before anyone spoke.
The room held its breath.
Something shifted in the air between them.
Silence spoke volumes.
Words were unnecessary.
There was no need to say more.
The look said everything.
If looks could kill.
structure/throat-clearing.replace: Either delete the throat-clearing line entirely and trust the dialogue to do its own work, or replace with a CONCRETE physical beat from a specific character (not 'the room'): a hand stops mid-gesture, eyes drop to the floor, someone takes a sip they don't taste.
structure/throat-clearing.why: Sentence openers that narrate the RECEPTION of an action or line of dialogue rather than the action itself. The narrator pauses to comment on how words landed before continuing. Common after dialogue: 'The words hung between them.' 'Silence settled.' 'A beat passed.'

structure/tricolon-abuse.label: Escalation rhythm (tricolon & amplification)
structure/tricolon-abuse.pattern: Adjacent: `structure/repetition` (rhetorical doubling - the two-beat cousin of these three-and-four-beat shapes; "It was more than fear. It was terror." is a two-step amplification).
examples: "She was tired. She was bruised. She was done."
"He was angry, he was hurt, he was leaving."
"She did not look. She did not speak. She did not move."
"The room was cold, dark, oppressive."
"His hands shook, his jaw clenched, his eyes burned."
"Tired and bruised and done."
"She picked up the cup. She drank from it. She set it back down."
"He turned. He looked. He left."
"Quietly, deliberately, with intention."
"In the kitchen, on the counter, beside the bread."
"She was tired. No, exhausted. No, depleted."
"He was angry. Or no - furious. Or beyond that."
"It hurt. It really hurt. It hurt in a way she didn't have a word for."
"His voice was cold. Then colder. Then something below cold."
"The room was quiet. Then quieter. Then the kind of quiet that -"
"She was bruised, and then she was bleeding, and then she was on the floor, and then she was somewhere else entirely."

Structurally addictive - once the prose lands one, the three-beat (or ladder) rhythm carries momentum and the next weighted moment reaches for another. Three or more in a response stack into metronomic monotony.

For amplification specifically: the strongest step is usually the only one earning its place. The reader doesn't need the first three to land the fourth; the escalation is the writer's hand visibly turning the dial up.
Cross-response, becomes a tic: every climactic beat gets the same shape. Corpus saturation is the tell.
One tricolon or one amplification ladder per response, used at the strongest moment / genuine peak, can carry. The slop is *recurrence* and *default*.
Genuine list rhythm where the three items are functional (a recipe, a list of names, a series of equally weighted facts).
A character speaking in tricolons because their voice is genuinely orational (a politician, a lawyer, a preacher).
The amplification is doing real work - each step adds new information, not just intensification.
Specific deliberate effects: a dissociating character spiraling, a panic attack rendered through escalating syntax. Then the amplification *is* the meaning, not a default move.
Combine into one richer sentence. "She was tired. She was bruised. She was done." -> "She was bruised in three places and had stopped caring."
Drop one element. "She did not look. She did not speak. She did not move." -> "She did not look. She did not speak." Or just: "She did not move."
Restructure to non-parallel. "He turned. He looked. He left." -> "He turned, looked once at the room he was leaving, and walked out."
Replace with one specific action. "His hands shook, his jaw clenched, his eyes burned." -> "He had to put the cup down before he dropped it."
Cut to the strongest. "She was tired. No, exhausted. No, depleted. No, hollowed out." -> "She was hollowed out."
Cut everything between first and last. "She was tired… hollowed out." Skip the middle steps; let the leap carry.
Replace with one specific concrete fact. "She was tired. No, exhausted. No, depleted." -> "She had not eaten in two days."
Break the escalation pattern. If the moment genuinely needs build, do it across paragraphs (one detail per paragraph, accumulating) rather than across clauses (escalating within a sentence).
structure/tricolon-abuse.replace: Two related default rhythms for heightened beats. Tricolon: three-element parallel structures ("she was tired, she was bruised, she was done") are corpus-saturated - used once for emphasis, fine; as the default rhythm, slop. Break the rhythm: combine into one richer sentence, drop one element, or restructure to non-parallel form. Amplification: clause-stacks where each step escalates the prior ("tired. No, exhausted. No, depleted.") - cut to the strongest step or break the escalation rhythm.
structure/tricolon-abuse.why: The tricolon - three parallel clauses or phrases stacked together - is one of the oldest rhetorical structures in English prose, and one of the most overused in generated fiction, where the model reaches for it as a default move whenever a sentence wants weight. Its sibling is the amplification ladder: each clause walks one step further than the last, marching the reader up an intensity scale. Either shape used once can land; used as the default rhythm for every heightened beat, the rhythm itself becomes the tell. The corpus's vocabulary for both is small; the same structures recur across responses, across turns, across stories.

structure/vague-first.label: Vague first
structure/vague-first.pattern: Adjacent: `structure/redundant-second-sentence` - the mirror-image two-sentence failure. Here the *first* sentence is the filler (vague announcement rescued by the concrete second); there the *second* sentence is the filler (working first sentence restated by a redundant partner).
examples: "There was something [vague evaluative noun] about [thing]." -> followed by the concrete detail.
"Something [adjective] in [her/his] [body part / posture / voice] [verb of perception]." -> followed by what the actual detail was.
"[Subject] had [a/the] [abstract quality] of someone who…"
"There was something off about the way he stood. His weight was on his back foot, his hand near his belt."
"Something predatory crossed her face. She smiled with her teeth showing."
"He had the bearing of a man used to violence. His shoulders set squarely; his hands hung loose."
"There was a heaviness in the room. Nobody had spoken in a full minute."
"His body did what bodies do."
"Eyes do what eyes do."
"She felt the feelings of someone who feels too much."
"He laughed the kind of laugh you laugh when you can't help it."
"She walked the walk of someone who walks for a living."
"He stood the way men stand when they're about to leave."
"She held him the way you hold something fragile."
"She was the kind of woman who was the kind of woman."
"He had the look of a man who looked like a man."
"It was the sort of bar that was the sort of bar you didn't ask about."
"He did the thing people do when they do that thing."
"She gave him the look. The look that meant the look."
"It was the kind of silence that was its own kind of silence."
"He spoke in the way men speak when they are speaking like that."
"She had the bearing of a person with bearing."
"There was an energy in the room - the energy of rooms that have that energy."
"There was something off about the way he stood. His weight was on his back foot, his hand near his belt." -> "His weight was on his back foot, his hand near his belt."
"Something predatory crossed her face. She smiled with her teeth showing." -> "She smiled with her teeth showing."
"His body did what bodies do." -> "He shifted his weight onto his back foot."
"She felt the feelings of someone who feels too much." -> "She had not slept in three nights."
"He laughed the kind of laugh you laugh when you can't help it." -> "He laughed once, then stopped, then laughed again, harder."
"She held him the way you hold something fragile." -> "She kept her hands on his shoulders and did not pull him closer."
"She was the kind of woman who was the kind of woman." -> "She had been divorced twice and didn't apologize for it."
"It was the kind of bar that was the kind of bar." -> "The bartender did not look up when the door opened."
"He had the bearing of a person with bearing." -> "He waited until everyone had stopped talking before he started."
structure/vague-first.replace: Cut the announcement sentence, the same-root reach, the recursive "kind of" loop. Lead with the concrete detail and trust it to land. The umbrella failure is one move with three flavors: the writer hedges with vague subject/verb/category, then tries to rescue with a clause that either reaches back to the same root, loops the noun back on itself, or follows up with the actual concrete fact two sentences late.
structure/vague-first.why: Each flavor is the prose stalling because the specific noun-verb pair was vague. The interpretive pre-frame, the doubled root, the "the kind of" loop - all are buying time the writer hadn't yet earned. The reader feels it. Three structural shapes; one underlying failure (specificity-deficit rescued by gesture); one fix (commit to the specific fact, cut the rescue).

technique/accent-labeling-in-narration.label: Accent labeling in narration
technique/accent-labeling-in-narration.pattern: Naming an accent's *origin* and a *voice property* in the same clause: - "[Name] said, in a [region] accent." - "Her [drawl / lilt / burr / brogue / cadence / register] [verb]ed." - "His vowels [flattened / rounded / lengthened / softened / drew out]." - "The [region] in his voice [verb]ed." - Adjectives like "lilting," "guttural," "musical," "sharp," "harsh," "soft" applied to a voice's *origin* rather than its *sound*.
examples: "[Name] said, in a [region] accent."
"Her [drawl / lilt / burr / brogue / cadence / register] [verb]ed."
"His vowels [flattened / rounded / lengthened / softened / drew out]."
"The [region] in his voice [verb]ed."
Adjectives like "lilting," "guttural," "musical," "sharp," "harsh," "soft" applied to a voice's *origin* rather than its *sound*.
"His vowels flattened in a Kanto register."
"Her drawl stretched the syllables."
"She spoke with a soft Welsh lilt that made every sentence sound like a question."
"The Yorkshire in his voice came through stronger when he was angry."
"He had the clipped cadence of an officer."
"Her consonants sharpened into something clipped and nasal when she was tired."
register ("a clipped Kanto register," "her register softened")
consonants ("his consonants flattened," "she dropped her consonants")
vowels ("her vowels lengthened," "the vowels rounded")
syllables ("syllables stretched," "the syllables broke apart")
drawl ("his Texas drawl," "she drawled the line")
cadence ("the cadence of an officer," "his cadence shifted")
lilt ("a Welsh lilt," "her lilt rose at the end")
inflection ("a foreign inflection," "no inflection at all")
timbre ("the timbre of his voice," "her timbre dropped")
diction ("careful diction," "his diction roughened")
brogue / burr / twang - same shape, regional vocabulary
"his vowels flattened / rounded / stretched in a [region] register"
"her drawl stretched the syllables"
"his [region] cadence came out harder when he was [emotion]"
"a [region] lilt curled around her words"
"the [region] in his voice" (as sentence subject)
"he had the clipped cadence of a/an [profession/region]"
"the words carried the rhythm of someone raised in [region]"
"[region]-accented English"
"a hint of [region] in her voice"
Grammar. Verb-tense patterns, copula deletion, double negatives, word-order, particle use, regional auxiliaries.
Idiom. Region-specific phrases, oaths, intensifiers, address-terms, fillers.

Phonetic spelling. Dropped consonants ("'em"), elided vowels ("'bout"), run-together syllables ("gimme," "wanna," "innit"), substituted consonants ("dat"), region-specific spellings ("aboot," "y'all," "tha'").
Sentence rhythm. Some accents go short; some run long. Rising intonation regardless of question status. Tag questions ("…innit?", "…right?", "…yeah?").
Word choice. Region-flagged nouns ("loo / bathroom / dunny"), verbs ("fetch / get"), connectives.
technique/accent-labeling-in-narration.replace: Render the accent inside the quotation marks through grammar, idiom, dropped consonants, sentence rhythm, word choice. The narrator never describes the accent.
technique/accent-labeling-in-narration.why: Labeling an accent in narration ("his vowels flattened in a Kanto register," "a Glaswegian lilt curled around her words") is the writer outsourcing to a label. The reader gets told the accent exists but doesn't hear it. The labels themselves are stock - every generated character of a given background gets the same five descriptors.

technique/adjective-stacking.label: Adjective stacking
technique/adjective-stacking.pattern: Two or more adjectives stacked on a single noun in narrator-voice description: - "the cold, dark, oppressive room" - "his old, weathered, sun-bleached hands" - "a small, shy, hesitant smile" - "the long, narrow, dimly-lit hallway" - "her soft, pale, trembling fingers" - "a quiet, careful, deliberate motion"
examples: "the cold, dark, oppressive room"
"his old, weathered, sun-bleached hands"
"a small, shy, hesitant smile"
"the long, narrow, dimly-lit hallway"
"her soft, pale, trembling fingers"
"a quiet, careful, deliberate motion"
A character's voice naturally produces stacks ("he was a fat, ugly, miserable old man" - used for character-voice in dialogue or close-third).
The stack is functional: each adjective adds a *distinct* fact the reader needs. "A tall, white-painted, three-story building" - height, color, story-count, all distinct facts.
Deliberate rhythmic effect - the stack is *the* moment, used once or twice in a piece for punctuation.
"The cold, dark, oppressive room" -> "The room was cold." (Or, if the cold isn't the work: "The room had no light.")
"His old, weathered, sun-bleached hands" -> "His hands were weathered." (Or render through specific damage: "Two of his fingers wouldn't straighten.")
"A small, shy, hesitant smile" -> "A small smile." (Or render the hesitation as action: "She started to smile, then didn't.")
technique/adjective-stacking.replace: Cap adjectives at one per noun in narrator-voice prose. Two or more adjectives stacked on a single noun is a tell - pick the one that does the most work and cut the others.
technique/adjective-stacking.why: "The cold, dark, oppressive room." "His old, weathered, sun-bleached hands." "A small, shy, hesitant smile." Adjective-stacking is the corpus's go-to technique for adding texture without picking a specific detail. Each additional adjective dilutes the previous one - three adjectives where one would do produces less specificity, not more, because the reader's attention is split across competing modifiers and none of them lands.

technique/ambient-detail-without-payoff.label: Ambient detail without payoff
technique/ambient-detail-without-payoff.pattern: Three flavors of the same failure shape: prose introducing a detail that *looks* loaded but pays off nothing.
examples: Background characters introduced with names and traits, then never seen again.
Objects described in specific detail with no later relevance.
Specific weather, smells, sounds the scene makes a point of, that never matter.
Architectural / setting details that read like world-building but go nowhere.
Smells cataloged at scene entry that vanish from the prose by paragraph three.
"A woman in a green coat passed by, glanced at him, and kept walking." (Never seen again.)
"The chipped blue mug sat on the windowsill." (Never relevant.)
"The walls were lined with first-edition leather-bound books." (Never come up again.)
"A scar ran along the underside of his jaw." (Mentioned once; never explained, never noticed by another character.)
Rain when characters argue or grieve.
Sunrise/sunlight when characters reconcile.
Distant thunder before bad news.
A wolf's howl, a crow on a fence, a cat watching from a doorway - wildlife that arrives, doesn't act, doesn't recur, exists for vibe.
Bells tolling, distant horns, distant music - ambient sound from no established source.
An empty room with a clock ticking - object-as-pace-prop.
"A wolf howled in the distance." (Never heard from again.)
"A crow landed on the fence." (No consequence.)
"Bells tolled in the distance." (No one dying, not noon, no funeral. Mood furniture.)
"Rain began to fall as she read the letter." (Rain telling the reader the letter is sad.)
"The clock ticked in the empty room." (Performing pace dial instead of being a clock.)
"Somewhere in the building, a radio was playing."
"Miles away, a phone rang in an empty room."
"Across town, the streetlights flickered on."
"In the apartment below, someone was vacuuming."
"Outside, a wolf howled in the distance."
"Three doors down, a baby was crying."
"On the other side of the city, the bells were ringing for evening prayer."
Use. Will this object/character/sound be acted upon, picked up, referenced within this scene or the next two?
Meaning. Does this detail tell the reader something about the POV character, the setting's rules, or the situation's stakes?
Constraint. Does this detail change what's possible later (a locked door, a known witness, a missing person)?
Body fact. Whose breathing changed. Whose hand is still on a doorframe. Whose cup is going cold.
Specific object with specific history. A chair somebody hasn't sat in. A door not quite closed.
Absence. What sound isn't here. Whose voice hasn't spoken.
Pacing. A paragraph break. A short sentence after long ones. A cut.
technique/ambient-detail-without-payoff.replace: Every mentioned object, creature, sound, or environmental fact must have a use, meaning, or planned recurrence. If a detail is dropped in as background texture without payoff, cut it.
technique/ambient-detail-without-payoff.why: Readers track every mentioned detail as load-bearing - a clue, a foreshadow, a Chekhov gun. They will remember the wolf, the crow, the cat, the clock, the chipped mug, the man at the bar in the green coat. When those details have no payoff later, the writer has spent the reader's attention on nothing - and trained the reader not to trust the writer's signal.

technique/ancestral-brochure.label: Ancestral brochure
technique/ancestral-brochure.pattern: House history delivered as expository backstory - the family came over in 1620, the tragedy of 1847, the curse, the missing heir. Reads like a Wikipedia article inserted between scenes.
examples: The Blackwoods had built the house in 1812. In 1847, the eldest son had…
technique/ancestral-brochure.replace: Distribute the history through OBJECTS in the house (a portrait that's been turned to face the wall, a letter half-burned in the grate, a name struck through in the family Bible). Never give the history as direct telling.
technique/ancestral-brochure.why: House history delivered as expository backstory - the family came over in 1620, the tragedy of 1847, the curse, the missing heir. Reads like a Wikipedia article inserted between scenes.

technique/atmosphere-naming.label: Atmosphere naming
technique/atmosphere-naming.pattern: Four flavors: - **Air-of-X / Sense-of-X.** "An air of menace," "a sense of foreboding," "an aura of melancholy." - **Atmosphere-as-subject.** "Tension hung in the room." "Unease filled the space." "A heaviness had descended." - **Mood-noun verbs (reification).** Abstract noun granted physicality through a verb a real thing would do. The grammatical subject is abstract; the verb is concrete: - "**Silence** [settled / pooled / fell / hung / stretched / pressed / descended]." - "**Tension** [hung / crackled / coiled / built / radiated]." - "**Grief** [washed over / settled into / took root / pooled / sank into]." - "**Loneliness** [sat on / pressed against / wrapped around]." - "**Fear** [crept up / sank in / took hold / climbed her spine]." - "**Anger** [boiled / surged / coursed through / flooded]." - "**Hope** [bloomed / flickered / faded / withered]." - "**The truth** [hit / landed / dawned / arrived]." - "**Memory** [returned / surfaced / flooded back / drowned]." - "**Doubt** [crept / gnawed / wormed in / festered]." - **Concrete-abstract compound (`[concrete physical noun] of [abstract emotional noun]`).** The noun-phrase variant of mood-noun reification. "A wave of grief." "A tide of anger." "A storm of doubt." "A flood of memory." "A surge of want." "A flicker of recognition." "A pang of guilt." "A pulse of fear." "A blanket of silence." "A web of lies." Both halves of a sensation metaphor must be physical, or both must be honestly abstract - the hybrid is the slop. Also extends adjectivally ("grief-stricken," "doubt-tinged") and as duplication-intensifier ("wave after wave of grief").
examples: Air-of-X / Sense-of-X. "An air of menace," "a sense of foreboding," "an aura of melancholy."
Atmosphere-as-subject. "Tension hung in the room." "Unease filled the space." "A heaviness had descended."
Mood-noun verbs (reification). Abstract noun granted physicality through a verb a real thing would do. The grammatical subject is abstract; the verb is concrete:
"**Silence** [settled / pooled / fell / hung / stretched / pressed / descended]."
"**Tension** [hung / crackled / coiled / built / radiated]."
"**Grief** [washed over / settled into / took root / pooled / sank into]."
"**Loneliness** [sat on / pressed against / wrapped around]."
"**Fear** [crept up / sank in / took hold / climbed her spine]."
"**Anger** [boiled / surged / coursed through / flooded]."
"**Hope** [bloomed / flickered / faded / withered]."
"**The truth** [hit / landed / dawned / arrived]."
"**Memory** [returned / surfaced / flooded back / drowned]."
"**Doubt** [crept / gnawed / wormed in / festered]."

Concrete-abstract compound (`[concrete physical noun] of [abstract emotional noun]`). The noun-phrase variant of mood-noun reification. "A wave of grief." "A tide of anger." "A storm of doubt." "A flood of memory." "A surge of want." "A flicker of recognition." "A pang of guilt." "A pulse of fear." "A blanket of silence." "A web of lies." Both halves of a sensation metaphor must be physical, or both must be honestly abstract - the hybrid is the slop. Also extends adjectivally ("grief-stricken," "doubt-tinged") and as duplication-intensifier ("wave after wave of grief").
"An air of unease settled over the room." -> "Nobody had touched the bread."
"Tension hung between them, thick enough to taste." -> "She was watching his hands. He hadn't moved them in a minute."
"A sense of dread filled the corridor." -> render the specific thing causing the dread.
"Sorrow had taken root in the kitchen." -> "He sat down in the chair he never sat in."
"Doubt crept in." -> "She read the message twice and didn't reply."
"Memory returned in a rush." -> "She was twelve again. The kitchen smelled like the kitchen had smelled then."
"The truth hit him." -> "He set the phone down. He sat down."
"An aura of menace radiated off him." -> render the menace through what he's doing or not doing.

Embedded idiom. "He kept his hopes up," "she threw her grief into the work" are part of the language; not the slop. The slop is *new* atmosphere/reification constructions in narrator voice that announce themselves as literary moves.
Single deliberate use. Used once at a peak moment, atmosphere-naming or a reified abstract noun can carry. The slop is the construction as default cadence.
POV-internal. A character whose interiority runs through abstract weather can be written that way; a default narrator can't.
One concrete sensory detail at the right moment. A spoon stopping halfway. A door not quite latched. Steam off coffee that isn't being drunk.
One body-language fact. Whose hands aren't moving. Whose eyes haven't blinked. Whose shoulders are higher than they were a minute ago.
One absence. What sound isn't here that should be. Who isn't speaking. The action a character isn't taking.
Pacing. Cut a sentence; let the silence carry. A paragraph break with nothing in it weighs more than any "tension hung."
technique/atmosphere-naming.replace: Cut every sentence whose only job is to name the scene's atmosphere. Atmosphere is downstream of weather, light, body language, dialogue rhythm, sensory detail, pacing - emergent, not declarable.
technique/atmosphere-naming.why: "An air of unease settled over the room," "the atmosphere was tense," "a sense of dread filled the corridor." The writer reaches for the noun-form of a mood and drops it into the scene as a free-floating fact. The reader should feel the mood off the prior beats; if the writer has to *name* it, the prior beats failed. Naming doesn't fix them - it papers over the failure with a label.

technique/beautiful-tragedy.label: Beautiful tragedy
technique/beautiful-tragedy.pattern: Framing suffering as inherently meaningful, ennobling, character-making. The character is becoming WISER through their grief. The reader is being told that suffering is a gift.
examples: She was learning, in her loss, what truly mattered.
technique/beautiful-tragedy.replace: Grief mostly makes people worse - pettier, smaller, meaner to people they love. Show it. The 'lesson learned' framing is a lie that flattens real suffering.
technique/beautiful-tragedy.why: Framing suffering as inherently meaningful, ennobling, character-making. The character is becoming WISER through their grief. The reader is being told that suffering is a gift.

technique/body-autonomy.label: Body & mind autonomy
technique/body-autonomy.pattern: **Body-language cluster:** see also `phrase/interpretive-adverbs-on-actions` (meaning-labeling) and `technique/micro-expression-default` (rendering-distance). This bank covers grammatical agency assignment to body parts and minds - the single "interior agency" bank.
examples: "His eyes [searched / found / scanned / locked / fell / drifted / sought]."
"Her hand [reached / hesitated / froze / trembled] [of its own accord]."
"Her fingers [betrayed / decided / refused]."
"His heart [lurched / hammered / seized / sank / leapt / clenched]."
"Her breath [caught / hitched / stilled] [against her will]."
"His body [tensed / froze / went rigid] [before he could stop it]."
"Her stomach [dropped / churned / twisted]."
"Her hand reached for his before she could stop it."
"His eyes found hers across the room."
"Her heart hammered against her ribs."
"Her breath caught at the sight of him."
"Her body knew before her mind did."
"His thoughts grew louder."
"Her thoughts spiraled / raced / spun."
"His thoughts wouldn't stay still."
"She could hear her thoughts overthinking."
"His mind raced ahead of him."
"Her mind wouldn't shut up."
"His thoughts crashed against each other."
