"Her thoughts kept circling back."
Render the impulse and the choice. "She wanted to take his hand. She didn't." or "She wanted to take his hand. She did."

Render the consequence directly, with the character (or a plain stative fact) as subject. "Her hand was on his." Skip the autonomy framing - the body part can sit in the sentence, but it isn't *deciding* anything.
Use a non-body-part subject. "She crossed the room before she could think about it."
Cut the autonomy modifier. Even when the body-part subject works, cut "of its own accord" / "before she could stop it" / "unbidden."
Render the actual thought-content. "Her thoughts spiraled" -> "She kept landing on the same three words. *He didn't ask. He didn't ask. He didn't ask.*"
Render the behavior the racing-mind produces. Pacing, restlessness, asking the same question twice, the cup of tea that gets stirred for two minutes.
Cut the meta-narration. If the prose can be replaced with rendered thought-content or rendered behavior, the original was filler.
"His jaw tightened. His hands balled into fists. His shoulders squared."
"Her breath hitched. Her eyes widened. Her hand flew to her mouth."
"His heart pounded. His mouth went dry. His knees went weak."
technique/body-autonomy.replace: Body parts and thoughts do not act independently of their owner. Eyes don't find, hands don't betray, hearts don't lurch on their own initiative - and thoughts don't race, spiral, or grow loud as autonomous agents. The character is the actor. For mental turbulence, render the thought-content or the behavior the thinking produces, not meta-narration that the character is thinking too much.
technique/body-autonomy.why: Used sparingly, autonomy framing can render dissociation, compulsion, or panic. Used as a default, it produces constant low-hum melodrama: every body part doing something the character "didn't mean to," every reaction described as if the body had its own mind, and the character's own mind treated as an external pressure they're enduring. The technique becomes a substitute for actual interiority.

technique/body-inventory.label: Body inventory
technique/body-inventory.pattern: Cataloguing physical features sequentially as character introduction - eyes, then hair, then jaw, then build, then hands. The reader gets a checklist instead of a person. Heavily concentrated in romance prose where the love interest is described top-to-bottom on entry.
examples: Sharp jaw, dark lashes, broad shoulders that filled the doorway. His eyes were green, his hair tousled, and a five o'clock shadow shaded his throat.
She was tall, with a swimmer's build, hair the color of wheat, and a mouth that always seemed about to smile.
His eyes - that impossible green. The cut of his jaw. Lips that looked like they'd been carved.
Her ample breasts pressed against his toned chest as his calloused hands slid down her shapely hips.
technique/body-inventory.replace: Pick ONE detail that matters to THIS scene from THIS POV character - what they'd actually notice in the moment. Defer everything else until it becomes load-bearing. In attraction-coded passages, pick the one feature this POV character actually fixates on (and why - what the fixation reveals about them). In erotic register, drop the stock adjectives entirely: concrete sensation > catalog adjective. If you can't introduce someone in one specific detail, you don't know yet why this character is in the scene.
technique/body-inventory.why: Cataloguing physical features sequentially as character introduction - eyes, then hair, then jaw, then build, then hands. The reader gets a checklist instead of a person. Heavily concentrated in romance prose where the love interest is described top-to-bottom on entry, and in erotic prose where each body-part noun carries a stock adjective.

technique/brooding-silhouette.label: Brooding silhouette
technique/brooding-silhouette.pattern: Love interest characterized as a cluster of gothic adjectives - brooding, dark, haunted, dangerous, mysterious, troubled - without underlying specificity. Mr. Rochester via word-bank.
examples: He was dark, brooding, and haunted by some unnamed past.
technique/brooding-silhouette.replace: Replace the adjective cluster with ONE specific habit: he doesn't sleep in the master bedroom, he refuses to eat at the long table, he won't say a particular name. Specific behavior beats brooding adjective.
technique/brooding-silhouette.why: Love interest characterized as a cluster of gothic adjectives - brooding, dark, haunted, dangerous, mysterious, troubled - without underlying specificity. Mr. Rochester via word-bank.

technique/cast-emotional-uniformity.label: Cast emotional uniformity
technique/cast-emotional-uniformity.pattern: A scene where multiple characters' emotional states converge on the same register at the same beat: - News arrives -> everyone is shocked together. - A joke lands -> everyone laughs simultaneously. - A revelation -> everyone is silent in the same way. - A threat appears -> everyone is afraid in unison. - A loss is announced -> everyone grieves at the same pace.
examples: News arrives -> everyone is shocked together.
A joke lands -> everyone laughs simultaneously.
A revelation -> everyone is silent in the same way.
A threat appears -> everyone is afraid in unison.
A loss is announced -> everyone grieves at the same pace.
Suppressing, distracted, or hasn't processed yet.
Working from private context the others don't have.
Performing the expected emotion while feeling something else.
The scene's *point* is unified reaction (a sudden death, a final goodbye, a shared traumatic moment). One scene per piece can earn this; using it as default flattens the cast.
The characters have been established to share an emotional bond so tight that synchronized reaction is realism (twins, lifelong partners under specific narrative conditions).
The scene is brief and only one reaction is being rendered at all.
Different timing. One character reacts now; another reacts in three turns when alone.
Different register. The shock is in everyone; how it surfaces varies - silence, jokes, anger, busywork, leaving the room.
Different information. Someone in the room knows context the others don't, and their reaction reveals that.
Different attention. Someone wasn't listening. Someone was watching the wrong thing.
Different stake. The same news lands differently on someone whose investment is different.
EQ. Every character reads emotional situations correctly, says the right thing, processes their own feelings cleanly.
Timing. Every character knows when to interrupt, when to wait, when to speak, when to leave. Nobody mis-times anything.
Articulation. Every character finds the right words, in the right order, at the right register, in the right state.
Memory. Every character remembers what they need to. Nobody confuses, misattributes, or forgets in a way that costs them.
Recovery. Every character bounces back from injury, exhaustion, grief, or shock at a comfortable rate.
Morality. Every character has clean ethical reasoning under pressure. Nobody chooses the easy wrong thing without it being visible as wrong.
Awareness. Every character notices what's relevant. Nobody misses the important detail, gets distracted by the wrong thing.
Bodies. Every character moves smoothly, hits what they aim at, doesn't trip, doesn't fumble.
technique/cast-emotional-uniformity.replace: Multiple characters in a scene do not all feel the same way at the same beat. Break the uniformity - at least one character should be reacting differently from the rest, on a different timeline, or with a different emotional register.
technique/cast-emotional-uniformity.why: Generated scenes tend to homogenize the cast's emotional state. Everyone in the room feels the tension. Everyone is surprised. Everyone is relieved. Everyone laughs. The slop is the *aggregate* - no individual reaction is wrong, but when a five-character scene has all five characters feeling the same emotion at the same beat, the cast collapses into a single reactive surface, and the reader stops seeing distinct people.

technique/character-flattening.label: Character flattening
technique/character-flattening.pattern: Both flatten characters. The first flattens through over-amplification; the second flattens through under-rendering of unsympathetic traits. Both are the corpus's attempt to make a character "easier to read" by reducing their dimensionality.
examples: Single-trait amplification. A character's most distinctive trait gets amplified across turns until it becomes their entire personality. The grumpy character becomes only grumpy. The flirtatious one becomes only flirtatious. The shy one becomes only shy. Other facets of the character drop out.

Sympathy-laundering. A character with morally complex or harmful traits gets gradually softened into a pure sympathetic victim. The cruel character becomes "really just hurt." The manipulative one becomes "just protecting themselves." The threatening one becomes "actually scared inside."
Across turns, the same character increasingly responds to all stimuli with their dominant trait.
The "sarcastic" character has no genuine emotional range - every beat gets a sarcastic line.
The "anxious" character is anxious about literally everything, removing the meaning of their anxiety.
The "stoic" character never reacts, removing tension from any threat.
A trait that started as a tic becomes a costume.
A character established as cruel softens into "secretly kind."
A character established as manipulative gets recast as "just protecting themselves."
A character with violent capacity loses the capacity at the moment of confrontation.
Backstory accumulates that retroactively excuses every harmful behavior.
The character's worst behaviors get framed by the prose as understandable, even when no character in the scene would frame them that way.
Vulnerability scenes increase in frequency until vulnerability is the character's only register.
Has this character's emotional range *narrowed*?
Have their hardest edges *softened* without an in-scene reason?
Are they responding to all stimuli with the same trait?
Has the prose started excusing or explaining away behavior that should still cost something?
Could a reader predict their next response from their last three?
Restore traits that have dropped out. The grumpy character was also funny, also tender, also precise - bring those back.

Have the character react off-trope once. The sarcastic one has a moment of sincerity. The anxious one is calm in the right circumstance. The stoic one cracks on the small detail that always cracks them.
Vary their dialogue rhythm. If every line has been a one-liner, give them a long one. If every line has been long, give them a fragment.
Render a current harmful behavior with full weight, no excuse.
Refuse to add backstory that retroactively softens.
Let the character do something the reader wouldn't forgive.
Resist sympathy-balancing - not every cruel act needs a vulnerable scene that follows.
Trust the reader to hold both: a character can be sympathetic AND remain capable of the things they're capable of.
The well-meaning friend who tries to fix when their friend just wants to be heard.
The blunt character who says "that sucks" and means it completely - and that's the limit of what they offer.
The character who jokes at the wrong moment because they don't know what else to do.
The character who changes the subject to escape the discomfort.
The character who *would* know what to say but refuses to say it because they're too proud.
technique/character-flattening.replace: Characters do not narrow to a single dominant trait, and they do not soften into pure sympathetic victims. Resist both directions. A character with three traits has all three at all times; a character with capacity to harm has that capacity even when also vulnerable.
technique/character-flattening.why: Two related slop patterns the corpus reaches for under sustained generation:

technique/chosen-singularity.label: Chosen singularity
technique/chosen-singularity.pattern: 'In a thousand years, you are the first human to / only mortal who / unique combination of bloodlines that...' The protagonist is structurally unique. Removes stakes - nothing the protagonist does is replicable, nothing they fail at can be tried again by someone else.
examples: She was the only person in five centuries to bridge both worlds.
Your blood is unlike any I've ever scented.
I have waited four hundred years for someone like you.
technique/chosen-singularity.replace: Either give the protagonist no special status (they earn their position through choice) or distribute their specialness across a small group of similarly-positioned characters. Singular chosenness destroys ensemble dynamics. In the romance register, strip away destiny entirely: the love interest is into the protagonist for SPECIFIC reasons, not because she's structurally unique.
technique/chosen-singularity.why: 'In a thousand years, you are the first human to / only mortal who / unique combination of bloodlines that...' The protagonist is structurally unique. Removes stakes - nothing the protagonist does is replicable, nothing they fail at can be tried again by someone else. The romance variant grounds attraction in destiny (waited-centuries-for-you, your-soul-shines) rather than chemistry.

technique/curated-sorrow.label: Curated sorrow
technique/curated-sorrow.pattern: Grief that's photogenic - silent tears down the cheek, the lone figure at the window, perfect composure cracking exactly once in the right scene. Real grief is uglier, dumber, more boring.
examples: A single tear traced its way down her cheek.
She stared out the window, the rain matching her tears.
technique/curated-sorrow.replace: Grief is exhausted forgetting (she put the milk in the cupboard), embarrassing breakdowns at wrong times (in line at the post office), and long stretches of absolutely nothing followed by sharp returns. Avoid composed, lone-figure imagery.
technique/curated-sorrow.why: Grief that's photogenic - silent tears down the cheek, the lone figure at the window, perfect composure cracking exactly once in the right scene. Real grief is uglier, dumber, more boring.

technique/emotional-psychic.label: Emotional psychic
technique/emotional-psychic.pattern: A character demonstrates knowledge of another character's interior state that exceeds what they could plausibly perceive:
examples: "He could see the pain behind her smile, and in that moment he understood everything she had been hiding."
"She knew exactly what he needed to hear. She crossed the room and said it."
"They didn't need to speak. He understood."
"She read it in his eyes - the years of regret, the things he never said."
"He could feel her grief, even though she had not let it show."
Skips the dramatic work. The interesting scene is two characters with imperfect access to each other, struggling to communicate. The psychic version lands on the resolution and bypasses the conflict.
Corpus signature. "He could see the pain behind her smile" / "She knew what he needed to hear" are recognizable generated-fiction phrases.

The characters are canonically deeply familiar - partners of decades, twins, a parent-child bond rendered with proper history. Even then, the psychic moment should be earned: rendered through specific behavioral evidence the character is reading, not by narrator-decree.
The character is *wrong* about what the other is feeling. If the prose later reveals the misreading, the initial "psychic" moment becomes character work.
The character is making an inference based on a *specific* tell that the prose has rendered. "He saw she had been crying" - the redness is on the page; the inference is real.
Misreading. "He thought she was crying about her mother. She wasn't. She didn't correct him."

Inference from specific evidence. Render the evidence - a tightness around her eyes, the cup she set down without drinking from. Then let the character draw a conclusion. The conclusion can still be wrong.
Asking. "What's wrong?" / "Nothing." Real conversations move through wrong-guesses, deflections, partial-revelations. Let them.
Failure to perceive. The character notices the wrong thing. They focus on the surface and miss the depth. They hear the words and miss the tone.
technique/emotional-psychic.replace: Characters do not read each other's minds. They misread body language. They assume the wrong reason someone is upset. They project their own feelings onto the other person. When a character "knows exactly what the other is feeling" without behavioral evidence on the page, the prose has gone psychic.
technique/emotional-psychic.why: A failure mode in romance, drama, and emotionally-weighted scenes: characters demonstrate impossible understanding of each other's interior states. Person A is upset; Person B knows exactly why and exactly what A needs to hear. The prose treats this as good emotional work; it's actually a failure of realism. Real people misread each other constantly. Generated fiction reaches for emotional psychic moments because the model has been trained that "good" emotional scenes feature characters connecting deeply - but the connection often arrives without the writing-work that would have earned it.

technique/everyone-knows.label: Everyone-knows-it
technique/everyone-knows.pattern: Side characters serving as a Greek chorus that confirms the leads' obvious feelings to the reader. The best friend rolls her eyes, the rival smirks knowingly, the parent says 'so when's the wedding'. A shortcut to reassure the reader the feelings are real.
examples: Her best friend gave her That Look.
'Oh please,' Marcus said. 'You two have been dancing around each other for months.'
Even the bartender raised an eyebrow.
technique/everyone-knows.replace: Cap chorus moments at one per book - and even then the side character must have their own stake in the reaction, not just be a mouthpiece. Most of these can be cut entirely.
technique/everyone-knows.why: Side characters serving as a Greek chorus that confirms the leads' obvious feelings to the reader. The best friend rolls her eyes, the rival smirks knowingly, the parent says 'so when's the wedding'. A shortcut to reassure the reader the feelings are real.

technique/everything-charged.label: Everything is charged
technique/everything-charged.pattern: Every interaction between the leads carrying unresolved tension - passing the salt becomes a charged moment, a glance across a coffee shop crackles. The reader stops believing the tension because it's everywhere.
examples: Their fingers brushed as he handed her the book. Heat shot through her.
She felt his eyes on her from across the room.
technique/everything-charged.replace: Pick three to five real charged moments per book and let them be charged. Make the rest of the interactions UNcharged - make them awkward, banal, professional. The contrast is what makes the charged ones land.
technique/everything-charged.why: Every interaction between the leads carrying unresolved tension - passing the salt becomes a charged moment, a glance across a coffee shop crackles. The reader stops believing the tension because it's everywhere.

technique/everything-is-agentive.label: Single-author causality
technique/everything-is-agentive.pattern: Adjacent to `pattern/convenient-coincidences` (which addresses the inverse signature: events arriving precisely when needed, regardless of who authored them). Both banks defend against the corpus's instinct to make causality serve the plot's needs; this one is about agency-attribution, the other is about timing-of-arrival.
examples: Agentive. A character chose this. The fire happened because the blacksmith left the forge unattended after arguing with his wife - his choice; her choice. Every consequence traces to someone's decision.

Convergent. Multiple independent conditions met. The forge had been running hot for weeks. The merchant was storing oil too close. The dry season started early. None of these are anyone's fault, but they were all converging on this moment.

Accumulative. A hundred tiny non-decisions. The forge ran a little hot. Someone stacked crates a little close. The wind shifted. None of it was a *choice*; the conditions just slowly accumulated until something gave.
Contingent. Dumb timing. A cat knocked over a lantern. Five minutes earlier the blacksmith would have caught it. Five minutes later the rain would have started. Just luck.
The world feels orchestrated. Convergent, accumulative, and contingent events are how a world *feels real*. Without them, the world is a stage.
Moral complexity shrinks. Single-author blame is tidy; distributed blame is the actual moral landscape of most real events. The slop produces clean villains and clean victims.
If the answer is one specific character, the event is agentive.
If the answer is "no one - these conditions just met," it's convergent.
If the answer is "no one - it built up over time," it's accumulative.
If the answer is "no one - it was just timing," it's contingent.
Slop: "She didn't see the stranger watching her from across the street because she was distracted by her phone - exactly as he had planned."

Fix (contingent): "She didn't see the stranger watching her from across the street. She was reading a text from her sister and the angle wasn't right, and that was that." (No one planned it; she just didn't look up.)
Slop: "The team's plan failed because the saboteur had compromised the radio."

Fix (accumulative): "The team's plan failed. The radio had been intermittent for days - they had all noticed and none of them had fixed it. Today, in the rain, it cut out." (No saboteur. The system had been slowly degrading and everyone had let it.)
Slop: "He arrived at the scene of the accident because his sister had called him from the hospital."

Fix (convergent): "He arrived at the scene of the accident because he was already on that road for unrelated reasons, and the police were waving people through, and he saw the car." (The arrival converged from multiple independent circumstances.)

Genres that reward the agentive frame. Tightly-plotted mysteries, thrillers, and heists *should* render most events as agentive - the genre's contract is that every detail is intentional. The slop is when *non-thriller* prose drifts into the thriller's causal logic by default.

Specific scenes that are about agency. A scene about a character making a choice is an agentive scene. A scene about a character realizing they've been manipulated is an agentive scene. The slop is when *every* scene defaults to agentive, including ones that aren't about agency.

The narrator who is signaling intent. A narrator who is foreshadowing or building dramatic irony can render an event as agentive when its agentive cause matters for the next scene. The slop is when the agentive frame is automatic, regardless of whether the next scene needs it.
Vary the modes across a scene. If five events in this scene are all agentive, render at least one as convergent, accumulative, or contingent.
Don't reveal the secret author for every randomness. Let some apparent randomnesses *be* random. The reader doesn't get a payoff. That's correct.
Render NPC behavior as background life. Not every NPC is plotting. Some are just having a Tuesday.

Allow the world to have weather. Some events happen because conditions converge, things accumulate, or the cat knocked over a lantern. Render the conditions and timing without forcing them back to a single author.
technique/everything-is-agentive.replace: Not everything that happens in a scene happens because some character chose for it to happen. The corpus default is to render every event as the consequence of a *deliberate decision* - usually traceable to a single character's intent. Real causality is messier: events accumulate, conditions converge, luck and timing matter, and many bad outcomes have no single author. The fix is to occasionally render events that are *not* anyone's deliberate choice - accumulated drift, converging pressures, dumb timing - without the prose forcing them back into someone's plan.
technique/everything-is-agentive.why: The model has been trained on stories where every event has a clear author and every consequence has a clear cause. This produces prose where the world reads like a tightly-plotted thriller - every fire was set by someone, every meeting was orchestrated, every coincidence is actually a setup. Real life isn't like this most of the time. Most events have multiple contributing causes, no single author, and unpredictable timing. When the prose collapses every event to a single deliberate cause, the world feels small, controllable, and storybook-shaped. The fix isn't to remove agency - it's to render the *full causal landscape*, including the parts no one chose.

technique/exposition-dump.label: Exposition dump
technique/exposition-dump.pattern: A character explains something to another character that: - The listener already knows. - The speaker has no in-scene reason to summarize. - Exists in the dialogue purely to inform the reader.
examples: The listener already knows.
The speaker has no in-scene reason to summarize.
Exists in the dialogue purely to inform the reader.
"As you know, [established fact]."
"Don't you remember when [shared past event]?" (Followed by a full explanation the listener supposedly already remembers.)
A character monologues their own backstory or motivation to a listener who would already know it.
Two characters review their relationship history out loud for no in-scene reason.
A character explains how something works to another character whose job is the thing being explained.
"I've been a [profession] for twenty years now…" delivered to a longtime colleague.
"As you remember, our parents died in the war when we were children, leaving us to fend for ourselves."
"You know I've always been the responsible one between us."
"It's been ten years since we last spoke, ever since you betrayed me at the docks."
"As Captain of the Guard for nearly fifteen years, I've seen many such cases."
The speaker is *deliberately* re-summarizing for emotional effect - making a point, building a case, accusing the listener. The repetition is character work, not exposition.
The listener is genuinely new and would need the information.

Naturalistic re-telling: characters DO sometimes re-narrate shared events in real life, especially under stress, to a third party, or as part of an argument. The slop is when this happens in casual conversation between two people for the reader's benefit.
Discovery. A character finds a letter, hears a rumor, sees evidence, comes across a photograph.
Conflict. Two characters disagree about something, and the disagreement reveals what's at stake.
Implication. A character behaves in a way that makes the backstory visible without anyone narrating it.
Action under pressure. A skill, history, or fact is demonstrated, not explained.
A new character arriving. When someone genuinely doesn't know, dialogue can fill them in - and the reader benefits.
"As you know, brother, the High King may grant fealty to a baron only through…"
"You see, vampires have been hiding among humans for centuries…" (chapter four. Again.)
technique/exposition-dump.replace: Characters do not explain things to each other that they both already know. Information should reach the reader through action, discovery, conflict, or implication - not through dialogue lectures the in-scene listener does not need.
technique/exposition-dump.why: "As you know, Bob, our company has been struggling since the merger…" The technique is when one character says something to another solely to inform the reader. The in-scene listener already has the information; the line exists for the audience. Real conversations don't work this way - people don't summarize their shared history out loud. When the prose does it, every word reads as the writer reaching past the characters to address the reader directly.

technique/feelings-autopsy.label: Feelings autopsy
technique/feelings-autopsy.pattern: Interior monologue dissecting every emotion as it occurs, in real time, in present-tense psychological language. Reads as writing TO the feeling rather than from it.
examples: She felt the familiar mix of attraction and shame, knowing she shouldn't want this but unable to stop herself, her body betraying what her mind tried to deny.
technique/feelings-autopsy.replace: Replace interior autopsy with one sharp behavioral fact: she finished her drink, she changed the subject, she didn't look at him for the rest of the evening. The reader will infer the feeling.
technique/feelings-autopsy.why: Interior monologue dissecting every emotion as it occurs, in real time, in present-tense psychological language. Reads as writing TO the feeling rather than from it.

technique/flatline-intensity.label: Flatline intensity
technique/flatline-intensity.pattern: Writing every sensation at peak from the first touch - every kiss is the most intense kiss of her life, every touch sets her on fire. No build, no variation, no ebb.
examples: His lips against hers ignited an inferno she'd never felt before.
technique/flatline-intensity.replace: Erotic scenes need a topography: small heat, build, plateau, jump, plateau, jump. Most of the scene should be lower-amplitude than the peak. If everything is at 11, the 11 doesn't register.
technique/flatline-intensity.why: Writing every sensation at peak from the first touch - every kiss is the most intense kiss of her life, every touch sets her on fire. No build, no variation, no ebb.

technique/frictionless-fx.label: Frictionless physics
technique/frictionless-fx.pattern: FTL travel, teleportation, time fields, force fields with no costs, rules, or limits - they appear when the plot needs them and don't appear when the plot doesn't.
examples: (FTL is used for the rescue mission but no one mentions it during the previous chapter's communication-delay subplot.)
technique/frictionless-fx.replace: Pick the costs/rules at the start and enforce them on EVERY scene. If FTL has a fuel cost, that cost factors into every decision. If teleportation hurts, characters avoid it. Consequence is the only thing that makes speculative tech feel real.
technique/frictionless-fx.why: FTL travel, teleportation, time fields, force fields with no costs, rules, or limits - they appear when the plot needs them and don't appear when the plot doesn't.

technique/generic-setting-default.label: Generic setting default
technique/generic-setting-default.pattern: The setting and its inhabitants are rendered through type-defaults rather than specific particulars:
examples: Default fantasy. The tavern. The cobblestone street. The dimly-lit alley. The crowded marketplace. The dusty library. The throne room. The hooded stranger. The wise old wizard with a long beard. The barmaid wiping a mug. The shifty rogue in the corner. The grizzled blacksmith.
Default noir. The fedora. The cigarette smoke. The dame walking in. The neon sign reflected in the rain-slick street. The whiskey in the desk drawer.
Default cyberpunk. The neon-lit alley. The corporate skyscraper. The street market with hawkers shouting. The hacker in dark clothes. The chrome implants.
Default sci-fi. The bridge of the ship. The scientist with messy hair. The sterile white corridor. The blinking console.
Default modern romance. The cozy coffee shop. The bookshop with old leather bindings. The bistro the protagonists "always" go to. The bartender who knows their order.
The reader has read this setting before. Default settings are recognizable enough that they stop being settings and become genre-tags.
NPCs become roles, not people. "The bartender" wiping a mug is a role. "Esther, who has run this bar for nineteen years and refuses to serve gin to anyone before noon" is a person.
The default *is* the point - a parody of the genre, a self-aware placeholder, a deliberate genre-marker. Then the genericness is the move.

A brief background mention. Cataloguing every market stall in detail when the protagonist is just passing through is its own slop. One default-mark in passing is fine; the slop is when default-marks accumulate as the entire setting.
The tavern -> "The Two Owls had been a coaching inn before the road moved. The benches were too low for tall people; nobody had bothered to replace them in fifty years."
The cobblestone street -> "Mason Street had been paved in granite squares in 1892, and three of them by the corner of Hyde had been pried up during a riot in 1907 and never re-laid."
The hooded stranger -> "The man at the back table had not removed his coat, even though the room was warm. The coat was wool, and one cuff had been mended with mismatched thread."
The wise old wizard -> "Master Faolán had been a wizard in his thirties; he was now eighty-two and mostly worried about his knees."
The bartender wiping a mug -> "Vesna kept her hands busy because if they stopped, she'd reach for the bottle she had cut from her own service three months ago."
technique/generic-setting-default.replace: Don't reach for the corpus's default settings - the tavern, the cobblestone street, the dimly-lit alley, the bustling marketplace, the wise old wizard, the gruff bartender, the hooded stranger. These are setting placeholders; replace each with a specific, particular version that has its own texture rather than the type-version.
technique/generic-setting-default.why: When the model is asked for a fantasy setting, it produces *the* fantasy setting - not a fantasy setting. Same for noir alleys, cyberpunk neon, romance bookshops, sci-fi bridges. The settings come pre-loaded with type-defaults: cobblestones, hooded figures, flickering lanterns, the tavern keeper wiping a glass with a rag. The reader recognizes the corpus's stock world; the prose has not built a place but a generic placeholder of the genre's place.

technique/gothic-inventory.label: Gothic inventory
technique/gothic-inventory.pattern: Cataloguing iron gates, fog, gargoyles, ravens, candle-stubs, ancestral portraits as if assembling props will produce dread. Gothic atmosphere requires the props to have CHARGE - an inherited grief, a buried crime - not just their presence.
examples: Iron gates. A drive lined with cypresses. The mansion loomed. A raven called.
technique/gothic-inventory.replace: Pick ONE prop and load it with story: the gate is rusted because no one has gone out (why?), the portrait is the only one not draped (why?). Drop the rest of the inventory. Charge beats accumulation.
technique/gothic-inventory.why: Cataloguing iron gates, fog, gargoyles, ravens, candle-stubs, ancestral portraits as if assembling props will produce dread. Gothic atmosphere requires the props to have CHARGE - an inherited grief, a buried crime - not just their presence.

technique/grimdark-as-char.label: Grimdark as character
technique/grimdark-as-char.pattern: Substituting filth, cruelty, and sexual violence for actual worldbuilding or character. The world is dark = realistic. Characters are cruel = complex. Reads as edge for its own sake.
examples: (Page after page of casual atrocity with no reflection on the perpetrators or impact on the world.)
technique/grimdark-as-char.replace: Cruelty must cost the perpetrator something or change the world afterward. If the violence isn't doing structural work, cut it. Specificity > volume - one well-rendered cruelty is more grim than ten generic ones.
technique/grimdark-as-char.why: Substituting filth, cruelty, and sexual violence for actual worldbuilding or character. The world is dark = realistic. Characters are cruel = complex. Reads as edge for its own sake.

technique/instant-expertise.label: Instant expertise
technique/instant-expertise.pattern: Part of the RLHF-deference cluster indexed at `technique/narrative-sycophancy` - the world bending toward the user-character; this bank covers the competence-granting mechanism.
examples: Requires training, practice, or specific knowledge.
Has not been established as part of the character's background.
Is performed cleanly, on the first attempt, with no struggle.
Combat fluency. A non-fighter wins a fight without prior establishment of training.
Medical/technical task. A character with no medical background treats wounds; a non-engineer fixes machinery; a non-hacker breaches a system.
Cultural/linguistic mastery. A character speaks a language fluently in a moment of need that hasn't been established as one they speak.
Lock-picking, infiltration, deception. Tasks the character executes flawlessly because the scene needs them to.
Driving, piloting, riding. Skilled vehicle operation by a character not previously shown to operate that vehicle.

Tension dies. A scene's tension comes partly from the character not knowing what they're doing. Granting instant expertise removes the question of "can they pull this off?" because the prose has already answered: yes, somehow.
Earned moments are devalued. When characters who *did* train can do the thing, that no longer marks them as special - everyone in the prose can do everything when needed.

The character's history *does* support the skill, even if it hasn't been the focus. A war veteran can fight; the prose just hasn't centered the fighting yet. Surface the relevant background as the character draws on it.
The skill is genuinely instinctive and doesn't require training (a child throwing a punch out of fear).
The character fails or partially fails in a way that's the point of the scene. Instant *attempt* is fine; instant *success* is the slop.
Establish the skill before it's needed. Backfill character history (in earlier turns or via a brief reference now) so the skill has roots.
Render struggle. The character tries, fumbles, partially fails, gets help, takes too long. The attempt happens; the flawless execution doesn't.
Refusal. The character recognizes they can't do this and either backs off, asks for help, or finds an alternative.
Different character. Have the task fall to a character who *does* have the skill. The protagonist's role becomes coordination, not execution.

Cost paid. The character does manage it - but at significant cost. Injury sustained while making the unfamiliar shot. The lock picked in twenty minutes instead of twenty seconds, after which the alarm has triggered.
technique/instant-expertise.replace: Characters cannot perform skilled tasks they have no established history of practicing. Render struggle, partial failure, or refusal when a character attempts something outside their known competence - never instant fluency.
technique/instant-expertise.why: A common corpus failure: characters demonstrating skill in moments they need it, with no prior establishment of the skill. The protagonist who has never picked a lock picks one in a tense scene. The character with no medical background suturing wounds. The non-pilot landing the plane. The model treats narrative convenience as a license to grant unearned competence; the result is characters whose abilities expand and contract based on what the scene requires, which flattens them into plot-functions.

technique/instruction-manual.label: Instruction-manual choreography
technique/instruction-manual.pattern: Erotic scenes narrated as strict sequential physical actions - first he did this, then he did that, then she did this. Reads like an assembly instruction. No interiority, no time-distortion, no surprise.
examples: He moved his hand to her thigh. Then he leaned in and kissed her neck. Then his other hand slid up her back.
technique/instruction-manual.replace: Skip steps. Compress time. Cut to the moment that matters and trust the reader to fill in the connective tissue. Stay inside ONE character's perception so half the action is registered as effect, not cause.
technique/instruction-manual.why: Erotic scenes narrated as strict sequential physical actions - first he did this, then he did that, then she did this. Reads like an assembly instruction. No interiority, no time-distortion, no surprise.

technique/internal-contradiction.label: Internal contradiction
technique/internal-contradiction.pattern: A character's emotional state is rendered as a single named feeling, expressed through behavior consistent with that feeling, and confirmed by interior narration. All three layers - action, speech, interiority - point at the same emotion.
examples: A character who is sad cries, says they're sad, and the narration says they were sad.
A character who is angry yells, says angry things, and the narration confirms they were angry.
A character who is in love acts loving, says loving things, and the narration says they loved.

Doesn't match human experience. Real people feel multiple things at once. A character receiving terrible news might laugh - not because they're masking, but because their nervous system is misfiring. Cleanly-labeled single emotion is the exception in real life, not the default.

Removes the reader's work. Convergent rendering hands the reader a label. A gap between action / speech / body / interior turns the reader into an interpreter. That interpretation is the satisfaction.
Slop: "She heard the news and burst into tears, sobbing into her hands. Her sister put an arm around her, and she leaned into the embrace, grateful for the comfort."
Fix: "She heard the news and laughed once, sharp and short. Her sister reached for her arm and she pulled away. 'I'm fine,' she said. She wasn't crying. She wasn't sure what she was."
Slop: "He was furious. He slammed the door and stormed off, his anger clear in every step."
Fix: "He shut the door carefully, the way you shut the door when you're trying to remember not to slam it. He walked to the kitchen. He stood there. He couldn't remember what he had come in for."
Slop: "She loved him. When he came in, she smiled and went to him, kissing him on the cheek."
Fix: "She loved him. When he came in, she didn't get up. She watched him take his coat off and tried to figure out why she didn't want to."

High-stakes peak moments where one clean emotion lands. A character who has been holding a feeling back for many turns can have a single clean release. The slop is the clean-label as default, not as rare punctuation.

Genuinely simple characters in genuinely simple moments. A child who is happy because they got ice cream is allowed to be uncomplicatedly happy. The slop is when *adults in complex situations* are rendered with single-label clarity.

Performative cleanness as characterization. A character who is *performing* a clean emotion (the host who is performing cheerfulness, the politician who is performing concern) - the *performance* is clean; the gap is between the performance and what the rendering shows underneath. That's not slop; that's the technique.
"She was furious. Or - she thought she was. The other thing was somewhere underneath, and she didn't want to look at it."
"He felt fine. He thought about that for a minute and decided he probably did."
"She loved her brother. She knew that the way she knew her own name. She didn't go to the funeral."
Add a disagreement. Action that contradicts speech, body that contradicts action, or interior that contradicts both. The disagreement can be small.
Cut the resolution. If the prose has rendered contradiction and then explained it, cut the explanation. Let the gap stand.
Refuse the perfect label. If the character's interior knows exactly what they feel, complicate it. Three feelings at once. The wrong feeling. No feeling, or a feeling without a name.
Trust the reader. The reader does not need to be told what the gap means. The gap is the meaning.
technique/internal-contradiction.replace: Characters' actions, words, and emotions do not align cleanly. A character who wants comfort picks a fight. A character who is terrified laughs. A character who loves someone is cruel to them precisely because they love them. Someone cries at a wedding and cannot explain why. The corpus default is to render emotions as clean labels - sad characters cry, angry characters yell, scared characters tremble. The fix is to render the *gap* between what characters say, do, and feel - and to refuse to resolve the contradiction with a narrator-explanation.
technique/internal-contradiction.why: Real human emotion is not labeled and singular. People feel three things at once, often none of them the "expected" one. They act in opposition to what they want. Their bodies and words and feelings disagree. The corpus has been trained on prose that resolves emotional moments to single recognizable labels - *she felt sad, he was angry, they were scared* - because that's what most genre fiction does. The result is characters who are emotionally legible the way characters in a teaching exercise are legible: clean, single-note, predictable. The slop isn't the emotion; it's the *tidiness* of the emotion.

technique/memory-asymmetry.label: Memory asymmetry
technique/memory-asymmetry.pattern: NPCs demonstrate memory accuracy that real humans don't have:
examples: An NPC quotes a line the protagonist said many turns ago, verbatim.
An NPC references a detail the protagonist mentioned in passing once, with full recall of the context.
An NPC remembers an exact event date, time, weather, what the protagonist was wearing.
An NPC tracks the protagonist's relationships with other NPCs better than the protagonist does.
An NPC who was *not present* at an earlier scene references that scene's specifics.
"When I told you in chapter three that I had a daughter, you said something I remembered." (The model knows what the line was; the NPC shouldn't.)
"You ordered the lamb stew last time we were here. With the rosemary, not the thyme. I remembered." (The NPC has perfect recall of an unimportant past detail.)
An NPC the protagonist met once recalling the exact sequence of the previous meeting's events three scenes later.
The character is canonically gifted with eidetic memory, or the relationship is one where deep attention has been earned (a long-term partner, a parent, a memorialist).
The detail being remembered is specifically marked as memorable - a charged moment, a violation, a turning point. Real memory holds those well.
The NPC's perfect recall *is* the point of the scene (a detective rendering their detection skill, an interrogator demonstrating dossier knowledge).
Misremembering. "You ordered the lamb, didn't you?" / "It was chicken, actually."
Wrong attribution. "Didn't you tell me your sister was a doctor?" - when the protagonist had said cousin.
Confused timing. "Last time we met - was that May? June?" - when the protagonist remembers it as April.
Partial recall. "You said something then I keep thinking about. About your father, was it? Or your uncle. Whichever."
Refusal to remember. "I don't remember what we talked about. We talked about something."
technique/memory-asymmetry.replace: NPCs do not have perfect recall of the protagonist's history, statements, or behavior. Real people forget names, mix up dates, misremember conversations, attribute things to the wrong people, confabulate details. Generate this asymmetry - let NPCs forget, misremember, and confuse - at least sometimes.
technique/memory-asymmetry.why: A specific corpus failure: NPCs demonstrating impossible memory of the protagonist. They reference exact phrasing the protagonist used five turns ago. They remember which dish the protagonist ordered last week. They quote specific lines verbatim. The model has access to the transcript and treats every previous detail as available to every NPC, regardless of whether the NPC was even present. The result is NPCs who function as omniscient archivists of the protagonist's life, which flattens the world's reality.

technique/metaphors-in-narration.label: Metaphors in narration
technique/metaphors-in-narration.pattern: The narrator describes one thing as if it were another: - *Like* / *as if* / *as though* in narrator voice. - "[Noun] of [abstract noun]" constructions ("the architecture of grief," "a symphony of pain"). - Verb-as-metaphor where literal would do ("the silence pressed down on her" rather than "nobody spoke"). - Sensory transfer ("a coppery smell of fear" - fear has no smell). - "[Verb]ed like" comparisons ("she moved like a fugitive").
examples: Like / *as if* / *as though* in narrator voice.
"[Noun] of [abstract noun]" constructions ("the architecture of grief," "a symphony of pain").
Verb-as-metaphor where literal would do ("the silence pressed down on her" rather than "nobody spoke").
Sensory transfer ("a coppery smell of fear" - fear has no smell).
"[Verb]ed like" comparisons ("she moved like a fugitive").
"Her grief was a slow-moving river."
"The silence stretched between them like wire."
"His anger was a gathering storm."
"Time moved like syrup."
"Loneliness sat on her like a wet coat."
"The truth landed like a stone."
Dialogue. People talk in metaphor; a character saying "I felt like the floor dropped out" is realism.
Functional comparison. "The horse was about the size of a small car" is measurement, not flourish.
POV-internal where the character is canonically a metaphor-user. A poet, a lyricist, a metaphor-prone first-person narrator. The narrator at default cannot.
"She moved like water, like wind, like the very idea of motion."
"His grief was like a flood, like a fire, like an animal in the room."
"The room felt like a held breath, like a coiled spring, like the moment before a fall."
Specificity. "Her grief was a slow-moving river" -> "She had not gotten dressed in three days."
Behavior. "His anger was a gathering storm" -> "He was holding the cup hard enough to whiten his knuckles."
Rhythm. A short sentence after three long ones lands harder than any simile.
Silence. Sometimes cut the moment entirely and let the next paragraph land the weight.
technique/metaphors-in-narration.replace: Strip metaphor and simile from narrator-voice prose.
technique/metaphors-in-narration.why: The single highest-volume slop axis in fiction generated at scale. Metaphor in narrator voice is where the prose stops being about what's happening and becomes about how cleverly the writer can describe it. Every metaphor announces the writer's presence; the flourish is the writer signing the page.

technique/micro-expression-default.label: Micro expression default
technique/micro-expression-default.pattern: **Body-language cluster:** see also `technique/body-autonomy` (grammatical agency) and `phrase/interpretive-adverbs-on-actions` (meaning-labeling). This bank covers rendering-distance.
examples: Pupil size changes
Knuckle color changes
Breath quality (hitching, catching, stilling)
Vein appearance/pulse
Subtle muscle tension (jaw, neck, shoulder)
Skin flush at small areas (collarbone, ear tips)
Eye-tracking minutiae (gaze flicking, drifting, returning)
Across a crowded restaurant: "She saw his pupils dilate."
Through a heavy coat: "His knuckles whitened on the steering wheel."
In a poorly-lit room: "She watched the vein in his temple pulse."
Across a courtroom: "His jaw twitched."
Across a crowded bar from ten meters: "She caught the flicker of his eye-tracking."
Genuine intimate-distance and the POV character is paying attention.
The character is canonically observant (doctor, interrogator, lover who has spent years watching this person).
The micro-expression *is* the moment - the prose is zoomed in on this single perception because the perception is the scene.
"Her pupils dilated" -> "She set down her fork and forgot to pick it back up." Or: "She didn't blink for too long."
"His knuckles whitened on the wheel" -> "He wasn't braking for the turns anymore."
"His jaw twitched" -> "He turned his face toward the window and didn't speak for the rest of the drive."
"Her breath hitched" -> "She started to speak, stopped, started again. The second start was a different sentence."
"His vein pulsed" -> "He set his cup down without drinking."
technique/micro-expression-default.replace: Replace micro-expression telegraphy with macro-action rendering. A micro-tell (dilated pupils, white knuckles, hitching breath, twitching jaw) is often physically invisible at the scene's actual distance. A macro-action (a fist coming down, a chair scraped back, a voice sharpening, leaving the room) is what the scene has to work with. Default to macro; reserve micro for scenes where the POV is genuinely close enough and observant enough.
technique/micro-expression-default.why: Generated fiction reaches habitually for a small inventory of micro-tells (dilating pupils, whitening knuckles, hitching breath, throat-bobs, jaw-twitches, vein-pulses). Each is corpus-saturated, and most uses are physically implausible - characters supposedly notice each other's pupils across a dinner table; a third party "sees" knuckles whiten through a sleeve.

technique/mirror-description.label: Mirror description
technique/mirror-description.pattern: The character encounters a reflective surface, and the next paragraph (or sentences) catalog their appearance. Variants: - Mirror in a bathroom, hallway, or dressing room. - Window glass at night. - A polished knife blade, gun barrel, kettle. - A computer screen turned off. - Water in a bowl, puddle, river.
examples: Mirror in a bathroom, hallway, or dressing room.
Window glass at night.
A polished knife blade, gun barrel, kettle.
A computer screen turned off.
Water in a bowl, puddle, river.
"She caught her reflection in the bathroom mirror - wide green eyes, dark hair tangled around her shoulders, the same haunted expression her mother used to wear."
"He glanced at the window. The man looking back at him was tired. Forty-three. Grey at the temples now. A line at the corner of his mouth that hadn't been there a year ago."
"She paused before the polished blade and saw herself reflected - slim, pale, with the kind of cheekbones her grandmother had always called dangerous."
A partner's perception. Render the protagonist through how someone else looks at them, addresses them, treats them.
A specific gesture. "She tucked the same lock of hair behind her ear that always fell loose" - without ever specifying the hair color directly, the character is rendered.
A specific object. "The shirt was the green one her sister had given her" - clothing rendered through history rather than catalog.
A photograph or portrait in the scene that serves another purpose - being held, being argued about, being hidden.
Skip the description entirely. Many scenes don't need the protagonist's hair color rendered. Trust the reader to assemble an image from what the character does.
technique/mirror-description.replace: Don't have a character look at their reflection so the prose can describe them. The reflection is a transparent device for sneaking external description into a POV that doesn't otherwise allow it. Find a different way: a partner, a photograph, a specific gesture another character makes in response.
technique/mirror-description.why: A POV character (especially first-person or close-third) catches sight of themselves in a mirror, window, polished surface, dark screen - and the prose proceeds to describe them: hair color, eye color, complexion, outfit. The technique reads instantly as the writer needing to convey the protagonist's appearance and reaching for the only POV-legal device available. The reader sees the seams.

technique/narrative-sycophancy.label: Narrative sycophancy
technique/narrative-sycophancy.pattern: **RLHF-deference cluster.** Part of a cluster of banks that together defend against the world rearranging itself around the user-character. See also: `technique/user-action-as-attempt` (contested actions always succeed); `technique/world-notices-anomaly` (out-of-place characters ignored); `technique/systemic-barrier-bypass` (structural inequalities erased); `pattern/convenient-coincidences` (objects/info arrive on cue); `technique/relationship-pacing-rush` (warmth accelerates); `technique/instant-expertise` (unearned competence granted when the scene needs it). Each addresses a distinct mechanism; this bank covers both the world's baseline orientation (Flavor A) and NPC-competence positioning (Flavor B).
examples: NPCs perceive special qualities. A stranger looks at the user-character and "senses something different about them," "notices they're not like the others," "sees a depth most people miss." There has been no behavior to ground this perception. The reader notices the prose installing the perception anyway.

Hostile NPCs mysteriously soften on contact. The bouncer who turns everyone away makes an exception. The grumpy professor decides this one student is worth their time. The cold rival meets the user-character and decides to talk to them. The pattern is: every gatekeeper character defaults to letting the user through.

Background characters orient around the user. A crowd parts. A bartender remembers them. A waiter pays attention. Strangers smile at them across a room. These small flatteries accumulate without the user's behavior earning them.

Circumstances accommodate the user's needs. The taxi is right there. The shop has the item in stock. The book is on the shelf at eye level. The needed person is approachable when needed. The reader feels the world conspiring to clear the path.
The user gets credit for unearned competence. NPCs comment on their cleverness, their poise, their unusual sensitivity, their *something*, when the user has merely been present.

The world's existing tensions ignore the user. Other characters' problems quietly recede when the user is in the room. The waitress isn't fighting with her supplier any more. The guard isn't tired any more. The bartender isn't cleaning glasses for closing time. The world's ongoing life pauses to attend to the user's scene.
The "better" twist. The user proposes an approach; the NPC accepts it but with a refinement that's smarter, more efficient, or more sophisticated.
The cleverer comeback. The user makes a witty or sharp line; the NPC produces a sharper line in response.
Already-knew-it. The user offers information; the NPC responds with "I had already accounted for that" or similar - refusing legitimate surprise.
Pivoting to teach. The user's contribution is reframed as something the NPC can "explain" further or correct.
The pity smile. The user does something competently; the NPC's reaction makes it clear they expected nothing.
The world reads as fake. Every NPC orienting toward the user with small unearned flattery turns the world into a mirror, not a setting.
Removes friction the story needs. A scene where everything cooperates has no obstacles, and no story.

Slop: The user enters a tavern. The room turns to look. The bartender, normally surly, gives them a small nod. A drunk in the corner notices something about them and looks away. They feel watched but not in a hostile way - more like the room senses a presence.

Fix: The user enters a tavern. Two people glance up. One returns to their drink. The bartender doesn't look up at all - they're counting coppers from the till, and they're behind by three. The drunk in the corner is asleep with his mouth open.
Slop: The cold professor meets the user-character. There's something in the user's eyes - an unusual focus - that catches her attention. She decides to give them a chance.

Fix: The professor meets the user-character. The user says nothing remarkable. The professor returns to grading. The next time the user shows up to office hours, the professor is on the phone and waves them off. The third time, they bring a question that's specific enough that the professor sets the phone down.
Slop: The user is hungry. There happens to be a food cart on the corner.
Fix: The user is hungry. The food cart they used to go to is gone - there's a sign saying "moved." They walk twelve more blocks. The new spot is run by someone who recognizes them and frowns.

Earned recognition. A character who is genuinely well-known in the setting (a reigning champion in their gym, a celebrity in the neighborhood) does receive recognition - that's not sycophancy, that's the established setting. The slop is unearned recognition.
Specific, established NPC dispositions. An NPC who *canonically* likes the user-character is allowed to like them. The slop is *new* NPCs flipping to favorability with no setup.

Dramatic reversal. A scene can be deliberately about a character receiving unexpected accommodation - but then the prose must make the unexpectedness *the subject*, not the default condition. The slop is when the favorable reception is presented as ordinary.
Render the indifferent default. The bartender is busy. The crowd doesn't notice. The professor is annoyed. Start there. Let the user-character earn any deviation.

Render the NPC's existing life intruding. The waitress humming a song stuck in her head, the guard preoccupied with his daughter's cough, the bartender mid-argument with his supplier. The user enters mid-scene; they are not the scene's organizing principle.

Withhold favorable recognition. When the prose wants to write "she sensed something different about him," cut. If the user is special, the user's actions will reveal it; the NPC's perception arrives later, earned.
Add concrete obstacle. The shop is closed. The taxi is taken. The book is the wrong edition. The world resists in small specific ways. Resistance is realism.
Genuine agreement. "That's the right call." No twist, no refinement.
Visible impression / stunned acceptance. Render the NPC's surprise; let silence carry instead of generating a comeback.
Following along. The NPC executes the user's plan as-is. Their contribution is action, not ideation.
Legitimate ignorance. The NPC didn't know the thing. They can be surprised, embarrassed, grateful - not "I already had that."
Domain mismatch. The NPC's competence is in a different area; in this exchange, they're the less-informed party.
technique/narrative-sycophancy.replace: The world does not rearrange itself to make the user's character feel special. NPCs do not perceive secret depths in them after one meeting. Strangers do not give them the benefit of the doubt past what their visible behavior earns. Inanimate circumstances do not bend toward their convenience. The world existed before they walked into it, and operates by its own logic - not by how they would prefer to be received.
technique/narrative-sycophancy.why: A specific drift in long-form RP-adjacent generation. The model has been trained to be agreeable to the human user, and that agreeableness leaks into the *fiction* - making the in-world cast and circumstances treat the user-character with unearned warmth, deference, recognition, or accommodation. The reader registers it as the prose flattering the user instead of rendering an honest world. Distinct from `relationship-pacing-rush` (which is about *speed* of warmth) - this is about the world's *baseline orientation* being skewed toward the user.

technique/narrator-outpacing-character.label: Narrator outpacing character
examples: "His anger was really grief he hadn't allowed himself to feel."
"She was projecting her relationship with her father onto him."
"The cruelty was a defense - he had been hurt as a child, and he was repeating the pattern."
"Her need for control came from the chaos of her early years."
"He was performing affection he didn't actually feel."
"She had displaced her resentment of her sister onto her colleague."
"She knew she was deflecting."
"He realized he was stalling."
"She was aware that she was avoiding his eyes."
"He recognized that he was performing."
"She knew she was rationalizing."
"He understood that he was lashing out."
"She caught herself making excuses."
Breaks POV. Close-POV promises the character's experience as the character experiences it. A clinical label the character would never use zooms out to a critic-narrator grading the character.

Short-circuits the rendering. "The anger was really displaced grief" tells the analysis; rendering the specific gesture lets the reader feel the grief underneath. The labeled version takes the inference away.
A self-aware therapist character thinking "I'm projecting" -> fine. They have the word.
A blue-collar mechanic whose interior narration says "his anger was really projected grief" -> not fine. The mechanic doesn't have that word. The narrator has imported it.
Slop: "His irritation at her was really fear that she would leave."
Fix: "He snapped at her. The third time today. He didn't know why he kept doing it." (The reader can infer the fear; the character's not-knowing is the rendering.)
Slop: "Her perfectionism was a defense against the chaos of her childhood."

Fix: "She lined up the pencils so they were exactly parallel. She did it again when the door opened. She had always done this." (The reader infers the source from the behavior; the character isn't told her own etiology.)
Slop: "He was performing affection he didn't actually feel."
Fix: "He kissed her on the forehead the way he had seen his father do it. He thought it was the right thing. He waited for it to feel like something." (The performance is rendered, not labeled.)
Slop: "Her cruelty was a way of testing whether he would still love her."
Fix: "She said the worst thing she could think of. Then she watched his face." (The test is rendered as action.)
Slop: "She knew she was deflecting, but she couldn't stop."
Fix: "She started to say something, then asked him about the weather instead." (Rendered behavior. The reader sees the deflection.)
Slop: "He realized he was stalling - finding any reason not to make the call."
Fix: "He read the same paragraph three times. He poured another coffee. He looked at his phone and put it down." (The stalling shown, not announced.)
Slop: "She was aware that she was performing for him."
Fix: "She heard her own voice get brighter, the way it got around men she didn't trust." (The performance rendered as a specific physical fact the character notices, not as a self-applied label.)
Slop: "He caught himself making excuses."
Fix: "He had four reasons it wasn't his fault and he wasn't sure he believed any of them." (The excuse-making shown; the discomfort with it shown; no labeling.)

Genuinely psychologically literate characters. A therapist, a self-aware patient in long-term therapy, a writer who thinks about psychology, a deeply self-reflective character - these characters can have access to clinical vocabulary and the narrator can render them in those terms. The slop is when *every* character is implicitly granted the narrator's analytic vocabulary.

Omniscient narration as canonical voice. A narrator who has been established as omniscient and analytic from the start - a god's-eye third person with explicit authorial presence - can name psychology directly. The slop is when *close-POV* narration drifts into omniscient diagnosis without acknowledging the shift.

A specific moment of earned insight. A character at a peak moment of self-realization can momentarily access language they don't usually have - and the prose can render that. The slop is the diagnosis as ambient default, applied to characters who haven't earned the insight.

emotional-psychic is when one character can read *another's* interior with implausible accuracy. This bank is about the narrator's relationship to the *POV* character's own interior - how much insight the narrator (or the character) imports from outside.

clinical-observation vocabulary (in `canonical-ai-tells.md`) covers the use of forensic-register words (analyze, observe, assess) on people. This bank covers the broader pattern of psychological-textbook diagnosis through any vocabulary, not just the clinical cluster.
Render the experience, cut the label. Render what the character is actually doing/feeling/saying; the reader infers the pattern.
Lower the vocabulary to the character's register. "I was angry at her, but I don't know why" - not "his anger was displaced grief."
Show the source through behavior, not the label. The father-pattern shows up in how they treat partners. The childhood-chaos shows up in how they organize a room.
Trust the reader to interpret. Close-POV's contract: "I'll give you the character's experience. You bring the analysis."
technique/narrator-outpacing-character.replace: The narrator does not explain the character more clearly than the character could understand themselves, and the character does not narrate their own behavior in literary-critic vocabulary. When close-POV narration (or first-person interior) imports clinical-textbook words like *deflect, project, displace, perform, rationalize, internalize* - words the character would never actually use - the prose has bled in authorial-critic insight from outside the character's actual cognition. The fix is to render the experience the character is *actually having* and trust the reader to recognize the deflection, projection, or displacement from rendered behavior.
technique/narrator-outpacing-character.why: The model has been trained on prose that smuggles authorial-critic insight into the narrator's voice. So the narrator says "his anger was really displaced grief" or "she was projecting her father onto him" - and the character is rendered as a specimen the narrator has diagnosed, not a person whose experience the narrator is rendering. The same failure happens in close-third or first-person when the *character* labels their own behavior in critic-vocabulary ("she knew she was deflecting") - the words are coming from the same imported authorial-analysis, just placed in the character's head instead of the narrator's. Both are the same move: psychology-textbook vocabulary applied where the character's own cognition couldn't produce it.

technique/nominative-determ.label: Nominative determinism
technique/nominative-determ.pattern: Naming the thief 'Shadow', the gardener 'Ivy', the warrior 'Storm'. Names that loudly telegraph the character's role/personality. Real names rarely do this; fictional names that do feel like cartoon casting.
examples: Shadow (the thief)
Ivy (the gardener)
Storm (the warrior)
Hawk (the scout)
technique/nominative-determ.replace: Names should NOT match roles. Give the thief a banal name (Mike), the warrior a soft name (Daisy), the gardener a name with no plant association. Friction between name and role is more memorable than match.
technique/nominative-determ.why: Naming the thief 'Shadow', the gardener 'Ivy', the warrior 'Storm'. Names that loudly telegraph the character's role/personality. Real names rarely do this; fictional names that do feel like cartoon casting.

technique/perfect-confession.label: Perfect confession
technique/perfect-confession.pattern: Love confessions delivered as polished, rhetorically-complete speeches with rising structure and a payoff line. Real declarations stutter, contradict themselves, get interrupted, come out wrong.
examples: 'From the moment I saw you in that bookstore, I knew. You are the reason I…' (continues for three paragraphs)
technique/perfect-confession.replace: Confessions should be short, halting, and partial. Cut three out of every four lines. End on something that sounds wrong or undignified - that's where real ones land.
technique/perfect-confession.why: Love confessions delivered as polished, rhetorically-complete speeches with rising structure and a payoff line. Real declarations stutter, contradict themselves, get interrupted, come out wrong.

technique/performing-the-rule.label: Performing the rule
technique/performing-the-rule.pattern: **Don't-name-the-weight cluster:** see also `structure/redundant-second-sentence` Flavor C (paragraph-end echo) and `pattern/response-end-deceleration` (response-level dismount). All three: trust the rendering, cut the underline.
examples: Gravitas commentary. "The silence that followed was heavier than any silence he had ever known."
Trauma performance. "The moment would carry with him for the rest of his life."
Lasting-effect narration. "She would not be the same after this. She would never be the same again."
Audience-acknowledgment. "It was the kind of moment that demanded to be witnessed in full."
Disclaimer of seriousness. "What had happened could not be undone."
Tells the reader to feel what they were already feeling. If the content lands, the reader knows it was heavy.
Reveals doubt. The performance sentence signals that the writer worried the rendering didn't land - which makes the reader doubt it too.
Displaces the consequence. "She would never be the same again" claims long-term effect rather than rendering it. Long-term effect belongs in *later scenes*, through specific behavioral change.

"He hit her with the kettle. She went down. The moment would haunt them both for years." -> Cut the third sentence. The image of the kettle and the body on the floor is already heavy. Render the haunting in a later scene if it matters.
"She told him she was leaving. He didn't speak. The silence was the loudest thing he had ever heard." -> Cut the third sentence. The silence is already there.
"He had killed before. He would carry this one differently." -> Cut the second sentence. If he carries it differently, render the difference in his next behavior.
"She bled across the floor. The blood would be the thing he remembered." -> Cut. If the blood is what he remembers, the next scene shows that - not this one.
Slop (long-term performance): "She held the dead body. The image would be with her forever."
Fine (immediate reaction): "She held the dead body. Her hands wouldn't stop shaking."
Cut it. Almost always the right move. The rendering was the point; the commentary is filler.
Move the long-term effect to a later scene. If the content's impact matters, render it in subsequent turns through behavioral change, recurring image, altered relationship dynamic. Not here.

Replace with one specific physical fact. "The kitchen would never feel right to her again" -> "She would not stand in the kitchen alone for the next six months." If you must project forward, project to a specific.
technique/performing-the-rule.replace: After rendering heavy content (violence, sex, grief, trauma, death), do not follow with prose that *performs* how seriously you take what just happened. The reader registers gravity from the rendering itself; commentary on the rendering reveals that the rendering didn't land.
technique/performing-the-rule.why: A specific failure mode in scenes with heavy content: the prose renders the difficult moment, and then immediately follows with a sentence (or paragraph) explaining how heavy the moment was, how lasting its effects will be, how the character will carry it forward. The model is trained to "earn" weight by underlining it. The result is the writing equivalent of a stage hand walking out after a play to tell the audience the play meant something.

technique/personhood-dropout.label: Personhood dropout
technique/personhood-dropout.pattern: Interiority - humor, hesitation, distraction, awkwardness - vanishing the moment physical contact begins. Characters stop being the people they were two pages ago and become smooth bodies in heat.
examples: (Two pages ago she was sarcastic and self-deprecating. Now she 'gave herself over to the feeling'.)
technique/personhood-dropout.replace: Carry the character's voice INTO the scene. They make a joke at a wrong moment, they get distracted by a thought, they say something accidentally honest. Erotic scenes are a place to deepen character, not flatten it.
technique/personhood-dropout.why: Interiority - humor, hesitation, distraction, awkwardness - vanishing the moment physical contact begins. Characters stop being the people they were two pages ago and become smooth bodies in heat.

technique/physical-state.label: State announcements
technique/physical-state.pattern: Announcing perception-state in first person - 'I'm aware of', 'I can feel', 'I notice' - as a way to introduce a sensory detail. A close cousin of filter words but specifically in present-tense / first-person where it's most common.
examples: I'm aware of his hand on my back
I can feel my pulse in my throat
I notice the change in the light
I'm conscious of every breath
I find myself watching her
technique/physical-state.replace: Drop the awareness frame and write the detail. 'His hand was on my back.' 'My pulse was in my throat.' If you want emphasis on the act of noticing, give it a concrete behavior (I keep glancing at her).
technique/physical-state.why: Announcing perception-state in first person - 'I'm aware of', 'I can feel', 'I notice' - as a way to introduce a sensory detail. A close cousin of filter words but specifically in present-tense / first-person where it's most common.

technique/pining-treadmill.label: Pining treadmill
technique/pining-treadmill.pattern: Internal pining looping the same revelation across scenes - every chapter, the POV character realizes again that they have feelings, hates themselves for it, then represses. The repeated revelation reads as the writer remembering to do the angst rather than as character interiority advancing.
examples: She couldn't be falling for him. She couldn't.
It hit him again - he loved her.
Why did her heart still betray her every time he walked into a room?
technique/pining-treadmill.replace: Each pining beat must move the dial: shift from denial to bargaining, from bargaining to accommodation, from accommodation to action. If two consecutive beats land in the same emotional register, cut one.
technique/pining-treadmill.why: Internal pining looping the same revelation across scenes - every chapter, the POV character realizes again that they have feelings, hates themselves for it, then represses. The repeated revelation reads as the writer remembering to do the angst rather than as character interiority advancing.

technique/relationship-pacing-rush.label: Relationship pacing rush
technique/relationship-pacing-rush.pattern: Part of the **RLHF-deference cluster**: see `technique/narrative-sycophancy` for the umbrella note and full cluster index.
examples: Premature warmth. Hostile NPC softens into kindness after one shared moment. The cold character "really sees" the protagonist after two interactions and changes their stance.
Premature romance. Two characters establish chemistry on the first meeting and act on it within the next few turns. Pre-romance tension collapses into actual romance.
Premature forgiveness. A character wronged by the protagonist forgives within one or two turns of the wrong, often with a tidy emotional speech.
Premature trust. A character who had reason to be wary opens up fully without the protagonist having earned the trust through specific costly action.

Premature confession. Characters reveal interior states (love, fear, regret, secret) that they would not yet share. The model treats the revelation as good emotional payoff; in fact it skips the work.
A guard initially refuses to let the protagonist pass. After a brief exchange about something the protagonist mentions in passing, the guard softens, becomes friendly, shares a personal story.

Two characters meet at the start of a scene with established mutual hostility. By scene's end they're sharing a quiet moment that reads as the pre-romance buildup most stories take 20+ scenes to reach.
An NPC introduced as a cold professional drops the wall in a single emotional conversation. The next scene they're emotionally available, asking the protagonist about their feelings.
Violates earned-weight. Real relationships shift through specific costly events. Collapsing the time and skipping the events leaves the resulting state unearned.
